### Grace and peace from God the Father, and
### our Lord IESVS CHRIST.

*Thou canst not at all meruayle (most Holy Spouse of Christ) that here is offered vnto thee a newe interpretation of this Booke of the Reuelation, seeinge in so great variety of interpretations old & newe, it is a matter with one consent acknowledged, that the Reuelation doth still require necessarily a Reuelation, and this voice of the Lord is sounding continually in thine eares: The Lord hath spoken vvho can but Prophecy, Amo.3.8. For the Lord hath not onely spoken by dreames and visions of old, but he speaketh also euery day, euen as often as he inlighteneth the mindes of his seruantes, that they may be able to search out the hidden truth of his Word, and to bringe it forth into the champion world. Nowe he with whome the Lord doth in this manner communicate his counsailes, can not but see a necessity lyinge vpon him, to declare abroad vnto others, what he hath receyued. For should a candle be lighted to be put vnder a bushell? Or should common danger be discouered to any one man in priuate, for his owne cause alone? and not rather for this end, that he beinge set as it were in a Watch-tower, should giue warninge to all others of auoydinge and preuentinge with all speede the euill &*

## To the Holy Reformed Churches of

*deſtruction that is ruſhinge in uppon them? wiſely doe the 4. Lepers conclude that they ſhould be culpable and liable to ſome punisſhment if they ſhould haue concealed but till the morninge that ioyfull newes 2. Kings 7.9. Then if one ſhould conccale an imminent deſtruction, what punisſhment were he worthy of? euen ſo much the more greiuous, by how much the worſe it is for one to be utterly undone, then to be depriued of ioy the ſpace of a fewe houres. Wherefore when as I had learned out of this Booke of the Reuelation both that a moſt greiuous triall was ſtraightwayes to come upon the whole Chriſtian worlde ſo as the ſword of the Lord was to be made drunke with bloud in the heauens, and all the hoſt of them was to be ſhaken, as alſo that yow the Chriſtian Churches of Germany, France, Britany, were by Epiſtles written by name unto yow, moſt mercifully admoniſhed concerninge this tempeſt, I that by Gods prouidence had found theis Epiſtles caſt abroad, and underſtoode by the inſcriptions to what Churches they were ſent, durſt not but giue them unto yow, leaſt by interceptinge, and keepinge them cloſe to my ſelfe, I ſhould both trecherouſly indanger your ſafetie, and alſo make my ſelfe worthily guilty of high treaſon against Gods Maieſtie. There is no godly man that liueth, or hath liued of a longe tyme, whoſe minde may not certainly giue him, by that contempt of Gods worſhip, mocking of his Holy word, extreme careleſnes and ambition of Paſtors, and the altogether diſſolute & wicked lyues of all men of euery order & condition, which are to be ſeene euery where, that ſome horrible calamity will ſtraightwayes enſue. But theſe Epiſtles doe not by a doubtfull coniecture gueſſe at the matter, but in expreſſe termes doe teach, that there is an unmeaſurable gulfe as it were full of miſeries already prepared, and that wee which liue at this day doe ſtand in the very brinke of it. Thou (ô Spouſe) looke I pray thee uppon the ſeale, take notice of the wordes, hand an ſtile of the Writer.*

*Thou knoweſt beſt the voice of thy husband, if they be Letters ſent thee from him, as they make open ſhewe to be, it is more then*

# To the Holy Reformed Churches of

*from the euent of this Prophecy, for whome, as shee draweth nearer the same, the more full knowledge is reserued: the other part is so strange and unexpected, that I could neuer finde, no not any propable suspition thereof gathered out of this Reuelation by any man. Al which effects though this newe hundred of the ages which wee are entred into, shall bringe vnto us, as our Interpretation, if I be not deceiued, doth make plaine~. For nowe is the last Act begun of a most longe & dolefull Tragedy, which shall wholy ouerflowe with scourges, slaughters, destructions, but after this Theater is once remoued, there shall come in rowme of it a most delightfull spectacle of perpetuall peace, ioined with abundance of all good thinges. And thus thou hast (most deare Spouse of Christ) the whole remaynder of the race of thy warfare, stand now vpon the hatches, and after a longe tossinge vp and downe, at length behold the land. Hitherto the cloude beheld a farre of hath deceiued thee, but now see where the shore, and take notice of the mouth of the hauen: Whither I be worthy or no to haue the reward of a good-newes bringer, I leaue it to the iudgment of thine eyes. For I am so far from thinkinge I should stand to the iudgment & umpirage of Rome alone, that I hope I shal by necessary arguments demonstrate, that shee is quite destitute of eyes by Gods iust iudgment, to the intent shee might at vnawares fall into euerlastinge destruction. Let her therefore thinke & iudge what shee listeth, shee shall shortly knowe what it is to deceiue herselfe & others with her iuglinge conueyances. Thou in the meane tyme (ô true & right-harted Spouse) thinke vpon this storme hanginge ouer thy head, and prepare thy selfe against it come, make lesse thy sayles that the winde may haue lesse force ouer them, labour hard at the sterne and pumpe of the shippe, least thou miscarry in the very entrance into the Hauen, which God forbid. And nowe see how exceedinge acceptable this Booke of the Reuelation ought to be unto thee, not onely because of theis euents of most great moment which are to come, but also in respect of the History of thinges past, unto which if thou wilt cast thine eyes, thou shalt see the perpetuall*

## To the holy Reformed churches of Brit. Germ. &c.

*somewhat repressed, thinkinge it worth my labour to make the Iesuites*
*see, how wickedly they rage, how foolishly they trifle, how they under-*
*stand nothinge of theis mysteries, how it can not be possible that they*
*should haue any wit or reach at all in this matter. That so, if they be*
*desirous of the truth, as they dissemblingly pretend, they might take*
*me for a helper at least to search it out; but if they shall still stub-*
*burnly despise it when it is offered them, a helper forward of theire*
*condemnation with my suffrage. And how soeuer it be that they wil*
*not hold theire peace, for I knowe they will fill heauen and earth a*
*while longer with theire ruffling and rustlinge noise, yet I hope I*
*haue here brought that power and euidence of light and Truth, that*
*beinge left destitute of all shewe of Arguments, hence forth they shal*
*doe nothinge but belch out meere blaspemyes against God and men.*
*Thou (ô Holy Mother) for thy kindenes and tendernes sake to all*
*thine, pardon I pray thee my weaknes, wherein so euer I haue offen-*
*ded; Aboue all, regard not, neither care for, the rudenies of my speech.*
*The truth alone is that which thou and I propound to our selues, suffer*
*me after my stammeringe fashion to talke with thee my Mother. Here*
*I bringe such Mandrakes as I could come by, which I found in the feild,*
*there are no herbes in my basket for such daintie fellowes, as make*
*more account of fine wordes, then sound matter, unles perhaps theire*
*heades akinge with the smell of so many elegancies, they may fetch*
*hence, if it please them, the perfume of brimstone and goates-beard,*
*wherewith, like to the Sabeans, they may be rowzed from theire dead*
*sleepe, & may awake theire dull senses. I beseech Iesus Christ, that yow*
*(o Christian Churches) may by understandinge proceede in godlines,*
*& that by true & earnest repentance, yow may either quite turne away*
*the euil hanginge over yow, or may at length be so defended by his*
*power, that yow may stand inuincible in all stormes and Troubles*
*whatsoever.*

-> Your most unworthy Contryman <-
-> and Foster-child, <-

-> **Thomas Brightman.** <-

# GENERAL
## VIEVVE
->Of the whole<-
# REVELATION.

Chapt. 1. 1. *The Preface declares the Argument of the Booke. 4. An Epistle giuen in common to the 7. Churches, after the Inscription, declareth who gaue the Prophecy, Who receiued it, the thinges heard and seene, by which he confirmeth his authority.*

<margin>A particuler Prophecy</margin>
Chapt. 2. *The Epistle are giuen ſeuerally. 1. The decayinge of the Ephesians is comprehended. 8. The Smyrnaeans are ſtrenthened against the aſſault of theire enemyes. 12. They of Pergamus are reproved for permittinge Balaam & the Nicolayts. 18. They of Thyatira are found fault with for toleratinge Iezabell.*

Chapt. 3. 1. *The hypocriſie of the Sardians is ſhortly and ſharply taxed 7. The pietie of the Philadelphians is commended. 14. The lukewarmnes and boaſtinge of the Laodiceans is vehemently rebuked.*

<margin>A cōmon Prophecy</margin>
Chapt. 4. *The common Prophecy ſetteth downe a general Type of the holy Church, Which is remarkeable by the Center, God. verſ. 2. 3. The Circumference, the faithful, verſ. 4. Gods protection, verſ. 5. Gifts, doctrine, rites, verſ. 5. 6. Miniſters, verſ. 6. 7. 8. And finally, by the purity of Gods publike worſhip, verſ. 9. 10. 11.*

<header>A VIEVVE of the vvhole</header>
<meta>catchword: Trompets</meta>

*Chapt. 5.  A Prophecy of thinges specially declared , whereof first the dignity is shewed. 1. By the weaknes of the creature. 6. By the Worthines of the Lambe. 8. By his extollinge from them all.*

<margin>The seales frō Iohn to Constantine.</margin>
*Chapt. 6.  The first speciall euents are the seales. 1. The truth is first of all opened, & ouercometh vnder Traiane, Hadrian, & Antonius Pius. At the voice of the first beast Quadratus, Aristides and Iustine Martyr. 3. At the voice of second beast (viz) the same Iustine, Melito of Sardis & Apollinarius, cometh forth the red horse vnder Marcus Antonius verus, confoundinge all thinges with warres. 5. The 3. seale beinge opened, the third beast Tertullian cryeth out vnder Seuerus the Emperour, when the blacke horse scourgeth the world with famine and barrennes. 7. The 4. seale is opened and then speakes the fourth Beast Cyprian, Decius beinge Emperour, when the pale horse wasted all with warre famine, pestilence, wilde beastes. 9. The fift is opened, and some intermission of the publike persecution is giuen under Claudius, Quintillus, Aurelian, & the rest till the 19. yeare of Dioclesian. 12. The sixt is opened, when Dioclesian and Maximian Herculius rage til at length they were cast out of theire Empire by the power of the Lambe, for feare of whome those Tyrants fled & hid themselues.*

*Chap. 7.  The seuenth seale offereth, first, a generall Type of all the ages followinge. 1. When wicked men were ready to trouble all the world with contention, ambition, heresie, warre, they are restrayned by Constantine the great, till he had sealed the elect by prouidinge for the faithful (who were fewe, & liuinge in obscurity) in that great calamity of the Church which straightwayes followed. 9. # A PRAYER.

> Forasmuch as I am to take in hand a matter that is be-
yond the povver of mā, I beseech thee (o Father of lights,
together vvith thy sonne the principal Prophet, & the Holy
Ghost the guide of truth) to make playne & manifest before
my face the vvay vvhich to this day uvas neuer sufficiently
knovvne of mortall men. Our minde is halfe blinde in thinges
that are euen before our feete; hovv litle, or nothinge at al ra-
ther doth it understād of high & hidden mysteries? Here-
vppon hovv great danger is there, either to thrust our selues
rashly into thy secrets, or els to passe by thinges that be true
& to adde of our ovvne head thinges absurd & contrary to
the truth? Notvvithstanding thou that hast giuen thy word
for a lanterne to our feete, thou who callest the most simple to
search thy hidden mysteries, & chusest cōmonly fishermen be-
fore the wise of this world, doe thou (I say) vouchsafe to assist
me in my pouerty & weaknes, graunt me a happie passage
amonge theis hard rockie matters, keepe me from runninge at
any tyme upon the steepe rockes of pride, neither yet let me
sticke in the shallowe foordes of blinde ignorāce; but let me by
thy conduct goe on forth right till I approach to the truth, &
then after I haue found it out, let me so holily & religiously
loue, honour & keepe it, that I may neither conceale it through
dishonest feare, nor yet corrupt & sophisticate it for hatred
or fauour of any man, but may purely & sincerely bringe it
forth into light to the glory of thy most great name, and to the
consolation of thy Church, vvhich to this day mourneth grei-
uously, through Jesus Christ our Lord, Amen.

# THE FIRST CHAPTER.

## *The logicall resolvinge of it into the partes thereof.*

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap initial 'T' featuring floral and scrollwork ornamentation.</image-desc>

The Books of the Revelation after the Preface, is wholy closed vp into an Epistle. The preface is in the 3. first verses, & declareth the Argument, the Authors , both principall & ministeriall , & the fruite of the Booke. The Epistle is spent in an Inscription, A Propheticall Narration, & a Conclusion. The Inscription is notable for the person of the writer , & of those to whome it is written, but especially of him, from whome health is wished. Of which one God the Fathers eternall truth, the holy spirits manifold grace vers. 4. The sonnes partly threefold office vers 5. partly exceedinge great benefit redoundinge to the elect, both present vers 6. as also to be looked for at his glorious cominge , is described & greatly extolled , which cominge of Christ the Tribes of the earth shall intertayne with exceedinge great lamentation , while yet the Saintes doe vehemently wish for it, as is expressed in those wordes , *yea, Amen*, vers 7. The Propheticall Narration concerneth either particuler Churches , or the whole , & those either joyntly in the rest of this Chapter , or els severally in the two next. The matters which are joyntly declared serve to this end, that the 7. Churches might knowe, that Iohn tooke not in hand to write this Booke upon his owne head & pleasure, but called & commaunded thereto by God. For the full credit whereof doe make the Person callinge him, which can be no other but God , vers 8. Also the Person called vers 9. 10. Lastly the manner of callinge him, by hearinge vers 11. by seeinge vers 12. A vision whereof is sett before us, vers 12. 13. 14. 15. 16. & a certayne consequence whereof is declared, on the part of Iohn an astonishment, on Christs part a consolation, vers 17. 18. then a commandement to write vers 19. & an Interpretation of the vision, vers 20.

<header>A REVELATION, / The Exposition.</header>

*Vers. 1. A Revelation.* The Argument of the Booke signifyinge a Revelatiō made by God from which all the vayles of obscurity are taken away, which did before keepe it from the fight of mortall men. Which kinde of matters were wont to be called of old, *visions, & Prophecyes,* but in the writinges of the Apostles the word *Revelation* is more vsed; *I vvill come, (saith Paul) to visions & Revelations of the Lord,* 2 Cor. 12. 1. & againe, *least. I should be out of measure lift vp vvith excellency of Revelations, vers. 7. So every one of you hath a psalme, hath Doctrine, hath a Tongue, hath a Revelation,* 1 Cor. 14. 26. Besides the knowledge of the gospell is attributed to a Revelation, as to the vnderstandinge whereof wee have no more power till it be opened vnto vs, then wee have to vnderstand thinges to come. *I give thee thankes (O Father,) that thou hast hidden theis thinges from the vviſe, & hast revealed them to babes, saith Christ Matt. 11. 25.* Now then is this the meaninge of this word, that no newe thinge is brought in the preachinge of the Gospell, but as the Gospell is an vnsealed & disclosed lawe, so when the vayles are removed, that onely is pointed out clearely which before lay hidden vnder the old coverings? Indeed so it might seeme, unles this word were used also in & belonging to the old Testament. *The sayinge (saith Balaam) of him that heareth the vvordes of God, that seeth the vision of the Allmightie, fallinge out, yet vvhose eyes vvere opened or revealed, Num. 24. 4.* So the man of God saith to Eli in the name of the Lord: *I have revealed my selfe to the house of thy father,* 1 Sam. 2. 27. Wherrefore there can no argument be drawne hence to make for this matter. This maybe certayne, that this manner of speakinge here & there vsed doth shewe, that it neither was at the beginninge, nor as yet is, in the power of mortall witt, to attayne by searchinge to such mysteries as theis, and that yet through the grace of our Lord Iesus Christ, all thinges are made easie to be passed through, so farre as may be behoofull for his Church. Thou therefore most excellent day-starre and Light-bringer, open our eyes, that wee may behold thy mervailous thinges.

Of Iesus Christ: Who is one of the principall Authors of the Revelation, the Mediatour betweene God & men. From the same Christ have allwayes proceeded all the old Prophecyes, but in theis last dayes God hath spoken to vs in his Sonne after a certaine singuler & peculier man-

<header>OF THE APOCALYPSE.</header>

ner, Heb. 1. 1. Whence there is a difference betweene the auncient inscriptions of Prophecyes, & that of this. There, the vision of Isaias, the vision of Obadias, The Booke of the vision of Nahum; The Prophecy which Habakuk saw; but never till now, the vision, or Revelation of Iesus Christ. It must needes be a Prophecy full of Maiestie, which is so notable in the title of it before all others, neither is it to be doubted, but that accordinge to the nature of the light of the Gospell, all thinges are here delivered more distinctly and exquisitely, then ever before.

Which God gave him; Namely the Father, the Author & head-springe of all thinges. Now he gave theis thinges to Iesus Christ, as he was Mediatour, not as his coessentiall Sonne. For theis thinges doe rather teach the order, wherein God imparteth knowledge to his Church, then the beginninge of knowledge in respect of his Sonne, as Theod. Beza doth most learnedly explane it. He is the Pipe whereby whatsoever may be for our behoufe, is derived unto us men from that endles depth of goodnes. Although to give whith an infinitive moode after it, signifyeth often to permitt, as 

> thou shalt not give thy Holy one to see corruption, that is, thou shalt not suffer him, Psal. 16. 10. 

And 

> Edom refused to give to passe by him, that is, to permitt, Num. 21. 21. 

After which manner Demosthenes speaketh, ioyninge the word of permittinge whith all, 

> Give & permitt unto me to discourse of theis thinges before you. 

But it falleth all to one, whither wee iudge it to signifie the beginninge of knowledge or power: Therefore I thinke it best to rest in the first answere.

To declare it unto his servants, The understandinge therefore of theis thinges is peculiarly proper to theis men. Hence away farre ynough, ye Prophane-minded-men. What have you to doe (ô Iesuits) once to touch this Booke? Theis are mysteries sealed & closed vp from you, make shewe of whatsoever diligence ye will of interpretinge. Here is nothinge to doe for the sworne vassalle of Antichrist. Leave of to trouble your selves, to deceive others. If ye doe indeed desire to understand theis thinges, renounce that Lord ye serve, to the intent that he whose name ye doe now belye, may impart theis secrets to you, returninge againe into his family, after you have, like a company of dead men, bene so longe strangers from it.

Which must shortly come to passe, A declaration of what thinges the Revelation consisteth; not of such as have bene past of old, but which are to be done hence forward. Now he saith the tyme is at hand, because the matters should be begunne by & by, & should flowe from thence whith a perpetuall course without interruption, although the finall con-

<margin>+</margin> *Iohn to the seaven Churches.* Thus farre the Preface. The Epistle followeth, whose writers person is sufficiently knowne by thinges allready spoken. The persons to whome it is written, are the seaven Churches in Asia; namely all Churches in generall that be in all places whatsoever, as Aretas & Beda, and all Interpreters, as I suppose, doe with one consent determine, and that aright. For neither doe the matters herein rehearsed suffer us to stay onely in theis 7. Wee shall heare in the severall Epistles often admonition, that all would hearken to such thinges as are written to the Churches. Besides it belongeth to theis 7. to take notice aswell of thinges to come as of thinges present, both of which thinges (as he declareth belowe vers 19.) He had commandement to write and to send unto them. And the last clause of the whole Booke, which wisheth the grace of Christ to them all, sheweth that this whole Prophecy was sent in stead of an Epistle to the 7. Churches, Chap. 22. 21. Nowe what had it concerned or profited theis 7. Churches, which should remayne in safety but for a short tyme after, to understand of matters to come after for many ages, which should not belonge at all to them? Moreover the number of 7. is an universall number, by whose revolution, all tymes are framed, al ages beinge in like manner wheerled about upon this Pole, as the whole frame of heaven is turned about upon the seven starres of Charles-wayne. For which cause this number as beinge full of mistery, is used throughout the Booke afterwards in the description of every thinge. And yet are not all Churches so to be comprehended, as if nothinge at all were indeed sent to those Churches, which are by name belowe noted out; but together with the signification of the mistery, the truth of the story is to be retained. Seeinge therefore theis 7. Churches doe extend further then theire names shewe for, is the estate of all tymes till the last cominge of Christ to be considered in them? No verely, but onely of that age, wherein the Church conversed amonge the Gentiles; which shalbe made plaine out of the thinges that followe. In the meane tyme, so expresse mentioninge of the Churches of Asia seemes to intimate, that the congregations of the Iewes are not to be mingled with theis. Which hath made me in my generall survey to distinguish the whole Prophecy, into that which is proper to the particuler Churches, and that which is common to them all.

person. The first of which persons, theis wordes describe. Aretas thinketh that theis 3. tymes belonge in speciall to the 3. persons, because the father, saith he, elswhere, is called he that is, as Exod. 3. 14. The sonne, he that was, Ioh. 1. 1. The holy ghost, he that cometh, Ioh. 16. 8. 13. But that so cleare a distinction which presently followeth gainsayeth it, which challengeth this circumlocution of that Ebei Exod. 3. 13. Which is common indeed to the whole deity, as proper here to the person of the father alone. Whence also wee are geven to wit, that this threefold difference of time, respecteth the unchangeable and constant truth of God in his promises. For the same is the force of this circumlocution, as of that compendious description of God, Exod. 3. 14. Which wee knowe was then used to teach Moses, that the time was then come, wherein the promise of old made to Abraham concerninge the deliverance of his seede out of Egipt, should be performed. Whence also it was, that God was not knowne to the Fathers by the name *Iehovah*, because they had not as yet attained to the promise. Certaine others will have this to be the name of the essence, whereof a created minde can perceive no part, as if God should take such names to himselfe, for his owne sake alone, not for ours, and so this is the meaninge as if he should say, from God the Father that is most true and constant in all his thinges, who giveth in present most plentifull proofes of his truth, by sendinge his sonne at length into the world; who of old times never failed in any thinges which he promised, who lastly hath given us such hope of performinge thinges yet to come, that he is every day carefull to performe them, thus hasteninge the full perfection of his whole truth. For this force have the wordes: *Who cometh, or is in cominge*, as if they should signify a present-future thinge, that I may so call it. For that which is cominge is not yet present, neither yet is it altogether absent. It is therefore farre more significant then if he had said, he that is about to come, as it is commonly translated. For this he that cometh, declareth that he will no longer deferre his promises, but that he is even nowe labouringe to performe them, which is a notable comfort to them, who are ready to wax faint by reason of the tediousnes of the delay. But what will some say, is truth onely given to the Father? It is indeed common alike to them all, but seeinge the office of the Sonne and of the Holy Ghost is exercised in executinge decrees, it is so spoken of, as if it were proper to him alone, whome the order of working maketh the Author of promises, and the Fountayne of benefits and mercies. The impiety of the Gentiles hath imitated this distribution in theire Oracle out of a Trivet, which they say Apollo used, because of

*And from the feaven Spirits.* The fecond Fountayne of peace is the Holy Ghoft, as who doth moft plentifully inrich and furnifh the Church, with all kinde of giftes, for which caufe this circumlocution is ufed. For he can be no creature who together with the Father and the Sonne, is a giver and an Author of peace and grace. Touchinge which point fee what the learned *Iunius* hath. Neither can this argue him to be a creature, as the Iefuite would have it, becaufe he is faid to ftand in the fight of the Throne, after the manner of thofe that rather are ad minifiringe fpirits unto God, then that he fhould be God himfelfe. For by this reafon, the fonne fhould be God neither, as who beinge the Lambe, came and tooke the booke out of the right hand of him that fitteth upon the Throne; as it is belowe, Chap. 5. 7. And more plainly in Dan. 7. 13. And before him, (*namely, fittinge upon the Throne*) that is, the Sonne of Man. Is nowe the Sonne therefore to be put out of the Deity? Wherefore wee muft knowe, that troughout this Booke, mention is made both here & elfwhere, both in generall of God, as the higeft & chifeft governour, for which caufe he hath a Throne given him, as alfo of the Sonne & Holy Ghoft as mini- ftringe unto him, as by whofe mearely-ioyned helpe all thinges are made and done. Wherefore they are faid to ftand before the Throne, as it were in a readines, and as though they did-wayte for the becke & bid- dinge of theire higheft governour. So the Revelation was given to the Sonne aboue, vers 1. and therefore the Holy Ghoft in this place feemeth rather to be noted out by his giftes which he worketh in the Saints, then by his proper name. But matters that ferve onely for order, are not to be drawne to the abolifhinge of the natures.

5. *And from Iefus Chrift, vvho is that faithfull vvitnes,* the defect of the relative beinge fupplyed, which is moft common in this Booke, after the manner of the Hebrwes. Theis wordes belonge to the third Fountayne, which is Chrift, whome wee call the third, accordinge to that place he hath here, not in the order of his perfon. He was put of to this place, becaufe there was a longer ftay to be made in his difcription; & the thankf- givinge was to be begune at him, as by whofe merit alone, wee are made partaker of all good thinges. Now firft he mentioneth his propheticall office, callinge him a faithfull witnes, that is, one that hath taught faith- fully, truely & plainely the whole will of God, as farre as requifite for mans falvation. called a witnesse,as it is in,Ioh.3.11. & 5.31.32. & 18.37. 1.Tim. 6. 13. Nowe can there be any vaine or false matter with in that testimony which floweth from so faithfull a witnes? Or doth it agree to his faithfulnes to conceale any thinge from vs, as the which is not to be fetched frõ any other place, but from out of the closset of the Bishop of Romes brest? Cheifely seeinge he hath no where no not in one word intimated any such storehouse, whence to fetch it? But these be the dotages of witnesses as vaine and as litle to be trusted,if it may be, as this heavenly & most true witnesse is true.

The first borne from the dead: Theis wordes belonge to his Preisthoode, wherein he overcame death by death,and made a full satisfaction for sinnes. For this is to be the first borne from the dead, himselfe first of all to rise agayne after he had vanquished death,whome death would never have let goe, if he had had the least right to keepe him still with himselfe. For which cause the Apostle saith that *he rose agayne for our iustification*, Rom. 4. 25. Nowe he seemeth to be called *the first borne from the dead*, after a concise manner of speech, and by way of distribution, which more fully should be set downe thus, *the first borne of them that rise againe from the dead*; In which wordes two thinges are signifyed; First, that he is the Prince and head of those that rise againe, as the Apostle explaneth it, Col. 1. 18. *And he is the beginninge & the first borne from the dead, that he might be cheife amonge them all*; And therefore also is he called *the first-fruites of them that slept*, 1. Cor. 15. 20. The second, that he shall at last raise vp others also from the grave by his owne power, even as he himselfe speaketh. *I vvill raise him vp at the last day*, Ioh. 6. 39. 40. Which two thinges belonge to the elect alone. For neither is he the head of the reprobates, neither wil he raise them vp at the last day,that is,in glory,as the elect, but onely,the force of that curse *at vvhat day thou shalt eate thereof thou shalt certanely dye*, Gen. 2. 17. Shall restore theire bodyes vnto them, in which they shall suffer everlastinge torments. Whence it cometh to passe,that seeinge this kinde of restoringe is onely for and vnto death, it hath hardly given it the name of a resurrection in the Scriptures. And therefore the Holy Ghost doth seeme not to speake collectively, *the first borne of the dead*, but distributively, *the first borne from the dead*, that is, of those that rise from the dead,as was said before, with a manifest difference betweene the elect and Reprobate that are dead.

Interpreter is very undiscretely, bragged of, (that I may not say impu-

have heard, in the next wordes before, that he is indued, for himselfe
alone, but that he doth powre them out upon the elect, to the intent
they might be made happie by theire partakinge of them.

*Kinges and Preistes vnto God.* Some read kingdome and Priestes, as also the voulgar. It much matters not for the sence, yet the cōioyninge of persons amonge themselves, is more likely, then of thinges & persons. The elect are Kinges by the participation of the Kingdome of Christ, wherein wee have overcome the lawe, death, sinne, wee triumph also dayly ouer the world, by tramplinge it vnder foote by faith, <margin>1 Ioh.5.4.5.</margin> By him likewise are wee Priestes, as who beinge dead in him, have God fauourable vnto vs, haue also an entrance made & layd open, to speake boldly vnto him. But he doth warily adde that wee are made Kinges and Preists to God, least wee should thinke that this honour is giuen vnto vs, either to trouble the ciuile State, or els to intermingle Church-governement with civile.

*To him be glory:* This is all that wee can render for exceedinge great benefits, to desire that he may be most renowned amonge all men with his owne iust praises. And this giuinge of thankes seemes to be taken vp because of the present gift of God, powred vpon the Gentiles by knowledge of Christ.

*7. Behold he cometh vvith cloudes.* The benefit to come, that is to be looked for at his glorious cominge. To come with cloudes is to manifest himselfe with storme and tempest, & with a mighty & fearefull apparition of great lighteninge, to revenge himselfe vpon the wicked, and to deliver those that be his. After which manner also speaketh Daniel touchinge the same cominge. *I savve in visions of the night, that behold there came vvith the cloudes of heaven, one like to the Sonne of Man,* <margin>chap.7.13.</margin> For so the notable iudgments of God are wont to be described, in which he poureth out the vehement heate of his fury vpon his enemyes, to make vs now thinke that all creatures doe fight for God, as also that he will make Heauen and earth to serue him for the aydinge of those that be his, and moreover, that the Reprobate cannot by any meanes escape. In like manner the Psalmist beinge delivered out of the handes of his enemies, doth magnifye God for his power shewed forth from heaven in deliueringe him, Psal.18. 13.14.15. In Mathew, he is said to come vpon the cloudes, chap.24.30. But perhaps in the same sence as in Psal.18.11. *And he sate vpon the Cherubins, & did flye, &c.* But yet the Angells avouch, that *he shall so come, even as they savve him goinge vp into heaven,* Act. 1. 11. <header>A REVELATION,</header>

But the tribes are of them that mourne , and therefore of them that pierced him , namely of the Iewes , whose this wicked fact properly was . Therefore theis wordes of the Apostle carry this sence , as if he should say , behold he cometh with cloudes , and all men of what kinde soever shall see him , even they that pierced him , that is , the Iewes , whose Auncestours did lift vp Christ vpon the Crosse , and gored his side with a speare , these men beinge dispersed every where amonge all Nations , shalbe at last converted to the true faith , and shall mourne with an earnest sorrowe , both for theire forefathers horrible wickednes , as also for theire owne so longe obstinacy . Even so Amen . And so the summe of all is this , that the benefit cominge by Christ is here celebrated , partly present , in the callinge of the Gētiles , (for that which he spake before of Kinges and Priests is referred to the seaven Churches of Asia , that is , to all nations of the Gentiles that imbrace Christ for the present , for which cause he giveth him the praise of glory and power) partly to come , in the callinge of the Iewes , which wee have declared vnto vs here , both in theire repentance , as also in the desire and wish of all the Godly .

*Even so Amen .* The fervent desire of the Godly wishinge for this cominge is expressed in Greeke and Hebrue , because this shalbe the wish of all nations . The former particle belongeth properly to him that affirmeth , signifyinge the certenty of a matter , wherein not withstandinge there may be vnderstoode the verbe of wishinge ; *Let it be done* , or some other such word . For so in the end of this Booke , even so come Lord Iesus ; it is as if he should say , I beseech thee so to come as thou hast promised , chap. 22. 20. It is likely that both particles are vsed in the same sence , els the diversitie both of the tongues and of the signification , would not note out any joynt desire of al people , for which end this double proprietie of speech seemes to be taken vp . *Amen* , is a word , not onely of one that ascertaines a matter , but of him also that prayeth and striveth vehemently by prayer for the cominge to passe and good successe of a matter , as Ier. 28. 6. *Amen , the Lord doe so* : the latter wordes by way of exposition explaninge the former .

8. *Iam Alpha and Omega :* Hither to the Inscription of the Epistle ; nowe he setteth vpon the Narration it selfe ; where first to give authority to the writinge taken in hand , the threefold property of the person that calleth is set downe , his very great power of creatinge , truth in

his promises and his soveraigntie of governinge. This power is first metaphorically expressed, then with proper wordes. For *the beginninge and the end* doe interprete the meaninge of A. and O. of which, that is the first letter of the Greeke Alphabet, this the latter last: by a figurative speech they are applyed to any beginninge and end. They are wordes that doe plainlye signifie a certayne order and relation of Christ to the creatures. For which cause, they cannot properly note out an eternity, which is an absolute matter, and not to be measured by the creature in any respect. This is therefore the meaninge, *I am Alpha and Omega*, that is, the efficient cause of all thinges, and the end also, whither all thinges are referred; who have at the first created all thinges, and that for mine owne glory alone. It is a compendious expressinge of that which the wise man saith: *The Lord hath made all thinges for himselfe, even the wicked man for the day of evill, Prov. 16. 4.* The constant truth of God in his promises, is declared by the distribution of the three fold tyme, as vvee have shewed vers. 4. His omnipotency in the end of the verse seemes to belonge to that supreme power of governinge all thinges at his pleasure, wherein his incomprehensible Maiestie shineth forth no lesse, then it did in the first framing of all thinges. For this sheweth that his strength was not quite spent in his first worke, but that it doth continue in the vigour of it for ever with ont any impayringe, as the which nevver waxeth faint with any wearisomenes, neither oppressed with any over-great waight of busineses, but beyond all force of a created minde doth hold out infinitely more then ynough for dispatch of all matters. Such is he from whome the commaundemēt <gloss>commandement</gloss> to write proceedeth, beinge the most powerfull creatour, the most faithfull promiser , and the highest Governour of all thinges.

9. I Iohn: The person also of him that is called hath great moment for the credit of this Booke. I Iohn the Apostle, brother, and fellovve in affliction, beinge banished into Pathmus for the word of God, inspired from God in spirit on the Lordes day. What would this man relate, that were not of most certaine truth?

*And in the sufferinge of Iesus Christ.* The vulgar, and *in the patience of Iesus Christ* so also Montanus. The Interpreter of *Aretas*, *by Christ Iesus*. But after a quite contrary manner of workinge, not onely in respect of

wicked Spirits doe tormēt men are violent and horrible, whence it is

they doe come into, but the one by bowinge thē most gently, the other
by cōpellinge thē most cruelly, as examples of both doe make playne.

*On the Lordes day.* See what *Th. Beza* hath of this point. It is verylike
that there was no holy meetinge in the Isle as vpon this day, otherwise
Ihon would neuer haue walked vp & downe alone on the shore, & so

him the same day, & so by perpetuall order to haue flowed, that there

one Epistle, & are not diuided seuerally into sundry Epistles. Nowe wee

selfe might teach, he gat God himselfe to be his Teacher: & thus after
he had thus dispatched these thinges, he goeth forward to the māner of
his callinge, out of which it is yet more manifest that this office was
imposed by God vpon him.

<margin>11.</margin> *Sayinge, I am Alpha and Omega.* Theſe wordes wee had aboue, in the 8. verſ. but there thẽ they were the wordes of Iohn, deſcribinge the person of him whoſe authority he followed, in writinge this prophecy, here they are the wordes of Chriſt himſelfe, pronouncinge the ſame thinges with his owne voice. Therefore Iohn vſinge this manner of ſpeech aboue, did not drawe it forth of the ſhop of his owne brayne but learned it from God, from whome nothinge that is not moſt holy can come. Aretas, the vulgar and Complutenſis read not theis thinges; but yet they ſeeme to be raſhly daſhed out by ſome man, perhaps becauſe they were repeated after the interpoſition of ſo fewe thinges. Neuertheles, there ought to haue beene a diſtinction made betweene Iohn and Chriſt, neither ought thoſe wordes to haue bene thought ſuperfluous, which teach what Author there was of vſinge them before.

*Write vvhat thou ſeeſt in a Booke.* That is, that which thou art ſtraight-wayes to ſee, and likewiſe alſo to heare. This expreſſe commaundement to write, and that withnaminge to whome he ſhould write, ſheweth, that this Embaſſage was not voluntary, but deputed and aſſigned to him from God.

Which are in *Asia* , *Ephesus*, &c. Aboue in the 4. verse, it was said in generall onely in *Asia* ; but nowe seeinge these Cities are named , wee vnderstand, that not the whole continent is designed , which is called by this name,and is much spoken of for a third part of the world,but a litle part of it onely,which is so properly called of the common sort: which lyinge in a place almost like an Iland by the *Euxine* , *AEgeum* and *Pamphilian* sea , is bounded on the Northside with *Bithinia* , on the west with *Hellespontus* and the *AEgæan* sea , on the South with *Licia*,on the East partly with *Licia*,partly with *Pamphilia* and *Galatia*. In this part of the world flourished once, these seven most renowned cities , beinge put in this place in stead of the whole Church amonge the Gentiles. As touchinge *Ephesus*,it is a most noble Citie lyinge by the shore of the *Icarian Sea* , not farre from a riuer in *Lydia* called *Cayster*,the head-Citie of *Ionia*,the greatest martinge place of all *Asia* with in the Mountayne *Taurus* , much praised and spoken of for the Temple of *Diana* ; most noble in renowne amonge Christians , for *Paules* three yeares holy labours there ; *Act*. 19. 20. and 20. 31. For that diuine Epistle of his written to that people ; for *Timothy* that was giuen them to be theire Pastour , and for the most happie watering it had in latter tymes before many yeares by the Apostle S. *Iohn*. *Smyrna*, a citie also of *Ionia* by the sea side , on the northside of *Ephesus*, distant from thence 320. furlongs,an vnder-citie of the *Ephesians*, with whome of auncient tyme they dwelt together , that was some times of great wealth and power , and hath a Iurisdiction in certayne nigh-adioyninge Cities , euen as *Ephesus* also, wherein the meetinges of the Cities that are subiect vnto it were made , as *Plinie* writeth, *Booke 5. Chap. 29.* *Pergamus*, is a Citie of *AEolia* on the North of *Smyrna*,very renowned and hauinge the principallitie among the *Mediterranean* cities,sometymes the seate of the Kinges of *Attalia*,which at length came into the *Romanes* handes, who were made heires of it by will from *Attalus* the last of that name and race , who turned the Country into a Province, and called it *Asia* by the name of the Continent,as deuouringe doubtles in hope that whole part of the world by this small beginninge , as if *Attalus* had bequeathed vnto them by Testament, not onely *Pergamus* but all *Asia* also,whence, if I be not deceiued , came the first distinction of the lesser *Asia*. *Thyatira* is the further most citie of the *Mysians* , a Colony of the *Macedonians* towards the west of *Pergamus*, to whose iurisdiction also it belongeth.

Neither doth it make a litle hereunto, that he appeareth in this habite in the mids of the Candleſticks, thereby plainly declaringe, that this manner of adorninge himselfe doth not agree absolutely vnto himsel-fe, but so farre forth as he is conuersant in the Churches of theis and these tymes. Wherefore in such visions as these, wee ought not so much to enquire of vvhat fashion Christ is in himselfe, as vvhat kinde of gouerninge his Church he vseth, and of vvhat fashion his Spouse is arisinge thence, vvhich he setteth forth to be beheld in himselfe as in a glaſse. To come therefore to the explaininge of the thinges one by one: The garment dovvne to the feete, is the perfect righteousnes of Christ imputed, vvherevvith the Spouse is couered throughout from the head to the heele, so as no filthy nakednes of hers can appeare. For this clothinge is not neceſſary for Christ, but serueth to couer his Spouse, vvhich yet Christ vveareth on his ovvne body, declaringe hovv beautifull shee should be at these tymes in this respect. Neither is lesse often then significantly the righteousnes of faith noted out by a gar-ment. *Bleſsed is the man, saith the Psalmist, vvhose sinne is couered, pſal. 32. 1.* And *the guest that vvanteth this garment is cast into vtter darknes, Mat. 22 12.* And afterwardes in this Booke, *they are pronounced bleſsed, that vvatch and keepe their garments, least they vvalke naked and their filthines be seene, chap. 16. 15.* And so elſevvhere oftentimes. Novv vvhat can more fitly resemble the righteousnes of faith, vvhich abhorreth our inherent righteousnes as a menstruous cloth, neither can rest in any other thinge, saue onely in this rayment of Christes righteousnes.

But the Spouſe hauinge obtained more plentifull grace at this tyme, ſhould remoue the girdle from the loines to the pappes, thus nearely and ſtraitly tyinge and bindinge theis garments to herſelſe by true faith of the hart, that ſo they might not ſlippe or hange looſely and ſcatteringly about her.

14. *His head and hayres.* Garments and girdle are common to all the members, in the head and the hayre there is a certaine diſtribution of partes, whereof the one reſpecteth thoſe that haue rule and authority in the Chriſtian congregations, and are as it were heades vnto them. The haires note out the common ſort, which dependeth on the holy Teachers drawinge nouriſhmet and garniſhhinge from them, giuinge them likewise comelines and defence. Both of them are white that is flouriſhinge in the ſeaven Churches, or rather in the firſt of the ſeaven Churches with a ſinguler puritie. For wee ſhall ſee that this order of the members hath referencẽ after a ſort to the order of the Churches. Although thoſe thinge which are here ſpoken of in the laſt place, are giuen in the Epiſtles to the firſt. Which invertinge of the order teacheth that theſe properties doe ſo cheifely agree to ſome of them, that they may be applyed as occaſion ſerueth to others alſo. But this whitenes is of woole and ſnowe ; of that, for her, ſimplicitiẽ of conditions, wherewith the Saintes are endued, who are every where called ſheepe, and not vnvvorthily, ſeeinge our head is a lambe ; of this, because this purity and whitenes is not naturall, but that which ſhee hath cominge from a nother. For woole naturally is defiled with greaſe, and is ful of duſt and many other pollutions, but beinge waſhed

*And his voice like the voice of many vvatters.* This similitude is ordi-
nary, and noteth out almost every where a mighty tumult. In this
Booke it is of a more full signification, declaringe besides the greatnes
of the noise, a certayne vnperceivable notion of thinges, that I may
soo call it. Such as is the disordered and confused roaringe of waters
that beatinge together with contrarie vvaues, and rushinge in vpon
the shore or the rockes, make a mighty noise, and yet one cannot
distinctly perceiue, what all that noise meaneth. Such should be by
meanes of Christes gouernment the voice of Christ in those Churches
in which the feete should be like to fine brasse burninge. The truth
should be a certaine vnfavoury thing without any pleasant tast of wi-
sedome vnto the heathen men, that should keepe euen in the most pure
Church of Ephesus, neither should it sound any other wise in theire
eares, then harsh and Barbarous. Cornelius Tacitus calleth the do-
ctrine of the Gospell a certaine pestilent superstition, by this impious
blasphemy, declaringe not so much his owne, as the common hatred
of all the Heathen against it, Booke 15. Suetonius telleth howe the
Christians were afflicted and punished, whome he describeth to be a
kinde of men of a strange and noyfome superstition, in Neroes life,
chap. 16. Plinie a very prudent and learned man, in a certayne Epistle
to Traiane, singeth the same songe, writinge that himselfe, *when as he
had by tortures enquired the truth of tvvo Maydens, vvhich vvere said to be
servants to certayne Christians, found out nothinge but a vvicked and an ex-
cessiue superstition, the contagion vvhereof had ouerrunne not the Cities one-
ly, but the villages and Cuntry-territories besides.* How rude a beatinge of
vvaues together and voyd of all sensible matter, seemed the noise of the
truth to these men? Theire eares were filled with a sound, whereof
they vnderstoode no meaninge. Wee shall see notwith standinge in
the next chapter, how these men though heathens belonged to Ephe-
fus. But not onely this kinde of men accounted of the sauinge truth
as a Barbarous thinge, but many also of the Christians, so called, in the
Churches of Smirna, Pergamus & those that followe next after them.
Errours and peruerse opinions did so possesse many of them, that
they waxed deafe against sound doctrine, neither perceiued they any
sweetenes thereof, as shalbe more playne in the next Chapter.

For how could the Hell of the damned be cast into the lake of fire?
Thus therefore seeme these two to be distinguished,that death should
be the seperatinge and partinge of the soule and the body ; Hell, that
state and condition wherein the body is after this partinge.

19. *Write vvhat thou hast seene,and vvhich are.* Here the commaun-
dement of vritinge is repeated,but more largly vnfolded. In the 11.
verse it was commaunded onely, *vvrite vvhat thou seest in a booke*,nowe
he teacheth how farre that which he sawe reached,namely, to thinges
both present, and to come. For both these beinge ioyned together
explaine those wordes, *vvhich thou hast seene*. And in the seueral Epi-
stles,to which the partes of this visiõ are applyed,accordinge to theire
diverse condition,wee shall finde fore tellinges of thinges to come; so
that those wordes : *vvhich thou hast seene*, cannot be restrained onely
to thinges present. Seeinge therefore the seaven Epistles to the seaven
Churches, conteine as well thinges to come as present,the whole pro-
phecy is not rightly diuided into thinges present & to come. For these
members meete together,as afterwardes wee shall see in the openinge
of each thinge one by one. Let vs hold this then which the wordes
openly teach, that this vision which is proper to the seaven Churches,
is of thinges both present and to come. The obseruinge of which small
matter , hath opened a way vnto me to vnderstand these particuler
Epistles,as I suppose,vvhich I leaue to the iudgment of the godly.

20. *The Mistery of the seaven starres:* In the last place is the Inter-
pretation,which teacheth onely concerninge two thinges, the starres
and the Candlestickes. Why giveth he no explanation of the other
partes? Because these fewe were ynough for the openinge of his
purpose in the whole. For after the same manner are the rest to be
applyed to the estate of the Church. And the holy Ghost would in
such sort helpe our infirmitie, that he would leaue some partes of it to
be searched out by our diligence. Although those partes of the vision
which remayne vnopened,wil easily be seene out of the Epistles,which
teach throuh the condition of the seueral Churches what meaninge
the rest haue which are nowe passed ouer in silence, as shalbe shewed
in theire places. As touchinge the wordes. The word misterye is in
the fourth case followinge the word write, which is to be repeated in
common; as if he should say, *vvrite the mysterie of the seaven Starres, &
and likewise in the clause follovvinge,and vvrite the seaven Candlestickes.
Defectively; for vvrite the mystery of the seaven golden Candlestickes.*

Nowe he interpreteth the Starres to be Angells. *The seaven starres (saith he) are the Angels of the seaven Churches.* That is, signify the seaven Angels. Which I would have them marke, who sticks tooth and nayle to the letter elswhere. Neither are these Angells spirituall substances, but men that are Pastours and Bishops, to whome the Scriptures giue this name; as although the *Angell of the Lord had ascended vp out of Gilgall to Bochim, Iudg. 2. 1.* So in the Prophet Haggee. *Then spake Haggee the Angell of the Lord, chap. 1. 13.* And Malachie speakinge of the Preistes; *For he is the Angell of the Lord of hostes, chap. 2. 7.* How great then is the worth of true Pastours, who are both starres fixed in no other firmament then Christes right hand, as also Angells? What matter is it with what opprobrious names the wicked mocke them, seeinge they haue this place and account with God?

And *those seaven Candlestickes are the seaven Churches.* They are excellently compared to Candlestickes, as in which the light of the truth shineth for euer, beinge lighted by Christ the high Preist morninge & eueninge continually. This similitude is taken from the Candlesticke of the Tabernacle, which was made of pure gold, with a worke the partes whereof claue fast together with out any seperation, consistinge of one shanke, and seaven branches. The multitude of the branches, signifyeth the multitude of the particuler Churches, both of the Iewes and of the Gentiles, theire common originall from one shanke, signifyeth the most neare conioyninge of all the particuler Churches, all which come forth of that one Church of the Iewes, as it were out of the shaft: which shaft was more beautifyed then the rest of the branches, with one bowle an almond & a litle floure, because, as it seemeth, the Church of the Iewes is to be at length more abundantly filled with the giftes of the holy Ghost then this of ours that be Gentiles, Exod. 25. 31. The Candlestickes then are the Churches, but such as doe by theire most costly matter summarily onely note out the excellent worthines of them; the comlines of euery member Christ himselfe hath severally represented in that figure wherein he was seene of Iohn.

### Of the Church of Ephesus.

Of the Citie of Ephesus wee haue spoken in a fewe wordes at the eleuenth vers. of the first Chapter : to which wee must nowe adde the reason of the order, the force of the name, and the Counterpayne thereof, that the purpose of the holy Ghost may be the better vnderstode. The reason of the order may be double, one because this Citie fetteth before our eyes the Church of the Gentiles most clearly of all the rest, beinge most like to that prodigall sonne that went a whoringe and wasted his patrimony riotously in a farre country, Luc. 15. 13. &c. Whome, wee know, Christ propounded for a resemblance of the conuersion and callinge of the Gentiles. For this citie, besides the horrible Idolatry wherein it was as it were a Torch-bearer to the rest of the Cities, was luxurious past all measure and hope of recouery, as the which cast out one Hermodorus for no other crime, but because he was a trustie and an honest man, addinge ouer and besides this sayinge to theire fact; *Let none of vs be euer good for ought, if he be, lett him goe to another place and gett him other Companions.* A speech fit for beastes, even in the opinion of the heathen, and worthy to be punished with death. Cicero; in his Tusculan quest: booke 5. And that death defined with a Halter; for so Strabo saith: *That all the Ephesians yonge and old were worthy to be hanged vp for so sayinge.* Behold here therefore this riotous sonne betaking himselfe agayne to his fathers howse, his father also together runninge to meete him, and fallinge vpon his necke and kissinge him. How greatly is the grace of God to be magnifyed, which hath conuerted vs Gentiles, that were a gulfe and dungeon of wickednes (the nature of all which wee see in this Citie) into a most glorious pallace of saluation. Wee were of old Princes and Captaynes of mischiefe, nowe wee are made cheife heades of holines, euen as this was amonge the seauen Churches; no lesse excelling for pietie, then wee were famous before for all detestable actes. Certenly this is that father in the Gospell who hath caused the cheife robe to be brought out, & hath killed his fatted Calfe for our sake. The other reason of the order is, that this Citie was the principall amonge al other of that region for embracinge the faith, whence it was deriued vnto the other neighbour places. For Paul cominge to Ephesus, disputed daily in the schoole of one Tyrannus, and that for two yeares, so that all that dwelt in Asia both Iewes and Grecians heard the word of the Lord Iesus, Act. 19. 9. 10. Wherefore worthily is the beginninge of the Cities accounted to be from thence,

whence the beginninge of the faith was. Nowe wee are to explaine the force of the name. For it wilbe cleare in euery of these Churches, that the holy Ghost hath chosen out aduisedly these Churches, which by theire very names, as it were by certayne markes written vpon the forehead, should declare theire whole condition. Wee let passe that warlike woman, one of the Amazones, whence they say it drewe the name; that which followeth after vers. 4. *That thou hast omitted or let goe, thy first loue*, sufficiently teacheth vvhat that vvas vvhich the Spirit respected in this Citie; Namely, that Ephesus was as it were Aphesus of the Greeke *Aphesis*, omission; where vpon wee call it languishinge Ephesus, as whose piety doth by litle and litle wax cold, so as at length it is quite extinguished. Howe is it to be feared least it beare the Image of the Gentiles in this thinge also? As touchinge the Counterpayne of it, seeinge these seaven Cities contayne the vniuersall condition of the Church amonge the Gentiles, as it is euident ynough by those thinges which haue bene said vpon the first Chapter, in every one of them, not onely the Citie it selfe alone is to be considered, but with all likewise wee must ioyne some fellowe-Church, which may answere directly vnto it. But what kinde of Counterpaynes shall wee call theis? For are these seaven Cities appointed for patternes of all Churches of the same tyme, or of a diuerse tyme? If wee shall say the first, so that the Church dispersed in euery age through the whole world, should agree with theis seaven, that is, so as one should be the Ephesien Church, a nother the Smyrnean, a third like the Church of Pergamus, and so of the rest, it should be allwayes vniforme, and such as it was in the first times, such a face should it carry at this day, contrary to that which the experience of all times teacheth. It is necessary therefore to make them seuerally types one by one, and in that order as they are nõbred; but those Churches are the Counterpaynes which beinge deuided, either in the different spaces of tymes, or els in the distances of places, agree to euery one of them in theire order: with what boundes they are limmited the correspondence of thinges will shewe sufficiently. Accordinge to this rule wee hold that the Counter copie of the Citie of Ephesus is the first Christian Church, which takinge his beginninge from the preachinge of the Apostles, indured vntill the tyme of Constantine the great; as those thinges which are taught afterwardes will plainly shewe. This is the principall of all other Churches, as Ephesus is the first of the feaven Cities.

I knowe *thy labour and thy longe sufferance.* For seeinge the labour which is spent in preachinge the word is toylesome and ful of troubles, it is wont to be called in the Scriptures *Kopos*, that is, a wearyinge or toilesome labour, as *vvee beseech you brethren that you vvould acknowledge them vvhich labour amonge you, &c. 1. Thess. 5. 12.* And they are *vvorthy of double honour that labour in the vvord and doctrine, 1. Tim. 5. 17.* Now vnto the labour of teachinge patience must be ioyned as a neccessary companion, which here the Holy Ghost declareth sayinge, *and thy patience.* As also Paul; *The servant of God ought not to fight but he ought to be gentle tovvardes all men, apt to teach, enduringe vvicked men, vvith meekenes instructinge them vvhich are contrary-minded, 2. Tim. 2. 23. 24.* This Church then was notable for faithfulnes and diligence in teachinge. Behold the example of Paul, who for *3. yeares together did not cease day and night to admonish euery one vvith teares, Act. 20. 31.* Make a coniecture likewise by those godly Bishops, who did so greatly and dearly loue Paul, whome he also loued agayne with no lesse loue, *Act. 20. 37. 38.* Consider also of Iohn and the rest; but a matter so cleare needeth not many wordes. As touchinge the Counterpayne thereof, the matter is also euery whit as cleare. There was neuer any time when there was more faithfull diligence and ernest indeauour in teachinge. That monstrous wickednes was not as yet hatched, that any should be a Pastour, who did not feede at all, or that any should fit in the Doctours chayre, who should be dombe and lazy, beinge distracted with other businesses. No man was then a Bishop that had the office of teachinge, who did not teach most diligently. That yea euen at Rome, where the misterye of iniquity was to bud forth more speedily, there was no cessation as yet from this duetie. The Pastour of the Church euery Lordes day at least, did plainely and clearly expound such thinges as were read out of the Bookes of the Apostles or Prophets, he did also admonish and exhort them to imitate those thinges which they had heard read, beinge so holy and good thinges. *Iustin. Apologie 2.* The same thinge Clement, Origen, Tertullian, Cyprian doe witnesse. But the matter is as cleare and manifest, as it is cleare that the contrary is done at this day.

*And that thou canst not indure euill men.* Thus was the care of teachinge. The manner of theire Discipline was no lesse sound and entier. Which is first of all generally sett downe, of what sort it was against all euill men; and then in speciall, of what sort it was against the

Cleargie it selfe, that I may so call it, in the next wordes ; *And thou hast tryed those that say they are Apostles, &c.* The general discipline did not in the least manner tolerate men that liued any way detestably , and that with the offence of others; but accordinge to the nature of theire crime, it reproued them either priuately, or before many , if priuate admonition had nothinge profited ; and then afterwardes it did also keepe them backe from the holy thinges, if they would not hearken to them that perswaded them to that which was good and right. And as touchinge Ephesus it cannot be doubted, but that this holy course was kept constantly there, seinge Paul taught there three yeares, who also commaunded Timothy so precisely and diligently euery thinge that belonged to this matter. The obseruation also hereof was famous in the primitiue Church, as euen Pliny the Heathen witnesseth, in an Epistle of his vnto Traiane the Emperour. *The Christians* (faith he) *are vvont to rise earely, and to magnify Christ as if he vvere theire God, and for the perseruinge of theire Religion to forbid manslaughters, adulteries, couetousnes, deceit, and thinges like to theis,* Euseb. in his 3. booke 33. Chap. of his Ecclesiasticall Historie, out of Tertullian. Out of doubt they did not onely forbid these sinnes in word by teachinge, but they also repressed them by holy discipline. And they did well and wisely iudge, that otherwise Religion could not be preserued, vnles vices were cutt and putt downe with this spirituall sword. Iustine witnesseth that *no man vvas admitted to the Sacrament of the Supper, but he vvho’se life did ansvveare to his profession of godlines,* in his 2. Apologie. But Tertullian more plainely, writinge thus ; *In the same place also exhortations, chastisinges, and the diuine censures are in vse ; for it is proclaymed, vvith great grauitie and earnestnes by the Church, that if any shall offend he should be banished from partakinge vvith the Church in prayer in euery one of theire holy assemblyes and meetinges vvhither publike or priuate ; euery one of the elders that are most approued are made the Presidents in these censures, vvhich honour they haue obtayned not by theire money but by theire good report.* Apologet. chap. 39. false Apostles, Gnostickes, Sabellians, Samosatenians, Manicheans, &c. Of whome some part was thrust through with the dart of the truth by the Apostles themselves; *Paul* gave over *Hymeneus* and *Alexander* to Satan; so dealt he with *Phygellus*, *Hermogenes* and *Philetus*, as it seemeth. And he cōmaunded *Titus*, that he vvould avoyde an Heretike after one or tvvo admonitions, *Tit. 3. 10.* But after they were gone to *Christ* there arose vp many other worthy lights, which draue away diligently all the fogge of Heresie; amonge whome was *Agrippa Castor*, as *Eusebius* reporteth, *Iustine Martyr*, *Ireneus*, *Tertullian*, *Cyprian*, &c. Who all did stoutly fight for the truth against these counterfaite Apostles. Wherefore as both that Citie, and that first age were in great danger, because of the impudency of those that made shewe of themselves through false Titles, as if they had bene Apostles, so were they no lesse happie through the faithfulnes and painfulnes of such Champions, who would not be deceived by theire vayne shewe, but bringinge the matter to the true touch-stone, made the whole Church to see plainly, that they were most filthy and vile Varletts, who would have bene accounted as most high and principall Masters.

3. And thou hast bene pressed vvith a burden, &c. Hitherto of theire faithfullnes in executinge theire function; Nowe he speakes of theire vertue of patience in overcominge outward euills, which were very many and mightie that came both against the Citie, & also against the whole Christian world The skirmeges of *Paul* against beastes at *Ephesus* are renowned *1. Cor. 15. 32.* & what rest frō troubles could be vnto the Angells that followed him, who should have a graplinge with greeuous wolues, that would not spare the flocke, *Act. 20. 29. 30?* It was therefore the praise of this Angell that he did indure calamitie valiantly, which is declared in a threefold degree, that he bare a burdē, that he laboured vnder the burden, and that yet for all that he was not tired out: as if he should say, there lay indeed vpon thee a great load of calamitie, vnder the burden whereof thou hast groned, yet not with standinge thou hast not cast away thy hart, so as thou shouldest be driuen to with drawe thy necke from the yoake, and to betray the truth. It is a manly courage to indure anguish and paines like a man. Many doe beare the yoake chearefully when they feele but litle trouble, but to goe on constantly amidst the stinges of griefe, this is the part of a stout minde and of an heavenly fortitude. Such was this Angel; So also was the primityue Church. *Nero* and *Domitian* had vehemently afflicted it before *Iohn* wrote these thinges.

> Behold it ſhall come to paſſe, that the Diuell ſhall caſt ſome of you into priſon, &c. verf. 10.

Or that vnto thoſe of *Thyatira*;
> But I ſay vnto you, and to the reſt of Thyatira, verſ. 24.

That I may not ſpeake any thinge of this, that in ſome of the Epiſtles, the exhortation to heare cloſeth vp the whole matter; as in that to thoſe of *Thyatira*, verſ. 29. To thoſe of *Sardis*, Chap. 3. 6. To them of *Philadelphia*, chap. 3. 13. To them of *Laodicea*, verſ. 22. Whence it would followe, that if the Church be reſerued for the concludinge acclamation, ſhee muſt open & ſhut her eares at once; for there followeth nothinge to be heard.

> To him that ouercometh I vvill giue to eate, &c.

The reward in euery one of the Epiſtles is fitted to the tymes, and it is one and the ſame euery where, Ieſus Chriſt alone. For what greater thinge can he giue to the elect? Or what ſhall wee want, if wee enioy him? But accordinge to the diuerſe ſtate of the tymes, he is ſett before vs after a ſundry manner. In this firſt Church; he is a tree of life in the middeſt of the Paradiſe of God. And why? Becauſe that firſt eſtate of the Spouſe, was altogether like to that firſt felicitie of Adam in Paradiſe, of which this was indeed a certayne liuely reſemblance in theſe laſt dayes reſtored againe to the world, after our ſo longe baniſhment from thēce. For there was the ſhadowiſh tree of life in the middeſt of the Garden; Here Ieſus Chriſt borne of a virgin conuerſed with vs in the middeſt of mortall men. There were all kindes of moſt pleaſant plantes for ſight, and moſt profitable for eatinge; Here moſt plentifull ſtore of all gifts that make either for the ſaluation, or the beautifyinge of the Church. There was one riuer, but yet ſo as it diuided it ſelfe forth of the Garden into foure heades; here one voice of truth amōge al the Apoſtles, but yet ſuch as takinge his beginninge from Ieruſalem, was diuided into the foure quarters of the world, fillinge all landes whither ſoeuer it flowed with the waters of peace and ſaluation. What pleaſant thinge could be wantinge there which the hart of a man can

Neither yet is the reward of ouercomers giuen to thoſe that be idle-bellies. The Angel keepes backe theſe alooſe of with his flaminge ſword, leaſt they ſhould at any tyme haue any pull at this Tree.

## The Analysis or Resolution of the Epistle to these of Smyrna.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'T' decorated with scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

*Thus much of the First Epistle. The second is sent to the Smyrneans, but inscribed as the manner is to the Angell, and then he describeth him that sendeth it, that he is the first and the last, then also dead once, but nowe aliue, vers. 8. The Narration partly commendeth them for theire patient enduringe of affliction, which the blasphemous Iewes did cause, vers. 9. Partly armeth them against newe calamitie, both by shewinge the Author kinde end and continuance of it, & also by promisinge them a Crowne, vers. 10. The Conclusion hath both the usuall Acclamation, and also a Freedome from the second death for a reward, vers. 11.*

---

# THE EXPOSITION.

8. To the Angell of the *Smyrneans*. Wee haue said that *Smyrna* was a Colony belonginge to the *Ephesians*, was also so called of *Smyrna* one of the *Amazons*; yet whose notation notwithstandinge of another meaninge the Holy Ghost respecteth. For hence is shee called sweetly-smellinge *Smyrna*, that is, *Mirrhe*, or shee that is farre more delightfull then any pleasant and sweete spices, as it is euident by that, that he reproueth no fault in her, but sheweth her to be most deare to himselfe, howsoeuer there was nothinge more contemptible, and despised of the world at that tyme. Neither must wee thinke, that the second place was rashly giuen to this Church after *Ephesus*. For the Holy Ghost doth not reckon up the Churches by leapes, without order, next after ioyning either *Sardis* or *Philadelphia*, or any one of the rest, but in that order wherein they are layd downe. First of all then he goeth on to the North, on which side about a hundred and twenty fadomes is *Smyrna* placed on the Shore. From whence *Pergamus* bendeth agayne further Northward; from *Pergamus* the rest bend in

This Counter-Church takes her beginninge together with Constantine (vntill which tyme the primitiue Church, the Counter-Church of Ephesus, proceeded(or) extended, ) and is continued vntill Gratian, about the yeare of our Lord 382.accordinge to Eusebius.

*These thinges saith he that is the first and last.* This is a description of him that sendeth the Epistle, and is taken from the 17. and 18. verses of the first Chapter. In which wordes wee shewed that Christ is said to be the Creatour and Gouernour of all thinges, at whose commaundement alone all thinges are made, and that for his owne glory; or rather, that by this honourable testimoniall, that wonderfull conioyninge partly of his Maiestie, partly of his humilitie is magnifyed. Which interpretation indeed is hence confirmed, because the condition of the Smyrneas was like; *Thou art afflicted and poore(saith he)but indeed thou art rich*. What is this els, but to say, though thou art accounted of the world one of the last and lowest, yet in truth thou art first and cheife. He doth withall shewe that changeable estate of the Smyrneans, whereby it came to passe, that the truth which at first flourished amonge them, & was in highest honour, was after despised & troden vnder feete by the wicked Hypocrites; as Christ was in the beginninge God with God of incomprehensible glory, but afterwardes takinge vpon him the shape of a seruant, he emptied himselfe, and became like to men. He taketh titles to himselfe which may agree with the present condition of thinges. Whence it is, that he scattereth sundrie beames of his glory in each Epistle, as the diuerse condition of the Church gaue occasion. Where by he teacheth, that part of his diuine infinite Maiesty is cheifely to be considered of, which may make most for the present purpose. But least they should thinke, that they should lye allwayes in this deiected estate, he addeth the other title, *that was dead(saith he)but leueth.* As if he should say; though, beinge at first cheife of all, I was after that last & lowest, yet I stucke not any longe tyme in this most base estate, but hauinge vanquished death with in 3,dayes, I attayned to my former dignitie, in which I nowe liue for euer. These thinges therefore declare that notable change which befell to Smyrna, & no lesse to that Church whereof it is a Type; where the first truth, which had bene for 300.yeares, founded & spread abroad with much bloud, at length came to be hated of the Christians themselves & had extreme hard measure

*And thy pouerty.* That is, how thou art made a laughinge-stocke,& art cõdemned as beinge beggerly ; but be it that thou art lesse regarded of those hypocrites then any poore Irus, thou art rich tho notwithstandinge in my account; so litle cause hast thou to care for theire wicked scornes and floutes : And to let the Smyrneans passe , the matter is cleare in the Counterpaine. Howe fewe were there of those of the sound beleife, who durst professe the truth ? Howe were these fewe proudly trampled vpon by theire enemyes ? Certaine it is that the Saintes were compelled to run vp & downe hither & thither, to entreate for ayde against theire Tiranny; Neither could they, beinge turned out from all theire owne goodes , by any other meanes maintaine theire life, but by the liberall contribution of other men. Athanasius alone may be in stead of many examples , out of whose often dangers, flight, lurkinge, and despairinge of life which he was driuen to , any one may see how those that were of right iudgment were not able to repell the iniuries of theire enemyes by theire owne power & wealth. Then indeed was the Smyrnean Angel poore, if wee measure his power by humaine ayde.

*But thou art rich.* That is , thou art not left naked and forlorne as mẽ thinke, but through my helpe and in mine account thou art aboundinge with all store of thinges neceſſary. Which wordes doe also together with this intimate, what defence and estimation Christ prouided for his seruantes, euen in spight of the world. Theire authority should increase together with theire affliction, as wee knowe it came to passe in Athanasius, who beinge vexed with all reproachfull wronges in the east, was in great honour in the west. Constantine the sonne , Constans the Brother, Iulius the Bishop of Rome, and the Bishop of Treuirs, who harboured him two yeares, & entertayned him very kindely and liberally, did honour this man as he deserued. Yea and Constantine the great himselfe also, after he had seene into the slauders of the aduerſaries, gaue honourable testimony of his innocency and vertue, and thought good to call him from his banishment.

*And the blas phemy of them.* Hitherto of theire present calamity. Nowe he sheweth how the Authors of those calamityes did arrogate that to themselues, which did not all agree vnto them. But is it a blasphemy for a Iewe to professe himselfe to be a Iewe ? The kinde of punishme̅t is imprisonme̅t, which one thinge doth conteine proscribinges, confiscations of goodes, banishments, slaughters, fiers, rackinges, or whatsoeuer other exquisite torment beside, as the story teacheth. By all theis meanes should the Deuill outragiously labour to drawe men from the truth. But this persecution should endure but for ten dayes. Nowe a day in this booke is taken for a yeare. The no̅ber also of ten doth sometimes signifie properly; it doth oftentimes also signifie an vncertayne nomber by a Synechdoche. I suppose both are here vsed, that the certayne nomber should belonge to the Type, that which is vncertayne to the Counterpaine. As touchinge Smyrna therefore, this persecution fell out in the tyme of Traiane, who beinge a Deuill, that is, an open enemy of the truth, raigned next after this Booke was written, beinge very cruell against the Christians, deliueringe the̅ ouer to Prison & death, to driue them through feare from the profession of Christ. Smyrna could not goe scotfree from a co̅mon calamitie, especially seeinge Bithynia that bordereth vpon it, did ouerflowe wholy with the massacres of Christians, as the Epistle of Pliny the second vnto Traiane speaketh. Whe̅ce wee may see it may after a sort be gathered, how lo̅ge this persecution lasted. For in the fourteenth yeare of Traiane, Pliny relatinge vnto him the multitude of those that were flayne, gaue an occasion to stay that rage, & to obtayne some breathinge. What yeare it bega̅, it is not plainly set downe by the writers of the History. Some thingke that it began as soone as euer he tooke vpon him the Empire; but in the fourth yeare he triumphinge ouer the Dacians & Scythians, seemeth to haue had the beginninge of his raigne so troubled, that he could not be at leasure to afflict the Christians. But it is certayne that he exercised his cruelty for ten yeares at the least; it is likely that the end of that warre was the beginninge of this tormentinge the Christians; Neither is it necessary to thinke, that this affliction should proper to Smyrna alone, but rather that is that vniuersall one, which should come vpon the whole world, of which mention is made in the Epistle to the Church of Philadelphia, ch. 3. 10. As touchinge the countercopyinge Church of Smyrna, Constans & Vale̅s the Emperours, beinge in name Christians, were indeed no lesse terribly cruel against the true Godly me̅ & those of sound beleife, then the heathenish Deuills were of old. In which number, the inferiour instruments of theire wickednes are also reconed. Amonge the Laitye, Syrianus the gouernour, & Sebastian
