Before the matter was handled with braules, raylinges & all kinde of ſlaunders. But after that when as (Conſtantine beinge takẽ away) the Deuill was to come forth vpõ the ſtage, what tragedies were raiſed vp? It was but a light matter to thruſt the holy men into baniſhmẽt, to caſt very many of them into priſon, to flay almoſt an infinite company of them, they played the raginge beaſtes againſt them with all kindes of torments & all reproachfull puniſhmẽts. Some of them were beaten with ſtripes to death, others were brãded in the foreheads, others were tortured & racked; yea the holy women had theire breſts cut of, others breſtes were burnt with a red hot iron, or with egges roſted as hot as could be. Who would thinke, that men that profeſſed Chriſtianity, could inflict any ſuch thinge vpon Chriſtians? It cannot be declared in a fewe wordes, how lamentable thoſe tymes were. But you may ſee more in Socrat. Booke 2. & 4. Theodoret. Booke; 2. & 4. Sozom. Booke 3. 4. 6. Now the time of this Tiranny though it exceeded the nomber here ſpoken of by fourteene yeares, yet it holdeth out to be the nũber of ten dayes, in that manner as wee haue ſaid.

> *Be thou faithfull to the death.* Here he inuiteth them to courage and conſtancy, by ſettinge before them the reward of eternall life. It is a profitable loſſe that is recõpenced with ſo great a gayne. What would not the godly vndergoe, that are ſure to haue ſuch a reward? It is applyed to the tymes, ſupplyinge comfort abundantly, againſt the loſſe of this preſent life; To which end alſo he ſaid before, that he liueth nowe who had bene dead, that they might learne by his example not to feare death, which they might know to be the procurer of eternall felicity.

11. *He that hath an eare.* An vſuall concluſion, admoniſhinge all men to hearken diligently to theſe precepts that are made cõcerninge vertue and valour of minde in induringe afflictions. Before wee were armed againſt inborne ſluggiſhnes, here wee are prouided with munition againſt outward force. The reward which is added in the end is cõmon to the whole Church. That which was before ſpoken of, was properly belonginge to the Angell, the knowledge whereof notwithſtandinge, did very greatly concerne the whole people as was ſaid before. <margin>Sweete smellinge Smyrna.</margin>
aswell as by the Pastours, there is comfort ministred vnto them by name, tendinge to the same purpose with the former, but after a diuerse manner. For there are two thinges, which are wont to kindle our desires to take vpon vs any worthy exployte; hope of reward and litle regardinge of danger. That was set before the Pastours, whose mindes beinge more furnished with knowledge & more noble, is wont to be rather led with reward; This is layd before the people, whome feare of danger principally doth fray from theire duty , & will not suffer them to doe any thinge worthy of commendation. He sheweth therefore that they ought not to feare to lose theire liues if neede were ; For there can be no feare of the second death, by which the body and soule doe perish for euer; accordinge to that of Christ; *Feare not them that kill the body, but cannot kill the soule, rather feare him that can destroy both soule and body in Hell, Mat. 10. 28.* This Hell, is that second death which hee here speaketh of; whereby the whole mã shalbe as much depriued from all comfort in God, as the body is destitute of all ayde cominge from the soule, when it is once seuered from it by the first death. This is that horrible death, which is truely to be feared, from which he deliuereth his seruantes, who hath ouercome death, the freedome from which he here promiseth them, & not from the first death, as which is a lighter matter, then either so mighty a Master of the prizes should giue, or his souldyers should looke for. Now what neede is there to be defended from the first death, which the necessity of nature would bringe at last? but to preuent that necessitie for the truths sake, doth make way to get a more ample crowne. He promiseth therefore that which is best, and doth not delude vs with a vayne shewe of a lesser & lighter good.

# THE EXPOSITION.

**12.** And to the Angell of the Church of Pergamus. Pergamus as farre as the holy Ghost seemeth to ayme at the notation of the word in this place, is as it were the Greeke *Pergamos*, that is the Tower of Troy, as Hesychius doth interprete it. For it is a towred Citie, high and proud, agreeing to that that followeth in the next verse, *vvhere Satans Throne is*. It is distant from Smyrna toward the North about 540. furlonges, further of from it, then Smyrna from Ephesus, in the vttermost bounde of the Northerne latitude, as touchinge these 7. Cities. There was a great diminition of the light made in the declininge of Smyrna vnder Constantine, Constantius, and Valens; euen in that first and least turninge aside from Ephesus, where was the primitiue purity; but nowe there is a passinge from Smyrna to Pergamus, into the vttermost darknes, the Church beinge nowe to suffer a more greiuous Eclipse of the light, then euer before this tyme since Christes birth. 13. I knovve thy vvorkes. Here is a Narration of the bitter & more commendable estate of this Church , which is amplifyed two wayes; that it had not denied the faith, though it dwelt in such a place , as where Satan had his Throne ; and then that it had not denied the faith in those dayes , in which Antipas was slayne. Nowe Pergamus was the Mother-Citie,belonginge to the Empire of Rome in Asia. For it is likely,when that Country was made a Prouince,after that Attalus Philometor, the Kinge of Pergamus , had by name made the people of Rome his heire, that the Proconsul sent to gouerne it, placed the seate of his Iurisdiction in that place. *To him that ouercometh I vvill giue to eate.* The reward is threefold, hidden Manna , a vvhite stone and an vnknowne name vvritten on it. All which thinges agree to the tymes meruailously. Touchinge Manna,it was meate, which God gaue the people abundantly in the wildernes, when as there was no possibilitie to come by any other. Nowe in this condition of the Church of Pergamus, when that sinke of filthines which came from the Nicolaitans and the successours of Balaam, that is, the Romish Idolaters, ouerspred all,the Church was lurkinge as it were in a wast, wofull and hideous wildernes, whither wee shall see the woman betakinge herselfe, when shee fled from the Dragon, Chap. 12.But Christ nourisheth her with the meate of the wildernes, as of old he fed the children of Israel.For he will not be wantinge to his seruants in most distressfull tymes , but will abundantly poure out the ioy of his Spirit , whereby they may not onely be preserued aliue, but may also reioyce exceedingly,as hauing very great cause and matter of ioy. This Manna that is the same meate,with that fruite of the Tree of life in Paradise , as wee obserued on the 7. vers. but here is a diuerse manner of conferring it. There in a most chast , pure and flourishinge Church it was the fruite of the Tree in the middest of the Paradise of God ; here whē the truth was spurned at,contemned, troden vnder feete,yea & altogether overwhelmed with darknes , it is Manna,the foode of the wildernes.This meate should not be seene of the world , who should thinke that they which had fled into this wildernes,were killed with hunger,because of the scarcity of vitailes,as the ægiptians thought that the Israelites would straight haue perished in this regard in the wildernes, but God sustayned his people extraordinarily with this bread of Angels,yet this is the difference betweene the Manna of the people of Pergamus , and this of the Israelites ;

> And I vvill giue him a vvhite stone.

The second reward. Aretas telleth vs that such a kinde of stone was wont to be giuen to wrestlers , that stroue in the Theaters. But it is not likely that that custome is here aymed at. For that was giuen onely when the battaile was at the onset, not when it was ended , and the conquerour was to be rewarded. In the games of Olympus , least the Champions should runne together at randonne , they drew forth stones out of a siluer Pott , they which light vpon those that were marked with one and the same letter ( for there were two of them on which were grauen the same Characters ) those the Iudges put together to be combatants. Neither was there any other vse of these stones in games , as I suppose. In Iudgments they were vsed for a nother purpose , namely , to giue suffrage by voices, wherein they were of sundry sortes, accordinge to the diuerse customes of people ; many tymes they were hollowe and boared through, wherewith they gaue sentence of condemnation; some times they were full and solid, wherewith they absolued. There was a tyme also when they were distinguished by theire colour onely, the blacke condemninge, the white contrary absoluinge. So saith Vlpian vpon Demosth.

Against Timocrates. Stones for suffrages (*saith he*) *vvere* sometimes peir-

great a company of the wicked, should be hated of all men, and con-
demned of schisme, errour, heresie and I knowe not of what wicked-

they should be cried downe for giltie vpon earth by all mens voices,
yet they should hereby knowe most certainly, that they are adiudged
for giltlesse before the heauēly Tribunall of God. Howe great a com-
fort is this against the reuilinges and reproaches of the world? Be of
good cheare, *If God iustifie, vvho shall condemne?* *Rom. 8. 33.*

But it is not likely that that custome is here aymed at. For that was giuen onely when the battaile was at the onset, not when it was ended, and the conquerour was to be rewarded. In the games of *Olympus*, least the Champions should runne together at randonne, they drew forth stones out of a siluer Pott, they which light vpon those that were marked with one and the same letter (for there were two of them on which were grauen the same Characters) those the Iudges put together to be combatants. Neither was there any other vse of these stones in games, as I suppose. In Iudgments they were vsed for a nother purpose, namely, to giue suffrage by voices, wherein they were of sundry fortes, accordinge to the diuerse customes of people; many tymes they were hollowe and boared through, wherewith they gaue sentence of condemnation; some times they were full and solid, wherewith they absolued. There was a tyme also when they were distinguished by theire colour onely, the blacke condemninge, the white contrary absoluinge. So saith *Ulpian* vpon *Demosth.*

And in that stone a nevve name vvritten. The third reward. He persisteth in the same custome of giuinge iudgmẽts, in some of vvhich stones theire names vvere vvritten and ingrauen, vvho came into iudgment. This name is also vnknovvne to all men, but to him that hath receiued it; For *the vvorld hath not knovvne vs*, 1. Ioh. 3. 1. 2. Therefore theire testimony is nothinge vvorth, vvhither it be vvith vs, or against vs. But behold besides

### The Analysis or Resolution of the Epistle to them of Thyatira.

<margin>Growing Thyatira.</margin>
*<image-desc>Ornate decorative drop cap 'S' with floral patterns and scrollwork.</image-desc>Such is the Epistle to the Church of Pergamus. This to them of Thyatira is inscribed also to the Angel, as also it describeth him that sendeth it to be the Sonne of God, with fiery eyes and feete-like to fine brasse, vers. 18. The Narration commendeth the increaſe of pietie, vers. 19. But it reproueth them for ſufferinge Iezabel, whose wickednes he describeth, first by the kinde of sinne, vers. 20. Then by her obstinacy, vers. 21. And her punishment, which is notable, both for the nature of the punishment it ſelfe, which is diverse, accordinge to the diverse condition of the offendors, for Iezabel her ſelfe is punished by her Bedde, they that commit adultery with her by great affliction, vers. 22. And her ſonnes with death: lastly by the honourable testimony of all the Churches, witneſsinge that Gods iudgment against her is iust and rigorous, vers. 23. To which at length he ioyneth a counsaile against this wickednes, unto which he intimateth a way in mercy, vers. 24, Requiringe constancy of the Church, vers. 25. And perſwadinge her unto it with a reward of power ouer the Nations, vers. 26. 27. And the morninge Starre, vers. 28. The Conclusion, vers. 29.*

from Pergamus, towards the South, but farther vpon the East, beinge

The Counterpaine of it, is the tyme from the yeare 1300. vntill the
yeare 1520. (or) 520. aboue 1000.

These thinges saith the Sonne of God. Nowe Christ maketh himselfe

clearely appeare out of the Counterpayne. As touchinge the name it
now first of all offereth it selfe vnto vs, beinge not expressed before
amōge the thinges that were either seene or heard, in the first Chapt.
There was mētiō made of the Sonne of man, vers. 13. but the whole
vision did sufficiently declare him to be the Sonne of God. It seemeth
to be named here, as if nowe he were returninge out of Egipt. He was
in exile nowe a lōge tyme, but in the renuinge of the Church he retur-

a more familiar fort to his seruantes, from whome he seemed to haue

such as in the brightnes wherof hee sheweth himselfe to the Thyatiri-

light of the truth should scatter the darknes, as it doth flee away at the
light of the fire; which came to passe at the yeare 1300. Whē as a newe
troupe of Doctours rose vp by the iudgmēts of euery one whereof the

Who this *Iezabell* in this Citie of *Thyatira* should be, the auncient Hystorie doth not teach vs. By this place wee vnderstand there was some Princesse,a woman of great place and account, who was an Idolatresse, an Inchauntresse and a whore,like to that other *Iezabell* of old recorded in Scripture, the wife of *Ahab*; who yet was herein more able and apt to worke mischeife then this *Iezabell* here, because shee shewed herselfe to be an open aduersary to the truth; this here would be counted a Prophetesse. 22. *Behold I vvill cast her vpon a bedd.* Here is the punishment of
Iezabell. A Bed is sometimes for deliciousnes and wantonnes , as in
the Prophet; *They stretch themselues vpon theire yuorie Bedds, Amos 6.4.*
Sometimes it is for diseases and sicknes, as the Lord *shall strengthen him*
*vpon the Bed of his sicknes , thou shalt turne his Bed in his disease, Ps.41.4.*
Which of these doth it serue to expresse in this place ? Not delicious-
nes , though that be a greious punishment, to be giuen over vnto an
occasion of sinninge, but languishinge , as it appeareth by that which
followeth presently after , where, *those that commit adultery vvith her,*

yeare 1300. wastinge away more and more like one that is sicke of a
consumption. For from that tyme, her face began to waxe wan, her
stomach grewe weaker , her life was painfull and her flesh was con-
fumed away ; yea so farre hath this her weakness preuayled , that if a
man behold her as shee is nowe at this day, he will say that shee is but
a drie carrion in regard of her former good likinge. O infinite wise-
dome of God ! Which euen with one word hath drawen vs such a
liuely portraiture of so longe a tyme. Could the languishinge de-
struction of Rome be noted out vnto vs more elegantly or signifi-
cantly ? God would not haue her perish with a swift disease, least his
people should forget it, but rather that shee should rot by peecemeale
with a consuminge Ptisicke , both that this lingringe punishment,
should by the longe lastinge of it, be an image of her eternall punish-
ment , as also that shee might be a spectacle to many ages, which had
drawne many ages into errour. Certainly vnles Rome feele and ack-
nowledge this Ptisicke of hers, her disease is not a consumption onely,
but a Phrensie also.

*And those that commit adulterie vvith her.* This is the punishment of the Adulterers, which are the Kinges and Princes of the earth, of whome afterwards; Chap. 17. 2. These men, vnles they make a defection from this Harlott, shall drinke of a cup of most greiuous affliction. Haue not the Kinges allready by vvofull experience learned this point, vvhile the most cruel Turke oppreffeth the Emperour on the one side, and the Spanish Kinge on the other? Call to minde the Ages past, from the yeare 1300. vvherein Iezabell began to languish; vvho can expreffe those huge euills, vvhich the Transiluanian, the Polonian, the Boemian, the hovvse of Austria, the Emperour, the Venetian, the Spaniard, suffered at the hands of the most outragious Turke? VVhy doe ye not perceiue that your adultery committed vvith this Harlott hath procured yow al these euills? But this calamitie of Iezabell vvhile shee keepeth her ficke Bedde, is nothinge to that, vvhich, vnles yow vvill renounce, and that quickly, all vvicked societie and intercourse vvith her, yow shall suffer at last, vvhen shee shall be givinge vp her last ghost, as vvee shall shevve aftervvardes. ## *The Analysis or Resolution of the Chapter , as*
### *also of the Epistle to them of Sardis.*

<image-desc>Decorative ornamental woodcut initial letter 'T' featuring scrolling floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>
There be three Epistles of this Chapter. One to them of *Sardis*; another to them of *Philadelphia* ; the last to them of *Laodicea*. Neither are they vvithout cause inclosed in one Chapter , seeinge they haue a condition somevvhat differinge from the former. For the former, as they vvere of a further distance one from the other, so they had Counterpaines of a larger distance of time. But these Churches are both disioyned vvith lesser distances of place one from the other , and vvee shall finde also the counter-ansvvearinge Churches to each of them , to be more nearely ioyned together in space of tyme.

*The Epistle to the Church of Sardis, after the Inscription to the Angell, describeth him that sendeth it, by seauen Spirits, and seauen Starres, after that he adioyneth the Narration: Which reproueth him, because he bearinge the name, and makinge the shewe of one that liueth spiritually, is in truth dead notwithstandinge, vers. 1. But yet it doth with all teach the remedie: Which is double, the first consistinge in confirminge of the residue that are readie to die. For it should come to passe that many should die by the iust iudgment of God, who would by that meanes auenge himselfe of there carelesnes of the right and due reformation, vers. 2. The second consistinge in remembringe the thinges which he had receiued, and repentinge. The which admonition, least it should through there negligence be of lesse strength, hath an edge sett upon it by a threatninge of his unexpected cominge, vers. 3. Then after this, he commendeth some of them for there pure garments: Which praise contayneth also a reward both proper to them, as also common to all Conquerours, vers. 4. and 5. Which is threefold, white clothinge, a name enduringe in the Booke of life, and a confessinge of him before his Father and his Angells. All which thinges are shutt up with there wonted Acclamation.*

# THE EXPOSITION.

1. Nowe to the Angell of the Church vvhich is at Sardis. Sardis is the second of the newe-springinge Churches tēdinge further Southward, and waxinge to some growth and strength, by meanes of the more ample light of the Truth. The Counterpaine is the first reformed Church, begun by the speciall prouidence of godly Martin Luther at Wittenberge, which is a Towne of Saxony by the Riuer Albis, in the yeare 1517. At what tyme that holy man did withstand the Romish Publicanes, the gatherers and farmers of the Popes reuenewes, that made a sale to the people of Pardons for there sinnes. The truth began to be reuiued vnder the Thyatirian state; but no reformation followed of it; this was first of all taken in hand at this tyme I speake of. For which cause indeed, wee shall finde no mention made either

It is a ſhamefull thinge to make merchandize of Gods word,by ſpeakinge rather to fitt the pleaſure of men,then to ſett forth the truth. Therefore layinge aſide all both hatred and fauour of men,if ſo be that which is ſpoken ſhall appeare vnto vs to agree with the truth,let vs rather tremble at the threats of the moſt iuſt God,thẽ be angrie with him, who hath endeauoured with all his power to diſcloſe vnto vs the truth that is hidden and hard to be knowne, that to the ende we ſhould not bee ſurpriſed at vnawares with ſuch euills as hange ouer our heades. The which requeſt I hope I ſhall eaſily obtayne of all the godly,ſo farre of will they be from pickinge quarrells at & againſt my paines. Vpon which hope, I will goe forward, God aſsiſtinge me, to that I haue in hand.

Because Sardis should by experience finde protection frō Christ in defendinge the Pastours thereof, like to that which he shewed in Ephesus, he doth therefore, and not from the purpose, vse that same similitude, where there is so great likenes of the thinges. But the story is silent in shewinge how this was verified vnto Sardis; which yet is most cleare in the Counterpaine thereof. For he that giueth his Spirit plenteously to whome, & when he will, poured out vpon these selfe same tymes, such rich store of all giftes, as he did neuer elswhere in these last dayes. Longe before this, for a longe tyme, good learninge lay as a thinge nought set by, as the which, by meanes of the barbarousnes of the Schoolmen, was chased away for many ages, till at last, after the wonderfull art of printinge was found out (the which artificious deuise flowed from this same springe of the Spirit) many excellent wittes were raised vp for the searchinge out of the truth. *I knowe thy vvorkes,that thou art said to liue,but thou art dead.* Heare is the reprehension, because of that counterfeite life of God whereof the Angel maketh a shewe,beinge voyde of all truth, whẽce it may bee called hypocriticall Sardis. The force of which notation appeareth by the very name of it. For *Sardis* is like *Zardianos Legos, Sardiã laughter* which in the Greeke Prouerbe, is a laughter that is rather in shewe then in truth; so called from the Citie *Sardi*, euen as *Sardonius risus* is called of the Isle *Sardonia*, as *Erasmus* noteth out of *Plutarch*. For that kinde of herbe called *Ramunculus*, by eatinge whereof the minde is distracted, may aswell growe in *Lydia*, as in the Isle. This Church was accounted as if it were aliue,but it was dead; like to this laughter, which fayneth laughter, beinge in the meane tyme full of deadly greife. And hence it may nowe appeare how *Sardis* may be opposed to *Smyrna*. That Church, in regard of outward matters, was in very great affliction, so as it was held for dead almost of all men, yet did it meane time liue the true life,and was most acceptable vnto God himselfe: This, without, in the opinion of men liueth, and flourisheth in a goodly manner, yet with in, death raigneth, true pietie beinge banished out of it; whence this second payre of contraries is made,as wee obserued in the generall resoluinge of the seauen Epistles into there parts. But wherein lay this counterfeitinge? As touchinge the Citie of *Sardis*, wee haue litle to see or shew for it out of the History. There flourished not longe after, that famous *Melito*, greatly praised by *Eusebius*, Booke; 4. Chap. 26. But hence it appeareth, that the matter was come to that passe when *Iohn* wrote, that though the Angell seemed to himselfe,and others perhaps, to bee notably furnished with all thinges requisite to saluation, yet he wanted many necessaries, and abounded in the contrary euills. Wee knowe that those that be aliue without,may be dead either through ignorance or corruptnes of doctrine, or through neglect and carelesnes of godly dueties, as *Christ* calleth them dead, who were voyd of faith and knowledge of saluation, *Ioh.* 5. 25. And the Apostle calleth the lasciuious woman,liue-dead,howsoeuer shee had giuen her name to *Christ*; 1.*Tim.* 5. 6. For which reason also vvorkes are said to be dead,*Hebr.* 6. 2. As the which declare them to be truely dead, who giue themselues to the study of such vvorkes. It may be that this Angell of *Sardis*, partly, by meanes of his neglect of pietie,partly,through his corrupt teachinge, fell into

Wee haue said that the Counterpaine, by reason of the order and consequence of matters, is the first reformed Church springing vp in Saxony, when Luther begā to teach. For the Church of Thyatira bare the blame of suffering the Romish Iezabell: This Church first of all, as it were another Iehu, tooke order for the castinge downe of this painted and shameles Harlott out of the windowe, so as it dashed her braynes out against the earth. Whence it is, that shee is not reproued, no not in one word, for this fault. This Church therefore hath a name that shee liueth, because of the truth that was restored in her; which shee brought light vnto in a meruailous manner; and not a little, for her notable courage, whereby shee broke and trode vnder foote the Romish Tyrāny, shakinge it of not onely from her owne shoulders, but exposinge it also to the derision of the whole world: Shee is dead tho, as beinge infected dangerously with no small errours and corruptions, aboue and before the rest, that Consubstantiatinge of the Body of Christ in the Sacrament of the Supper, vpon the which, many other absurdities doe follow, which creepe like a leprosie, and doe vtterly take away the life of those members that in themselues were aliue. Yet are not these thinges to be vnderstoode of the seuerall men, one by one; but of the whole gouernment & forme of the Church, which was to be seene of the world, a draught whereof the holy Ghost doth pourtray vnto vs; which is also to be obserued in the rest of the Churches.

2. *Be thou vigilant and strenghten the thinges that are ready to dye.* Heare is the first remedy of diligence in confirminge the rest; who vnles there were care had of them in tyme, were readie to rush into deadly destruction. By which wordes wee are taught, that if the Teachers would bestowe theire paines faithfully and diligently in purging thoroughly the whole Doctrine, and Pietie, they might take from many an occasiō of fallinge, but if they should carry themselues more negligently in this matter, the ruine of many would be lamentable. In the Counterpaine the matter is so cleare, that a man might doe better to prosecute it with teares then with wordes. For how many excellēt men hath that monster of Ubiquitie tumbled headlonge into death? The seedes whereof indeed Luther sowed in the yeare 1526, and 28. in his disputation against Zwinglius & Oecolampadius.

Yea and heare I finde wantinge thy faithfullnes and diligence (oh holy Philippe)(that thou didst not stabbe this foule & mischeiuous errour at the hart as it deserued. Thou thoughtest perhaps it was to be hādled more nicely & gently, partly for the loue thou barest to thy frend, partly because thou hadst a conceite, that it might more easily be buried with silence, then with any sharpe inuectiue of bitter wordes. But errours, which are not confuted and reproued as false, seeme to be approued, & so much the more doth there authority growe, by how much more mildly and moderately they are dealt wilth. For they are Gangrenes, which the more gentle the remedies be, the more doe they stirre and increase them, rather then cure them. Therefore while neither of yow watcheth and doth his duetie, many dye; and those how many & what worthy men are they I pray yow? Truly an infinite nomber of all rankes, whose standar-bearers were Iohn Brentius, Iacobus Andreæ, Selneccerus, Kirchnerus, Chemnitius, & others like to these, who haue so increased that monster of Vbiquity, that was horrible ynough by it selfe, with such an heape of notorious errours, that there hath bene scarce at any tyme a more hideous and pernicious thinge extant. Lamentable truely was the case of those worthy men, whose labour had bene once very doughtie, and no lesse profitable against the common enemyes: And what a Crowne of victory had they gotten at last, if they had stoode out to the ende in the same warfare, & had not like to maddish Elephants, turned themselues from there enemyes to batter downe there frendes? But it is my part to interpret, not to make complaintes. Therefore I surcease these. This death did not onely come vpon some particuler men, but also vpon many whole Cities and Provinces, as may be manifest out of the Booke of Concord set forth in the yeare 1580; Which doth not so forcibly stablish this errour by the consent of many, as it doth serue to testifie this miserable calamitie of the brethren. For I haue not found thy vvorkes perfect. These wordes contayne a reason why so many dyed. The Church of Sardis as it seemeth , did not admit of the whole entier truth,but retayned much of the heathenish superstition, The Church of Germany cast away many of the popish errours , yet as touchinge the Sacrament of the Supper, shee stucke as it were in the mire of the corporall presence; not like to Rome,dreaminge that the substance of the bread and wine was changed into the true and reall flesh and bloud, but no lesse strangely from the truth, holdinge that the true flesh and bloud was ioyned with the outward signes, and was present here vpon the earth. This leuen Luther neuer cast out , but contended eagerly with Zuinglius and Oecolampadius to defend and retain it still. Suffer the neglect of reformation herein to goe vnpunished. A tast of which punishment to come,was then layde vpon them, when Luther was compelled for the patronage of his bad cause to flee to the ubiquitie and to maintaine many other thinges about the humanitie of Christ, which were dissonãt from the truth.But by reason of the heate of contention he could lesse giue his minde to consider of thinges , that so he might haue vnderstoode by those beginninges and lighter preambles, that God was angrie with him. How came it, that he did not take heed to keepe himselfe from that errour , which drewe with it such a cõpany of wicked opinions ? Why feared he not what might happen to others , hauinge tryed in his owne experience , to what freightes he was driuen in disputation? But his eyes were holden , that he could not foresee and turne away this so greuous a iudgment that vvas to come vpon those that were of his side. Wherefore there workes were not full , because there was no full reformation made, but one errour was onely changed into another no lesse dangerous. Now God is wont to reuenge sinne with sinne.

What godly man doth not conceiue great greife, recountinge with himselfe the destruction of so many of the brethren by meanes of that pernicious errour, so lōge a disagreinge of mindes, such bitter cōbates both by word & weapon? But yet he must needes be more vexed, as oft as he considereth that there is as yet no ende of these euills, but that somethinge more greiuous then any thinge that hath yet befalne them, doth presse sore vpon them, vnles they doe quickly repent. I could not but admonish the brethren concerninge the danger, least those whome I doe in the bowells of Iesus Christ desire to be in great honour & happines, I should heare to be wretched & plagued of God, to my great harts greife. And I hope, how soeuer my iudgment may bee troublesome, yet my good will shall not bee vnacceptable.

But *if thou shalt not vvatch, I vvill come.* The dāger which hee threatneth is his cominge as a Theife, & that at a tyme not looked for. Hee doth not expresly name what kinde of euill shall come vpon them, though it may in some fort bee gathered out of the similitude, which is often vsed in the Scriptures, to signifie the vnlooked for inuasion of an enemy, but seeinge the next wordes aime at this *neither shalt thou vnderstand vvhat houre I vvill come against thee:* he doth perhaps meane here some other thinge, that is, a certaine force and violence, such as Theeues vse in robbinge of houses. Who doe oftentimes not onely robbe the owners of there goodes; but they doe defloure there virgins, & commit villany with there wiues, & compell them with tortures to confesse where there mony is hidden; which hauinge once gotten they flay all without difference of sexe or age, that there villany be not bewrayed. Christ therefore seemeth here to threaten the like mad crueltie of some sauage enemy. Cōcerninge whose cominge wee must not determine by the iudgment of sense, seeinge it shall not be knowne what houre he shall come. Neither ought wee much to labour, to search out who this enemy should bee. The holy Ghost who fetteth it downe that his cominge shalbe suddaine, would not haue him to bee knowne who hee should bee. It may be it is the Turke, to whome the raines shalbe loosed, till God by his meanes, shal haue punished those that are to be chastened. But whither it be this or some

*And therefore they shall vvalke vvith me in vvhite.* That is, garments. These are the same garments with the former, but of a litle diuerse condition. For those were of profession whereby they did appeare vnto others to be stout soldiers of Iesus Christ ; These are of glory triumph and ioy, which they shall both enioy with in themselves from the sense of Gods loue shed abroad into there hartes , as also which they shall conceiue out of the open and common speeches of others, who shall magnifye God for there cause for giuinge them such courage and victory. The white and pure gowne is in great vfe and request at solemnities , both amonge the Heathen, and with the people of God : Whence it is that the wise man alludinge to this custome , saith : *Let thy garments be vvhite at all tymes, Eccles. 9. 8.* But aboue all I thinke that that place of Marke is respected heare , where was a certayne footesteppe of this heauenly glory ; He appeared in a *shininge garment very vvhite, such, as no fuller vpon earth can vvhiten like vnto it, Chap. 3.* At the sight whereof, Peter beinge ouerwhelmed with vnmeasurable ioy, thought vpon this one thinge alone howe he might enioy it for euer. So that this reward of the Saints shalbe most ample, as wherein they shall so rest themselves with there whole hartes, that they shall desire no greater thinge in this world. Yea if any mā should aske the brethren themselves whose these garments are , I doubt not but they would answere, that this ioy which they haue by Christ in holdinge fast the truth, is greater & of more account with them, then that they would exchange it for all the delights of this present life. Certainly great is there glory with all the godly, which with our whole harts wee pray may be perpetuall vnto them.

*For they are vvorthy.* The Popish sort doe picke much glee and gladsome matter out of this word *vvorthy* ; as if it were a worthy Patrone of there <term>Merit of Condignitie</term>. But let them consider this, that this merit is giuen to the garment, not to the Body; that is, to the imputation of Christs righteousnes , which wee put on as it were a garment , not to our owne inherent sanctitie. For it cannot be of more account, not to defile the garment , then the garment it selfe is. And whereas there are diuerse significations of garments , as wee haue taught, the worthines ariseth not, either from the profession, or from the care to doe good workes , whereby wee seeme to be holy vnto others, nor yet from the ioy of the Spirit, which wee feele with in our selves, but from thence onely that the father counteth vs for iust when

Booke, commaunded of old, that the Genealogies of euery one of the
Tribes should bee diligently preserved amonge the people of Israel.
Whither also belōged that lawe for raisinge vp seede to the deceased,
least his name should be cutt of from his people, Deut. 25. 6. For
which cauſe alſo the Psalmist curseth certayne Reprobates, that held
a place in the Church, as if they had bene true Citizens, wishinge, that
God would at least seperate them from the Assembly of the Saints, &
that he would openly shewe them to be meere hypocrites, Ps. 69. 29.
Wherefore all those are rased out of the Booke of life, which forsake
the societie of the holy Church, whither it be by errour and heresie,
or els by some wicked fact, or for any other cause; not that they are
therefore putt out of the booke of election, but that they doe this way
make it manifest, that they were neuer billed in that Booke, as Iohn
saith: *They went out from vs, but they were not of vs*, 1. Iohn. 2. 19. Nowe
the other Booke of Election is neuer blemished with any blottinge &
dashinge out, but the names that are once written into it, remayne
constantly in it without any crossinge out. And yet these Bookes are
not so open, that they can be read promiscuously of all men, but it is
declared by the Spirit to euery one seuerally, that is found in this Regi-
ster, in what place and number hee is.

*But I will professe his name.* The third reward is that he will professe
his name. The which declareth not onely the declininge of many,
but also that there shalbe violence offered by them to make others
decline by force; so that there would be neede of the great power of
the Spirit, that so a man might not depart from the truth, beinge put
cleane out of hart with the iniuryes and threats of the aduersaries. For
this confessinge of there names before his Father, is for the comfort
of those that professe Christ & his truth freely & without dismayinge
before men. Thus Christ sendinge out his Apostles on embaſſage to
preach, armeth them against the feare of affliction, Mat. 10. 32. And
who knoweth not how farre the hatred of those that call themselves
Lutherans, proceeded in inhumanitie against the professours of the
truth? Anno 1580. There was thrust vpō the Ministers of the Church,

des , Anno 91. When Christianus the Duke of Saxony was dead , Paulus Creilius the Chauncellour, beinge suspected for Caluinisme,as they call it,was cast into prison. Vrbanus Pierius , the Professour of Wittemberge was led away captiue into prison. Gundermannus was committed at Lypsia. The next yeare a newe visitation was made,and it went scouringe through all Saxony ; They that would not subscribe to the Articles were put out of there functions. What should I speake of the vproare at Lypsia the yeare after that, the vniuersitie men flockinge together from all places to breake downe the houses of the Caluinists ? Or of that sauage crueltie of those of Dresda , exercised vpon the dead corpse of Iacobus Lossius , whome they would not suffer to bee buryed , no not among malefactours, because when hee was aliue he was well affected to the more sincere truth ? These fewe thinges I here relate against my will, & I should be ashamed to make mention of them , but that the brethren haue not bene ashamed to commit such thinges. But how much better is it for you to heare of these thinges from your frendes,then from your enemyes ? These doe as much as they can with wordes exaggerate your sinfull facts , to your perpetuall ignominy ,yea to the shame of the whole Religion ; I onely shewe the agreeinge of the Prophecy, that ye seeinge what reckoninge God maketh of you,might seriously thinke of reforminge your errours,and makinge peace with your brethren. God graunt ye may take such a course, as that the consentinge together in one truth, may turne away from your shoulders that iudgment which otherwise hangeth ouer you,& will come most certainly vpon you.In the meane tyme,if I shall doe no good with you (which iudgment of me and my wordes I pray God may bee farre from you) yet it will doe me good to admonish the brethren to be of a good cheare and courage , who for the truths sake doe endure many troubles and miseries amonge you. Christ will not be ashamed of them before his Father , if they will constantly continue in there profession. Doe not therefore feare the sterne and stately lookes of men , but trustinge vpon this hope, bringe forth that into the open light, and the eyes of men,which you haue hitherto maintayned and loued in the darke for feare.

## The Analysis or Resolution of the Epistle to Philadelphia.

<margin>Godly Philadelphia.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'S' featuring scrolling floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>
*So much for the Epistle to the Sardians. This unto the Philadelphians, is inscribed also to the Angell. He that sendeth it is remarkeable for holines, truth, and the key of David, Which he carryeth not idely but he opens and shutteth with it, as beinge part of the highest soueraignetie that he hath, vers. 7. The Narration doth first tell his good thinges, both present, that of the open dore, which is illustrated by the cause of it, his litle strength, & constant keepinge of his word, vers. 8. As also that is to come, both that of subduinge his enemyes, vers. 9. And that of affordinge aide unto him in a common triall, the reason whereof is rendred to bee his constancy in the profession of the Gospell, vers. 10. And then hee inflameth him with desire of preservinge that good, because his cominge is swift, and there may bee danger, of havinge there Crowne taken from them, vers. 11. Then there is a very great reward, when as he shalbe made a Pillar, and shall haue written upon it both the name of God and of the newe Ierusalem, and also the newe name of a Sonne, vers. 12. To all which thinges the common Conclusion is added in the end, vers. 13.*

---

## THE EXPOSITION.

*7. And to the Angell of the Church of Philadelphia.* Wee shewed on the 11. vers. of the 1. Chapter, that Philadelphia was situated in a dangerous place, and was therefore lesse populous, the Citizens for feare of the often earthquakes in the Citie, dwellinge scatteringly in the feildes and villages, yet it hath a sweete name, and such as doth alone contayne in it selfe all vertues. These thinges saith he that is holy, and true, that hath &c. These wordes contayne a description of him that sendeth the Epistle, whose two first properties are taken out of the nature of the sonne of God, which yet are not expressely mentioned in the vision of the first Chapter. They doe very greatly serue to declare unto vs the government of this Church. 

<margin>Godly Philadelphia.</margin>
Concerninge the Citie of Philadelphia, wee haue no further notice in the stories, saue that there remayned there in the age followinge a famous company of the faithfull, whose governour was Danias, as wee gather out of the Epistles of Ignatius. In the Counterpayne, the divine power of Christ shineth forth in speciall manner, sanctifyinge the Church by kindlinge in it a carefull loue of pietie, and by makinge it fitt and chearefull in Christ Iesus unto every good worke. Loth would I be to provoake any man to envie, or to greiue him with my wordes, yet this I must say, there is no place where the doctrine soundeth out more purely, the worship of God is exercised more uncorruptly: where more faithfull diligence of the Pastours doth flourish, or more free and willinge obedience is given by the people, nor yet where there is greater reverencinge of the whole Religion amonge all orders. But this holines seemeth cheifely to respect theire manners; For which purpose, the notable testimony of Iohn Bodin speakinge of the men of Geneva, is not to be passed by. *Amonge whome (saith he) that is praiseworthy if any thinge amonge any people and that which maketh, theire common wealth to flourish, if not with Wealth and greatnes of commaund and dominion, yet indeed with vertues and godlines, namely, that censure of theire Pastours, (whome he calleth Pontifices, Popes, or prelaticall Bishops) then which nothinge can be devised of a more divine and great force to bridle the lustes of men, and to restraine such vices as cannot be any wayes reformed by lawes and iudgments of men. Yet this bridlinge is directed by the rule of Christ, first secretly and in frendly manner, then a litle more sharpely, then unles you obey, there followeth a graue and effectuall for bidding to come at the holy things, after that prohibition followeth a punishment inflicted by the Magistrates. So it cometh to passe , that those thinges which lawes doe not punish and by punishinge keepe in elswhere, are there kept in without force and tumult. Therefore there is no whore hauntinge, no dronkennes no dancinge, no beggar, no idle person to be found in that Citie.*

These thinges saith he in his Booke of the Methode of Histor. Chap. 6. Worthily is that Sanctifyer of this Church to be magnified, who hath wrought in the Saints to will and to doe such thinges of his owne free pleasure. The same care also, with the like fruite of it is in the rest, accordinge to that stinted portion of grace which Christ vouchsafeth to euery one of these reformed companyes. And his truth is no lesse notable, both as he is a Prophet in teachinge and as he is a free Couenantour in promisinge. Wee shall see that this double truth in the Church followinge is distinguished by the proper wordes for each of them, both of which this word *True*, seemeth here to contayne, seeinge it is put absolutely and by it selfe. Nowe for the truth of doctrine, where is it more chast and entier, euen in the whole world? Popery is here wholy cut in the throate; Anabaptists, Antitrinitarians, Arians and such like monsters raised vp from Hell againe, partly in Germany partly in Transiluania, haue neuer met with more fierce aduersaries; yea what hath it not done to try if it could plucke vp these errours out of the Churches of Germany? Neither doth it onely keepe the doctrine of saluation free from corruption, but it doth also both deliuer in writinge and exercise in practise, that sincere manner of gouernment, whereby men are made partakers of saluation. Certainly the whole will of God is communicated vnto these holy ones of his, so that Christ may iustly take to himselfe this title of truth to commend himselfe withall in gouerninge this Church. He did also shewe himselfe in this Church to be aboundantly faithfull in makinge good that his word of promise whereby he hath bound himselfe to preserue all those safe and found that seeke him with a sound and vpright hart. What mischeife is it that the Frenchman, Spaniard, Sauoy, and Pope haue not plotted and indeuoured to worke for the rootinge out of the men of Geneua, a small people, inuironed from all places with enemyes, and barred out from all aide of neighbour-Cities and Churces? Yet it flourisheth to this day (blessed be God for it) and shall flourish hereafter, maugre the enuie and malice of all aduersaries, though they burst againe with it so longe as it shall obserue constantly these holy ordinances of God. But he is true and trustie of his word, that hath promised to giue this honour to his Saints, that they should binde Kinges in chaynes, & theire honourable men in fetters of Iron. *Pfal. 149.8.9.* And to run through every thinge, it is thy protection alone most high and mightie God, who art constant in thy promisse, whereby they could be safe, as who are persecuted with deadly hatred by almost infinite enemyes, and to whome many of theire fayned frendes cannot wish very well for very enuie they beare against them.

He that hath the key of David. The third propertie of Christ belongeth also to the same goverment of his. Christ openeth and shutteth the way to the kingdome of heaven to whome it pleaseth him, of his owne kingly power. Which power of his, he graunteth to all his servants, that doe purely and sincerely preach the word, but yet it is most clearely to be seene in that parte of his government, wherby obstinate sinners, which will not yeald to admonitions, are given vp to Satan by the ecclesiasticall censure, and are cast out of the Church, yea the very kingdome of heaven; accordinge to that, *vvhatsoever ye shall binde on earth, it shalbe bound in heaven, and vvhat thinges soever ye shall loose on earth they shalbe loosed in heaven, for vvhere tvvo or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the mids of them. Mat. 18.18.20.* By these wordes therefore it is declared, that there is a very effectuall power in theis Churches of openinge and shuttinge, of bindinge and loosinge, yea even of the whole administringe of the censures. And what godly man doth not from his hart giue thankes to God, and extolleth not with condigne praises the holy labour of this Church, by meanes whereof he hath restored the decayed discipline, and hath recalled it to the square of truth, and to the practise of the primitive Church? But wee must observe that this Key was called aboue *Chap. 1. 18. the Key of Death and Hell*; notinge out by this one other part, the whole power of the Keyes. It is therefore a fearefull Key to the wicked (how soever they doe securely despise it) which bolteth vp the gate of heaven against the wicked that are cast downe into Hell; and no lesse joyfull it is to the godly, which doth vnlocke this dore to them, that so they may enter in by it to everlastinge life. But why is it called the Key of David, when it is rather the Key of Aaron, to whome it belonged to keepe backe the Lepers and vncleane persons from the holy thinges, and to shutt them out from comming into the Temple? > *And they shall know that I haue loued thee.* For till this tyme thou art made a mockinge-stocke, neither doe vnthankfull men acknowledge my loue by that singuler gift of Godlines which I haue bestowed vpon thee; But then will I adorne thee with those thinges which are in account with the world also; thou shalt set vp a victorious ensigne against thine enemyes, and thou shalt inrich thy selfe with there spoyles, so as there shalbe none that shall not be inforced to confesse, that thou art Gods onely beloved darlinge, when hee shall see thee so meruelously, aboue all hope, promoted and aduanced. Nourish and cherish thy hope with these thinges (ô holy Philadelphia) and bee not perplexed in thy minde, vvhatsoeuer the vvorld prateth of thee vvith many foolish vvordes.

10. *Because thou hast kept the vvord of my patience.* That is, That vvord and doctrine vvhich I taught the vvorld vvith very great patience, as also vvhich is to bee preached vvith like patience allvvayes, vvhich I see thou hast used to thy great danger, and hast for all that continued constantly in thy duetie.

> *And I vvill saue thee from the houre of temptation.* But vvhat is it to saue them from the houre? VVhat vvould not God suffer the Philadelphians at all to bee touched vvith the triall? It could scarce bee that they bee altogether free in the common calamitie of the vvhole vvorld.

To saue them then, is to deliuer them; as God saued them out of the hand of theire enemyes: That is, He deliuered them, Iudg. 2. 18. It is as much as if he should say: *I vvill not suffer thee to quaile in that triall, but I vvill giue thee strength, vvhereby thou shalt not onely beare the calamitie manfully, but shalt ouercome it also and proue a Conquerour.* But vvhat is this houre of temptation? In the Type it is that no doubt that vvas vnder Traiane, vvhich Philadelphia sustayned together vvith all other Churches.

It is an Hebraisme of a nominatiue case put absolutely , such as wee obserued,Chap.2.26. The reward is ,that hee shalbe like a Pillar in the Temple of God, that is, hee shall remayne firme and stable in the Church, neither shall he feare any ruine or slidinge , how soeuer the tempestuous raine shall fall, the floudes shall arise , the windes shall blowe,and all thinges shall rush together vpon him with one assault. He alludeth to those two brasen Pillars placed in the Temple by Salomon,which did resemble the stabilitie of the sonnes of God, 1.King. 7. 15. And so is this Church , by Gods mercy , not defiled with any schisme , or filthy reuolt , as wee haue seene the Church of Sardis to bee , which because shee tooke no care to plant a full and through reformation , did by Gods iust iudgment lose many of her Citizens, like as the figge tree loseth her greene figges ; so farre of was it that they should bee Pillars. But Philadelphia should bee without this greife , not but that it should haue some runnagates from there holy profession which for a tyme they should dissemblingly make , but because these fewe false-harted ones , should rather make the faith and diligence of this Church to shine forth in examininge and castinge forth these hypocrites, then that they should cast any blot of schisme or apostasie vpon it.

Neither shall he goe forth any more. This Pillar is declared by a double property, the one of perpetuitie, the other of a name written in it. That is signifyed in these wordes, *neither shall he goe forth any more*. The force of which wordes seemeth to bee an answeare to a secret doubt, which might perhaps trouble the minde of some man, because those Pillars,in the Temple were broken,when the Citie was taken by Nebuchadnezzar , and the brasse of them was carryed into Babell,Ier.52.17. Least any man should feare that the same might happen here,namely, that though a man should bee setled for a tyme in this Temple,he should at the length be banished thence;he biddeth them be of good cheare,for he promiseth that he shalbe such a Pillar, as no Nebuchadnezzar shall euer breake in peices,or carry away by force any whither. The Sonne abideth in the howse for euer,Ioh.8.35. The handmayde with her sonne is cast forth, but the aire shall liue allwayes in his fathers sight. Gal.4.30. &c.

And I vvill vvrite vpon it the name of my God. The name written vpon it is three fold, of God, of the new Ierusalem , and the new name of a Sonne. All which thinges are spoken agreably to those Pillars in the

The Temple, the fashion whereof the Holy Ghost as it were pointinge
at, doth here explaine, by the way teachinge vs, that there was nothing
ordayned in that old Temple in vaine, although it seemed to be of no
moment at all. Salomon called his two Pillars which hee erected by
two notable names, that on the right hand hee called *Iachim*, that is,
*he vvill stablish*; that on the left hand he called *Boaz*, that is, *in it there is*
*strength*, *1. King. 7. 21.* Shewinge not onely by the matter, but by the
names also of those Pillars, what stedfastnes the elect stand in before
God, both for the present, and for tyme to come. For the present, the
sonnes of God haue strength in themselues; for tyme to come, God
will stablish them so with his grace, that they shall neuer wholy de-
part from him. And yet, that I may by the way touch this point, these
two names seeme to note out besides this, the two Churches of the
Iewes and Gentiles. That of the Iewes, by *Iachim* on the right hand,
as which God would at length establish in his tyme, though as yet it
had not attayned to this stablenes, through the obstinacye of there
mindes wherewith they should reiect Christ when hee should come;
this of the Gentiles, by *Boaz* on the left hand, because of the present
strength that should bee in her, when shee should embrace Christ at
the first hearinge. Thus Christ shall write vpon these Pillars better
names then those of *Iachim* and *Boaz*. For first he shall write vpon
them the name of his God, that it may bee made plaine to all men, that
these men are chosen out from the rest, to bee Gods peculiar people,
as is in vse with all matters that are openly marked, which doe by
there titles declare to euery one whose they are. In which sence it was
said, *And they shall knowe that I haue loued thee, vers. 9.* For which
cause also: *Holines to the Lord*, was written vpon the litle belles that
hange vpon the horses in the Prophet *Zachary*, chap. 14. 20. The
second name is of the newe *Ierusalem*; of which Chapter 21. 2. &c.
To which tyme this reward belongeth: whence it is cleare, that these
seauen Epistles respected not onely the present condition of the seauen
Cities, but doe after the manner of Types comprehend the ages
followinge for a longe tyme, as wee haue interpreted them. But
as touchinge this newe *Ierusalem*, wee shall shewe in the proper
place, that it is not that Citie which the Saintes shall enioy in the
Heauens, after this life, but that Church, that is to bee looked for vpon
earth, the most noble and pure of all other, that euer haue bene to that
tyme.

The rewardes doe in a peculiar ſort ſerue for the tymes ; but if *this* felicitie ſhould be after the reſurrection, it ſhould bee common to all the Saintes,not proper to this Philadelphia. This therefore doth ſignifie,both that the Philadelphians ſhould endure vntill that reſtoringe of the Church, wherein the newe Ieruſalem ſhall come downe from heauen, and ſhall conuerſe with men,as alſo that they ſhalbe ioyned with it in Couenant and ſocietie,to bee endowed with the gift of that heauenly Ieruſalem, and to enjoy the ſame right and felicitie with it. At which tyme all men ſhall acknowledge, that thy reformation is not a deuiſe of mans braine, as contentious brablers will needes haue it to bee, when they ſhall ſee the ſame ordinances to flouriſh in the newe Ieruſalem. But at laſt hee ſhall ariſe and take the clubbe into his handes,hee ſhall deface all his enemyes,hee ſhall giue his Spouſe the triumph, & hee ſhalbe magnifyed of all men throughout the whole world,for this Kinge of Kinges : Hee ſhall take his ſeruants into the fellowſhippe of this glory, hee ſhall deliuer them from thoſe calamities wherewith they are nowe oppreſſed, he ſhall giue them power ouer there enemyes, and ſhall impart vnto them the whole honour of his Kingdome, ſo farre as mortall mẽ can be capeable of it. Nowe there is ſome difference betweene a newe name putt abſolutely;chap.2. 17. and the newe name of a ſonne in this place.For that belongeth to the certainty of adoption by Chriſt,which faith was very weake in the ſtate of Pergamus ; This is referred to the fellowſhippe of that Kingdome, which ſhalbe communicated with his ſeruantes in the latter tymes.

## The Analysis or Resolution of the Epistle to the Laodiceans.

<image-desc>A large, ornate woodcut drop cap 'S' decorated with vine and floral motifs.</image-desc>
*So much for the Epistle to the Philadelphians. The last of all written to the Laodiceans remayneth, the Inscription whereof is to the Angell like as of the former. The description of him from whome it is sent, is taken out of the double propertie, first of his truth, partly in his promises, that hee is Amen: partly in his Doctrine, that hee is a faithfull and true Witnes: then of his power, whereby hee is the beginning of the creatures of God, v. 14. The Narration first reproueth him and sheweth the greiuousnes of his sinne, both closely, by omittinge the mention of any good thinge in him, contrary to the course he tooke with all the former Churches, as also openly, both by cōparinge it with coldnes, as a lesser euill vers. 15. And by settinge downe the punishment that is to bee inflicted, which is vomitinge out of his mouth, vers. 16. After that hee sheweth the way to heale this disease, both by openinge the cause of it, which is a false persuasion of his owne worth and excellency, and the ignorance of his misery, vers. 17. As also by prescribinge the remedie, which is to bee fetched from Christ alone, vers. 18. And not this onely but also by perswadinge him to use it, both by threatninge a chastisement fitt for sonnes, if they shall neglect it, vers. 19. As also by layinge downe the easines of applyinge it, vers. 20. And the reward, vers. 21. The last Conclusion is the usuall Epiloge of hearinge what the Spirit saith to the Churches, vers. 22.*

## THE EXPOSITION.

<margin>Luke-warme vaineglorious Laodicea.</margin>
14. *And to the Angell of the Laodiceans.* Laodicea by the Riuer Lycus, was of old a great and renowned Citie, aboundinge both with Citizens, and wealth, and all thinges, as wee haue shewed; Chapter 1. 11. It was built by Antiochus the sonne of stratonice, and was called Laodicea for a fauours sake to Laodice his wife, as who would say, a Princesse of the people, to whome shee gaue lawes, and amonge whome shee executed iustice. Whence it is that wee call it glorious or gloryinge Laodicea, as beinge both by her name, and in her owne conceite a great Citie, bragginge that shee is rich and wanteth nothinge, vers. 17. It is distant Eastward rather then Southward from Philadelphia, not aboue ten scruples of ground, accordinge to Ptolomy. It is the third Citie, since the mention of Iezabell was last of, whose infamy and villany the Church of Sardis tooke away from the Churches. This Church hath this proper to it selfe, that shee hath none sett against her as the former Churches had.

Thyatira was set against Ephesus, Sardis against Smyrna, Philadelphia against Pergamus; Laodicea the seuenth Citie wanteth a Parallele to match her, as beinge a peerelesse Paragon. The Counterpaine is the third reformed Church; Which before that I doe by name specifie, I must put away from me by all earnest intreatie, the uniust suspicion which some men may raise against me, & the offence which they may take at my wordes. It was not truely any distempered affectiō of my hart, that hath set me on worke to seeke out an odious application of this Epistle. God is my witnesse that I am not greiued through enuie either at the wealth, or yet at the honours of any man. That litle estate which I haue of mine owne, doth fully content mee. Neither did I euer count any thinge more foolish, then for a man to goe about to please himselfe by displeasinge others. Yea how foule and shamefull a thinge is it for one to ly rakinge in the vlcers of his brethren, like a flye? My minde and disposition is and hath bene allwayes such, that I could neuer abide such courses. But when as I perceiued that these seauen Cities, were propounded for a Type of all the Churches amonge the Gentiles, and when I did more ouer see

clearely, both the order of the tyme, and the meruaylous agreeinge of all thinges together, I durst not perfidiously burie the truth in silence, least I should make my selfe accessarie to so bloudie a sinne, as is the damnation of other mens soules.

God forbid that I should willingly distaine that Church with any the least blot of infamy, which by the mercye of God hath brought me forth, hath brought me vppe, and doth sustaine me, the which therefore I doe with my daily wishes and endeavours, desire to bee, and to make a most blessed Church. But seeing a Bile cannot bee healed vnles it bee handled, neither handled without some paine and smartinge greife, I thought it my duetie to cast my selfe rather vpon whatsoever troubles, then to betray the saluation of that Church, whose estate ought to bee of more account with euery one of vs, then his owne Truely hee that gathereth the teares of his children into his bottle, knoweth right well, that I haue not with drye eyes taken a suruaye of this Laodicea. I could not but poure forth teares and sighes from the bottome of my hart, when I beheld in it Christ himselfe loathinge of vs, and prouoaked extremely to anger against vs.

Wherefore let no man blame me for speakinge that, which not so much mine owne minde, as the duetie of a faithfull Interpreter constraineth me to vtter. And I hope that those which loue the truth will not disdaine and reiect so equall a petition ; on which hope relyinge, but cheifely on his helpe ; who is the guide of my way and of my life, I will forthwith addresse my selfe to come to the matter. The Counterpaine (I say) of Laodicea, is the third reformed Church, namely : Our Church of England. For all the purer Churches are in a threefold difference to bee considered : for either they followe the steppes, which Luther trode out before them, of which sort are the Churches of Germany, cheifely, that of Saxonie, and those of Sueueland and Denmarke that border vpon it ; or els they abhorre that errour of Consubstantiation, as doe all the rest with one consent ; which yet doe not in all thinges conspire together, but follow a different manner of gouernment ; the French Churches and those that bee in league with them, one ; and ours of England another, and that a certaine proper and peculiar one, as it were an A, per se A, Gouernments.

Whence there are three that are distinguished each apart from the other, to which three are three Types correspondent, Sardis, Philadelphia, Laodicea, after the ouerthrow of Iezabell, that is, after that the yoake of the Romish Tyranny was shaken of. Nowe ours of England suteth with Laodicea the last most of them, as whose beginninge was last of all; which it tooke from the yeare M. D. XLVII. When as Kinge Edward of most noble memory came to the Crowne, beinge then at length a confirmed & established Church, when eleven yeares after our most gracious Queene began to Raigne. The most mightie Kinge Henry her Father had cast out the Pope, but hee retayned the Popish superstition. And before hee began but to stirre against the Pope, the Churches of Germany and Swizerland were founded. The Scottish Church was after ours in her birth and vprisinge, yet is it iustly nombred amonge these reformed Churches, with whome it consenteth in her forme of Church gouernment, with whome therefore it is reckoned as beinge of the same Originall, which is more to be esteemed by the agreement in the substantiall matters, then by the difference of tyme alone. Wherefore our one Church of England onely maketh a Counterpaine point-uice answeringe to Laodicea, as the which was last extant of those, in which a diuersitie of any moment is apparant.

These thinges saith that *Amen*. *Amen* is heare used as if it were a proper name, and vndeclinable, *ò Amen* as were *ò o'n*, *he that is*, *that vvas, and that is to come*, before in the first Chapter. This threefold propertie giuen to Christ in this place, tendeth to teach vs, what kinde of Gouernour Christ should shewe himselfe to bee in this Church of England. The first propertie is taken out of the first Chapter, vers. 18. Though *Amen* there wanteth the Greeke Article *ò* that goeth commonly with nownes, neither is it read at all by the vulgar Interpreter, which yet this place may make vs coniecture a litle, that it should bee read. The second is taken, not out of the vision of the first Chapter, but out of the Inscription of the common Epistle, vers. 5. Neither is the third to bee had there in expresse wordes, but in the 8. verse hee is called the beginninge and the ende, whence this here may seeme to be deriued, the beginninge of the creatures of God. The two first properties serue to expresse his double truth, the one in promisinge, the other in teachinge. In regard of that hee is called *Amen*, accordinge to that of the Apostle, *In him are all the promises of God yea and Amen, 2. Cor. 1. 20*

looketh vpon it with eyes that bee matches & indifferent, it may seeme to him and that worthily, to bee voyd of all vertue what soeuer. It is an horrible euill, that doth as it were say vnto all goodnes , what haue I to doe with thee ; gett thee hence farre ynough from me. And though wee may well coniecture by this kinde of silence , which the holy Ghost here vseth , howe desperate the disease of this Church is, yet in the next wordes following , the qualitie thereof is in a more plaine and liuely manner described vnto vs. And first for more plainenes sake , by a denyall of contraries. *I knowe* (saith he) *that thou art neither cold nor hott*, but some odde strange thinge moulten and compacted together of them both. So that this euill consisteth of certaine contraries strangely tempered and blended together. Nowe hee calleth that man cold , who can well indure that the dueties of godlines should lie dead, & out of request, litle or nothinge at all caringe what manner of way hee himselfe or others take to worshippe God. Hee calleth him hot , who boyleth with heate and feruency of Spirit, in his due and full regards of Gods worshippe , beinge like to boylinge water, that seetheth and plaweth (as wee say) in the Pott, with a certaine restles motion. For so doth the word *hott* in the Greeke signifie , to wit, such an one as can by no meanes indure superstitious and impious religions , but will hazard all hee hath , so farre as may bee, to effect a reformation. For wee must not thinke, that to bee hot is vitious in this place, as if it were an inconsiderate zeale, as the case stãdeth with the habits of morall vertues, wherein both the extremes, strayinge frõ the mediocritie, either in excesse or defect, are faults & vices , as wee see in liberalitie, fortitude, temperance, & the rest; but it is a matter of commendation, as beinge the onely vertue, from which both coldnes and lukwarmenes swerue.

This wee see, in that Apollos is said to haue bene *feruent in the Spirit* <margin>Act. 18. 25.</margin> And Paul exhorteth men *to be feruent in the Spirit*, <margin>Rom. 12. 11.</margin> Againe if to bee hot, should bee in this place to degenerate from the right constitution of minde by an excesse, then to bee luke-warme, should bee in the nature of vertue, that keepeth the middle betweene two extremes. *And thou knowest not that thou art wretched, &c.* The other cause
of the euill is, the ignorance of his owne miserie. For the pro-
speritie of the world blindeth the minde that a man cannot behold
in what state hee standeth. Therefore doth the Holy Ghost in many
wordes explane this misery of the Angells, because in so deepe and
dead a sleepe, a slight kinde of vpbraidinge him with it could not
make any sensible impression. Hee maketh fiue degrees of it, of
which the two first, are as it were certaine common affections and
accidents of the disease; the three latter, declare the very kinde and
nature of it. For the threefold remedy of gold, garments, and eye-
salue, in the verse followinge, sheweth that the disease consisteth
cheifely in these three. The accidents are referred, either to his
owne feelinge, or to other mens commiseration: in respect of that,
the Angell is *wretched*; in regard of this, hee is *miserable*, or, as the
word giueth, *pitifull*, or, one that is in a *pitifull* case. That man is
counted wretched, who is worne and forlorne with any grieuous
sorrowe of minde, whether it arise out of any publike calamitie, or
els out of a mans owne priuate and home-bred greife. Neither is
there any man, though placed in neuer so high dignitie, that can quite
himselfe free from this wretchednes. Whence it is, that the Kinges
in the Tragedies, are brought in so often lamentinge, and callinge
themselues by the name of wretched men.

Such a kinde of infelicitie did of old lye heauily vpon the Angel
of *Laodicea*, and is lyinge as hard vpon our *English Angell* at this
day. Howe can that bee, will some say, whereas no publike nor

If they had allwayes beene lyinge asleepe in the snares of the Deuill, the matter had not bene so much to bee bewayled; but after that they had escaped and awaked out of his ginnes, through the sauing knowledge of the Gospell, that they should bee againe intangled in them by this meanes, what godly hart is there that cannot lament, not there case onely, but the common miserie also of our whole Church and people, who are dragged into the same pit of destruction with them, and that a thousand wayes. These then are the Symptomes of the disease, greiuous indeed of themselues, yet but a flea-bitinge to the disease it selfe; which let vs nowe come to rubbe, as gently as wee can, and with a minde to heale it, not to exasperate it. The first filthy matter that is to be purged out, is his *Pouertie*: And knowest not (saith he) that thou art *Poore*. What kinde of poore man? not in spirit surely, of which *Christ* speaketh, *Matth. 5. 3.* For this is a blessed pouertie, that is a miserable one. Besides the *Angell* glorieth in this, that hee is and hath bene rich, and wanteth nothinge, so that hee is farre from that holy humilitie.

This pouertie therefore is a timorous kinde of beggarlines, whereby a man both trembleth for feare at the sight of one that is richer then himselfe, and dareth neither speake nor doe any thinge but what may please him that is of more power and authoritie then hee, as also is fayne to maintaine and sustaine a miserable life, with importunate begginge of an almes. For so the word <term>*Prokòs*</term> in Greeke, that signifieth a poore man, hath both the name of fearfullnes, and signifieth with all such an one as hee was, that lay prostrate at the threshold of the rich man, desiringe to bee filled with the crumes that fell from his Table, *Luk. 16. 20.* But how can either of these agree to our *Angels*? Is not all this base beggarye farre remote from them, & from such wealth and pompe as they abound with all? I would to God it were so. But as at all times, so here in this place, I am constrained to admire the infinite wisedome of God, which hath opened our hidden impostume with a word so fitly applyed to the matter, that nothinge could bee euer spoken or deuised more fitt for the purpose. For first, how base and seruile a feare hath seized on our *Angell*, may thence very easily appeare, in that hee speaketh nothinge in a manner, that may prouoke any man that is his better and superiour to anger or displeasure against him. <header>Chap. 3. A REVELATION,</header>

If they had allwayes beene lyinge asleepe in the snares of the Deuill, the matter had not bene so much to bee bewrayled ; but after that they had escaped and awaked out of his ginnes, through the sauing knowledge of the Gospell, that they should bee againe intangled in them by this meanes, what godly hart is there that cannot lament, not there case onely , but the common miserie also of our whole Church and people, who are dragged into the same pit of destruction with them, and that a thousand wayes. These then are the Symptomes of the disease, greiuous indeed of themselues, yet but a flea-bitinge to the disease it selfe ; which let us nowe come to rubbe, as gently as wee can, and with a minde to heale it , not to exasperate it. The first filthy matter that is to be purged out, is his *Pouertie*: And *knowest not (saith he) that thou art Poore*. What kinde of poore man ? not in spirit surely , of which Christ speaketh , Matth. 5. 3. For this is a blessed pouertie, that is a miserable one. Besides the Angell glorieth in this, that hee is and hath bene rich, and wanteth nothinge, so that hee is farre from that holy humilitie.

This pouertie therefore is a timorous kinde of beggarlines, whereby a man both trembleth for feare at the sight of one that is richer then himselfe, and dareth neither speake nor doe any thinge but what may please him that is of more power and authoritie then hee, as also is fayne to maintaine and sustaine a miserable life, with importunate begginge of an almes. For so the word *Ptokòs* in Greeke, that signifyeth a poore man, hath both the name of fearfullnes, and signifyeth with all such an one as hee was, that lay prostrate at the threshold of the rich man, desiringe to bee filled with the crumes that fell from his Table, Luk. 16.20. But how can either of these agree to our Angels ? Is not all this base beggarye farre remote from them,& from such wealth and pompe as they abound with all ? I would to God it were so. But as at all times, so here in this place, I am constrained to admire the infinite wisedome of God, which hath opened our hidden impostume with a word so fitly applied to the matter , that nothinge could bee euer spoken or deuised more fitt for the purpose. For first, how base and seruile a feare hath feazed on our Angell, may thence very easily appeare, in that hee speaketh nothinge in a manner , that may prouoke any man that is his better and superiour to anger or displeasure against him. The Bishops feare the Noble-men ; The Parish-Parsons and Vicars stand in awe of the Bishops , as whome they

riches and estate was more ample the thine, there authority greater,
there power more dreadfull,yet because the Vulgar sort sawe them to

beggarly cominge to Benefices and Ecclesiasticall functions. For the former riches were not true, as which keepe not the Angell a whitt from beinge a most base and abiect beggar : But the gold of Christ driueth this beggary farre away indeed. It is therefore that most holy manner of callinge, chusinge, ordayninge and giuinge of authoritie to Ecclesiasticall men, euery one in his function, which Christ himselfe hath appointed, whereby it cometh to passe, that Pastours sue not, but are sued for and vnto, and are promoted not by there money, but by there honestie, not by fauour, but by learninge, not at any one mans pleasure, but by the voices and consent of theire flocke. This gold Christ will haue bought of him, because he it is that hath plainly described this whole order, and hath not left it free for men to doe as they list in this matter. As longe as the matter shalbe in the power of the Patrone and Bishop alone, there will neuer want bribe-giuers, nor bribe-takers that wil suffer thẽselues to be corrupted with gifts : *But if Christs rule take place, this begginge pouertie will flee away & neuer returne agayne. For this gold is tryed in the fire, often approued and throughly refined. Wee see the excellency of it in the primitiue Church, yea euen at this day in our neighbour Churches. It feareth no touchstone, it fleeth not away for feare of any fire, it doth not burst asunder by batterie of any hammer, but standeth to this day, as it hath stoode of old, inuincible, to the great glorie of those that are growne rich by it.* The *vvhite Garments* are opposed to the former honours and nakednes, that is, contempt. Christ will haue these also to bee bought of him, as which hee hath alone, and those most pretious and most praise-worthy. For what can contempt hurt them, whome there worthines hath chosen, there learninge hath ordayned, there sanctifyed hart and carriage hath preferred? Whom many men haue earnestly desired for there approued pietie, doe admire for there diligence in teachinge, doe stand in awe of because of the truth that hath a most free passage in there ministerie, and doe reuerence as ensamples of all vertue and goodnes? Be thou (saith Paul) an ensample to the faithfull in speach, in conuersation, in loue, in spirit, in faith, in chastitie, neither lett any man despise thy youth; *1.Tim. 4.12.* Behold, here is a way to deliuer a Minister from contempt. But such trifling pointes of thine as these, doe easily of themselves fall to the ground, so that I neede not trouble my selfe with confutinge of them.

19. *As many as I loue, &c.* These wordes contayne an exhortation to vse the remedye; & first of all from the chastifinge of those whome hee looueth. A reason verily of great moment. Whosoeuer hee bee, hee is either amonge the sonnes of God or Reprobates. If hee receiue no sonne whome hee doth not reproue and chasten , what will become of the rest of the rout ? A horrible Iudgment abideth for these men , whome, hee that will not cocker his owne sonnes, will not surely spare in the least manner. There hangeth therefore a chastisement ouer them vnles they repent in tyme , and that a very greiuous and wofull one , as the very wordes doe intimate , which are wont to bee vsed for a solace in any sharper affliction then ordinary, whereby the minde is so beaten downe, as if a man were forsaken of God. For this cause hee telleth them that they are sonnes whome hee is wont to strike with so sharpe punishments , least they should despayre of his fatherly goodnes by meanes of the greiuousnes of the punishment. It is nowe therefore no tyme to brabble and contend together with hatinge of and raylinge vpon one another, but wee must rather listen diligently to Christes Alarum, and either forthwith bethinke our selues of the remedie , or els must shortly expect some great and lamentable calamity. Now heare wee must obserue, that hee doth reproue and chasten, that is, conuince & smite. For both these thinges are to bee ioyned together.
