Whence it is that a chastisement is rightly called discipline , or a displinge, whereby the offender feeleth payne and findeth matter to learne by all at once. In both which Christ communicateth himselfe to his members, keepinge a mutuall feast with them, he beinge first intertayned of vs by hearinge, and then hee intertayninge vs againe with the supper of his body. > Blessed be thou therefore (ô most meeke lambe of God) who findinge the dores shutt vppe against thee, dost not presently and speedily conuay thy selfe away from vs enraged with anger against vs, and dost not depriue vs of all meanes of saluation, as wee haue deserued, but dost still leaue a libertie to enioye thee in a goodly and abundant manner, and that to all those who doe open vnto thee when thou knockest by the word, and doe not despise thy most sweete inuitement by the Sacraments. 

The errour therefore of those men is full of euill, yea of blasphemy, who doe in such manner make a departure from this Church, as if Christ were quite banished from hence, and that there could be no hope of saluation to those that abide here. And therefore neither must wee hold our selues contented with these corruptions, neither must they seperate themselues from vs for any blemishes. Returne therefore to the vnitye of that Church, which hath begotten and nourished yow. If yow flee from this Christ that suppeth with the elect in our Congregations; & doth againe for his part intertaine them, certainly yow shall finde him no where. Such then for all the world , is the power of a naturall man to belieue , as is the loue of the truth in the Popish Teachers , who though they see it , doe yet wickedly reiect it with scorne and hatred.

21. *Hee that shall ouercome , I vvill giue him to sitt.* For , I vvill giue to him that ouercometh : So puttinge the nominatiue case absolu-tely ; as wee haue obserued aboue , chap. 2. 26. Here wee haue a third reason taken from the reward of a fellowe-Throane. Not that the glory of euery one of Gods children shalbe equall to the honour of Christ as hee is man ; but that the brightnes and Maiestie of the head-shall redound to euery one of the members. And therefore these thrones are not proper to the 12. Apostles , of which wee read , Mat. 19. 28. But common to all the elect , though they are giuen to the Apostles in that place after a peculiar sort , as perhaps wee shall shewe elsewhere. ### *The Analysis or Resolution , of the 4. Chapter.*

*Hitherto wee haue spoken of the Prophesie of the particuler Churches. The Prophesye of the whole Church followeth, the which doth first propound the matter summarily in this chapter, and then in speciall in the rest. This contayneth a newe callinge of Iohn, consistinge in the thinge that was seene, a dore opened in heauen, in the first voice of the trompett that was heard, vers. 1. And lastly in the effect, whereby hee became straightwayes in the Spirit, in the beginninge of the 2. vers. As also it contayneth an Vniuersall Type of the future Church, Which is described throughout the whole Chapter besides. The Prince whereof, as it were the Center, is most glorious by meanes of his Throne, most amiable to see to, glisteringe round about with heauenly brightnes, vers. 2. 3. The members, as it were the circumference of this Center, are the foure and twentie Elders, full of Maiestie, honourable, by reason of there thrones, age, holines, Crownes of gold, vers. 4. The thinges that accompany these persons, are partly the gifts which God bestoweth on this holy Company partly that worshippe which the company of the faithfull redreth backe againe unto him. The gifts are first, of protection, whereby great flashes of lightninge, thunders and voices come forth from the throne, for the vengeance of the wicked world because of there attempts against the congregation of the Saintes, vers. 5. And after that,*

Accordinge to that custome, after which God is worshipped in the Cristian Congregations. Such is the Company of the Godly before God, and some such company as this should allwayes bee extant, though not remarkeable of the world, in euery age with equall glorie.

# THE EXPOSITION

1. After that I looked. The Holy Ghost havinge hitherto reuealed those thinges that were to bee accomplished in a certaine short and determinate tyme, nowe inlarginge those boundes, hee goeth on to write in a continued order, of such thinges as might offer unto our viewe a common & perfect portraiture of the estate of the Church, from the writinge of this Booke euen unto the last end. The handling of which thinges wilbe admirable, and such as cannot bee performed but onely through his helpe, who did at the first reueale them unto his seruant. Trustinge therefore on the grace of this Almightie God, I will goe forward in the worke which I haue taken upon me. For the absoluinge and perfectinge whereof, howsoeuer other thinges requisite shall bee wantinge, certainly faithfullnes and diligence in searchinge out matters shall not be wantinge to the uttermost of my power. These first wordes belonge to a newe preparation for a newe

For Iohn is no longer conuersant vpon earth, but is lift vppe into heauen it selfe, where through a dore that is opened, he beholdeth meruailous changes of matters, that could not be knowen by any other meanes. The condition therefore of this ensuinge prophesie is diuerse from the former. That is of a narrower compasse, euen as the place also where the thinges were seene was a litle Island invironed with the sea; This is spread abroad infinitely farre and wide, like as is the heauen it selfe, that contayneth all thinges within the Circuite thereof. Moreouer there was a certaine visible tracinge out of thinges to come in those seauen Cities.

For the Churches that were afterwardes to bee propagated in order, should bee, by the will of God, pourtrayed, after the expresse image of those Cities as they were at that present, but there was no resemblance amonge mortal men of the thinges that are to be spoken of in this second Prophesie. For peculiar iudgments, of which, for the most part, speach is made here, are to be fetched onely from secret Reuelation. To the place therefore, of heauen, where power was giuen to behold this Vision, the Booke sealed vppe with seauen seales is in the next place added; besides the creature is vnable to vnseale those same seales, neither is the power of any other saue of the lambe alone sufficient for that worke, as wee shall see in the proper place. All which thinges, as they doe declare the excellency of this Prophecye, so they require greater attention and diligence on our part. As touchinge the wordes, *the first voice is heard, because the Authour of both the Prophecyes is one and the same, and it soundeth like a Trompett,* to the intent that the thinges that were heard might be more certaine and better perceiued of Iohn, as it was obserued on Chap. 1. 10. Hee biddeth him come vp hither, where onely, those thinges might bee seene, of which there was no tracke chalked out vpon earth: and he would haue him looke through the dore, by which meanes he might be deceiued, or could not see plainly ynough, but he would haue him be present, and before his face, that so he might haue the certaine and vndoubted knowledge of all thinges. But that which followeth hath some ambiguitie in it; howe he can say, that he will propound a Vision of thinges that must be done after these thinges: For should not this ensuinge Prophecy: take his beginninge, before that former as touchinge the seauen Churches should come to an issue? whole Prophecye into thinges present and to come. The Holy Ghost
followeth no such diuision, but mingleth many thinges to come
amonge thinges present, as they come to hand. For which cause, these
wordes, after these thinges, are not referred, in regard of there Origi-
nall, to the end of the former Prophecy, but to the present tyme of

reuealed these thinges vnto him; from whence takinge a newe begin-

anexeth those thinges which could not be sufficiently understoode
out of the former Types. Well therefore doth Theodore Beza tran-

regard of the end, this second Prophecy is worthily recorded after
the former, as the which is of a more longe lastinge tyme, reachinge
vnto the last cominge of Christ, whereas that former one is limmited
with farre more narrowe boundes. Out of these thinges therefore
we gather two thinges, that are very greatly to be obserued. The first,
that speach is made from this place, concerninge such thinges onely,
as followe after the tyme that this Reuelation was made. For so doth
he plainely speake, *And I vvill shevve thee vvhat thinges must come to passe*
*hereafter*. The which thinge seeinge it was perceiued by some of the
Interpreters, I meruaile that it was not obserued by them in there
exposition, but that they should rather confound the tymes as it were
with a violent whirlinge of them about throughout the whole Trea-
tise, so as all thinges are couered over with most grosse darknes. Wee
beinge better taught by there example, will hence borrowe light for
the commentary followinge. The second is this, that this Prophecy
is commõ to the whole Church, beinge neither tyed to any particuler
Congregations, nor yet bounded with any other limitts, then of the
whole vniuersall world. The holy Ghost hath sett that particuler one
in the first place, that hee might relate common thinges in common,
and not interrupt the order of the narration.

doth most excell aboue all other thinges, whence it is that they may

the head and Center of the Church, whome alone, the faithfull doe

As touchinge there age, they are all Elders, not because there strength is weakened & ouerworne with olde age, but because of there reuerend hoarie haires, & there mature and graue iudgments wherewith they imbrace the truth, as also because they haue a certayn present possession of there dignitie, such as is meete for mẽ of perfect age and stayed yeares. prognosticates, or the stinges of conscience, whereby they are tor-

6. *Nowe there was before the Throone a sea of glasse.* The first outward gift, which serueth to worke and increase those that be inward, as an instrumentall cause, is the Sea of glasse. Which seemeth to be some vnmeasurable vessell and huge Vatte as it were to the similitude of that Sea that was of old in the Temple, of which, *1. For howe can that which is before the Throne, compassed with a company of elders standinge round about it, bee poured out on all sides, like the Sea so properly called? The circuite indeed of the Elders may reach as farre as the whole world, but wee must remember that heare the matter was shewed to Iohn in a vision, that so wee may not co~ceiue of any such vnmeasurable space. Both the name and amplenes of the vessell, doe shewe the fullnes of all giftes which the Church draweth forth of Christ to saluation, who receiued the Spirit without measure, and out of whose infinite riches God bestoweth freely vpon vs, *Iohn. 1. 16. and 3. 34.* For els to what end should theare bee a vessell of that capacitie for Aaron and his sonnes to wash there handes & feete in, for the clensinge which any litle pitcher or ewer would haue sufficed?

And indeed this Sea doth afford vs very well and fitly, a certayne resemblance of the whole outward worship that is to bee performed vnto God. For the Doctrine, that is very often compared to waters. *Ho (saith Isaiah) euery one that thirsteth, come to the waters.* For the carryinge away of which waters he biddeth them bringe no other pittchers but there eares; *Incline your eare (saith he) Chap. 55. 1. 3.*

But glaſsie in this place is as much as made of glaſſe , rather declaringe a matter that ſhineth, ſo as one may ſee through it, then a colour without matter, for ſignifyinge whereof the other attribute ſerueth , like to Christall. It is called then a glaſsie Sea to lett vs ſee the difference of this frō that legall Sea, the which beinge made of braſſe, which is a thicke and darke matter , was not able to bee pierced through with any mans ſight , 1. after this patterne. Others doe otherwise interprete these thinges. Some there are that doe referre this Sea to Gods iudgments ; but there was ynough foreshewed as touchinge them in the thunders and lighteninges. Others thinke that they signifie the multitude of men that liue vpon earth. But if this multitude be holy , it was noted before in the foure and twentie Elders : if it bee wicked, what hath it to doe before the Throane ? Or howe can the puritie of Christall agree to it ? There is no neede for me to confute the diuerse and vnmeete interpretations with more wordes ; the very order of thinges sheweth easily , what that is which cometh most neare to the truth. This onely will I say , which is common to this whole booke, that in euery allegoricall interpretation, the purpose & scope of the allegory is aboue all to be respected , for want whereof euery interpretation wilbe waueringe, vncertayne , and of no moment , but if wee shall throughly knowe that , and shall wisely adde the rest of the circumstances, wee may drawe forth a meaninge no lesse constant out of an allegory, then out of any other easie and euident place.

And betvveene the Throane, and the thinges that compassed the Throne, vvere foure beastes. The second outward gift are the Beastes ; whose qualities come first to bee considered, which belonge to the fittinge of them to there function , when wee haue once seene of what kinde these beastes are. Which is indeed hard to bee determined by the iudgment of the Interpreters , they beinge so many wayes differinge each from other. Wee will accordinge to our vsuall course , in a word sett downe that , that seemeth to be most neare vnto the truth. They are the seruantes and Ministers of God , whose whole labour is spent in preachinge the word, and in caringe for those other thinges, which belonge to the Ecclesiasticall government. For first it is playne that they are men ; for so they singe together with the Elders : *Thou hast redeemed vs to God, by thy bloud, Chap. 5. 9.* Besides, seeinge there is a double kinde of mē that are redeemed, one of the people, another of the Ministers, the very place wherein they serue, sheweth that they are of this second order.

For they conuerse betweene the Throne, and the Elders that are placed round about it. So that they come nearer vnto God himselfe , and are as it were the Ambassadours betweene both. More ouer they are the leaders of the publike actiō, as it is manifest after, vers. 9.

There is a double function of this sort in the Church; one of succouringe the poore another of gouerninge manners; 1.*Cor.* 12. 28.

That belongeth to the Deacons and widowes whome the Apostles did of old by Gods appointment make ouerseers to care for the poore, and for such as are diseased through any infirmitie of the body, that so they themselves might not be forced to neglect theire dueties about prayers, and preachinge of the word, whiles they were diligently ymployed in such a busines as that was; *Actor.* 6. 2. &c. 1.*Tim.* 5. 9. &c. This belongeth to the Elders, who are putt in authoritie to gouerne the manners of men onely, and are the Moderatours of the discipline.

## The 5. Chapter.

### The Analysis or Resolution.

<image-desc>An ornamental drop-cap letter 'T' featuring intricate scrollwork and floral patterns.</image-desc>

*Thus much hath bene ſpoken ſummarily of the common Type of the whole Church militant. The ſpeciall Prophecie contayneth partly the ſurpaſſinge dignitie of this Reuelation, in this Chapter, partly the euents themſelues, in the reſt of the Booke. That is declared, first in regard of the creature, and then in reſpect of the Lambe. In reſpect of the creature, it is altogether vnſearcheable, as it appeareth partly out of the ſealinge of it vppe with 7. ſeales verſ. 1. partly, out of the teſtimony of all the creatures, which doe all of them acknowledge there owne impotencie, after that the matter was ſett forth to be inquired into, by the proclamacion of the Angell as it were of a Cryer, verſ. 2. As alſo after that triall had bene made at last what they could doe, verſ. 3. And the conſequent hereof is lamentable, euen the weeping of Iohn. Which this weakenes of the creatures, and his deſpayringe to enioy ſo notable a benefitt, wrunge from him, verſ. 4. In reſpect of the Lambe onely, it is able to bee ſearched out; as first the Elder teacheth who comforteth Iohn verſ. 5. After that the Angell cominge in the nicke, and takinge the Booke, verſ. 6. 7. Whence at last ariſeth a ſinguler ioye and thankſgiuinge of the whole creature, but in ſeuerall first of the Church, verſ. 8. 9. 10. And of the Angells, verſ. 11. 12. And then of the reſt of the creatures, verſ. 13. Last of all ioyntly, the Church ſubſcribinge to the common reioycinge & gladnes of all the reſt, verſ. 14*

# THE EXPOSITION

1. *Then I savve at the right hand.* The vulgar readeth, *in the right hand*; so doth the Interpreter of Aretas also; but all the Greeke Copies doe vvith one consent read, *at* or *vpon the right hand*. They translated it perhaps in the ablatiue case, because it follovveth beneath in the seuenth verse, that the Lambe tooke the Booke out of the right hand. But this vvas not a sufficient cause to depart from the natiue proprietie of the vvordes, seeinge it might be of purpose said for the better conuincinge of the vveaknes of the creatures, that the Booke vvas at first, not in the right hand, but at the right hand of him that sate on the Throne. VVhence it vvould follovve, that if they had no abilitie to open it vvhen it vvas offered & sett forth of purpose to there vievve, much lesse abilitie should they haue had, if he had held it in his handes. Then aftervvardes vvhen the impotencie of the creature vvas conuicted, it is said that the Booke vvas taken into his hand, that so the vvorthines of the Lambe might be made more notable, vvho did not catch at the Booke as it lay hard by his side, but takes it into his hand, out of the hand of him that sate on the Throne. As touchinge the purpose of this Vision, it seemed good to the Holy Ghost after he had pourtrayed the true Church in the former Chapter (the vvhich vvas to be layed as a foundacion of all the buildinge follovvinge, before hee came to the speciall predictions one by one) to giue men a vvatchvvord concerninge the incomprehensible excellencie of this Prophecye. For vvee are vvont (such is the dulnes and vntovvardnes of our nature) to passe by the greatest and most diuine thinges negligently and carelesly, vnles perhaps there be some to pull vs by the eare, and to call earnestly for our paynes, by tellinge vs of the greatnes of the matter vvee are about. Least perhaps this selfe same thinge should befall vs in this place, hee maketh vs to see that this Prophecy is such, as doth contayne in it all the dangers and extremities vvhich the Church is to vndergoe throughout the vvhole race thereof vpon the earth, and yet that it is invvrapped in so great obscuritie, that no created minde can behold it, no not aloofe, much lesse vnfold it vnto others. VVhich is a matter indeed most vvorthy to bee knovvne, and

wise then was meete they should.

*A Booke vvritten vvithin and on the back side.* The first commenda-
cion of the Prophecie is from the Booke, the plentifull writinge in
it,and the seauen seales in this verse. It must needes be a thinge most
certayne that is sett downe in a Booke, which is a most faithfull hel-
per of memory, where as that which dependes vpon memory alone
may easily in longe continuance of tyme be either wholy extinguished
or at least corrupted. Whence it is that God bidds Ieremy for the
greater credit of that prophecye, to write all the wordes wherewith
he speakes vnto him in a Booke,Ier.30.2. Thus hee prouides against
our doubtinge, least wee should thinke otherwise of these thinges,
then of such thinges as are committed to publique instruments and
recordes,yea and are as it were grauen in brasse,so as they can neither
be changed nor perish. The plentifullnes of the writinge is declared,
in that the Booke was vvritten vvithin and on the backside, on both
pages; Nowe hee speaketh accordinge to the auncient manner of
writinge in longe parchments,which were afterwardes rolled toge-
ther about some round peice of woode, where vpon Bookes were
called volumes or scroles, and Christ is said to haue vnfolded and
vnwrapped the Booke,Luk.4.17. Nowe (to use the wordes of the
most learned Theod. Beza) the outside did commonly abide cleane &
vnwritten, vnles the inside were not able to contayne the whole wri-
tinge,for then they filled the outer part with letters, which kinde of
writinges were called backside-writinges. This so great prolixnes
therefore did not onely contayne the cheife heades of thinges,which
might perhaps haue bene comprised euen in a narrow roome, but
euen all the most small matters also, that so there should bee no neede
to fetch ought from any other place, and that also wee might knowe
nothinge herein at all to come to passe without Gods speciall proui-
dence. The Complutense and some other copies reade *vvithout*, but the
vvord *on the backside*, is more often vsed in this matter, vvhence came
the name of backside-vvritinges, as vvee said right novve. To con-
clude, hovv pretious are these mysteries, vvhich God keepeth by him-
selfe sealed vvith so many seales? The creatures could not so much as
looke vpon the Booke, vers. 4. So farre vvas it from needinge seales
for the concealinge of matters from them. But thus hee vvould de-
clare vvith hovv great honour vvee ought to reuerence his secrets.

2. *And I savve a stronge Angell vvhich proclaimed* : Great is the wor-thines of the Prophecie by meanes of the certentie, prolixitie and the feelinge of it, but nowe it appeareth to be farre greater in asmuch as it exceedes the reach of all created vnderstandinge. For it is not of such a nature, that the wiser sort of men may be able by some quicke-witted foresight to comprehend it, but such as wherein all men must of necessitie acknowledge theire ignorance. For the better conuincinge whereof, here is an allusion made to the manner that Princes vse,who in matters of great difficultie, are wont to inuite theire subjects with great rewardes by the voice of a Cryer to make triall of theire strength ; neither is there any allmost who will not thrust forth to make triall in such a buisines. Some small hope of acheiuinge the reward, so that if there be no man that dare come forth ; what is this els but an open confession of theire weakenes & disabilitie ? Euen so the Angell is heare sent out to enquire, *vho should bee vvorthy to vn-seale the Booke?* If no man offer himselfe, lett vs acknowledge our owne impotencie,and the vertue of *the Mediatour* : And with all lett vs admire with due reuerence these holy mysteries : for the which end, God doth in this sort bringe vs thus to feele our pouertie and neede,as of old he dealt with *Adam*,before whome he set all the creatures ere hee gaue him a wife,that when as he sawe he could finde out no fitt helper for himselfe amonge them all, he might make the more account of the wife that was after giuen him.

*Who is vvorthy:* He enquires not of strength and might,but of merit and worthines. For euen all the creatures, if they would conspire together can not auayle one whitt to wringe matters from God by force. Whatsoeuer wee obtayne from him, wee enioy it,by our entreatie, and at his pleasure ; And the right Lord in conferringe dispo-singe his gifts,respecteth the worthines of those on whome he bestoweth his benefitts: so that vnles they bee commended by some due desert either of theire owne or of some other for them, they cā hope for no good thinge from him. But nowe if the bare fore knowledge of thinges to come bee of so great reckoninge, of what place and price then is the knowledge of saluation to be esteemed?

3. *And no man vvas able.* Here wee haue an ingenuous confession of the creatures that they could doe nothinge at all in this matter. Lett them therefore looke to it that make a creature a Patronesse

5. Behold hee hath preuayled : As if there were many that 
stroue, but one onely obtayned the prize beyond the rest. He seemeth 
to speake from the manner of the former proclamation, whereby the 
matter was putt as it were to a publike combate, wherein Christ car-
ryed away the cheife praise, yea euen all in all.

*That Lyon* : A circumlocutory description of *Christ* as he is *Kinge*, 
taken out of Genes. 49.9. But what hath a Lyon to doe with seales? 
Our sinnes did keepe & remoue farre away from us all the mysteryes 
of God : The which when as Christ hath powerfully abolished, and 
hath subdued our enemyes the Diuell and death for euer , hee doth 
worthily come forth with this name as it were an ensigne of victorye 
to obtayne that thinge for us from which our enemyes did before 
hinder us.

*That stemme or branch of Dauid.* So doth Th. Beza reade it very 
well. For the Hebrue word that signifyes a roote, to which the Greeke 
word for a roote answeareth, is sometimes taken for a plant or stem-
me of a tree ; as in Isai , *He riseth vp indeed as a tender plant before him,* 
*and as it were a roote out of a dry ground,* Chapter 53.2. Nowe a roote 
doth noth rise properly out of the earth , but that which groweth 
from it, a plant of the roote, but yet this plant is such an one indeed, 
as it is also the roote the roote of Dauid, namely, the fountayne it selfe 
and the springe-head , whence saluation and life floweth vnto Dauid, 
so that nothinge could bee spoken more significantly , neither hath 
there euer bene besides any plant of this kinde. See Psal. 110.1. Math. 
22.43. &c.

of the faithfull in the middest of the Church.

The seauen hornes; are that soueraigne power, by which Christ

This most meeke Lambe therefore doth not want those weapons

seeinge here are seauen hornes giuen to a lambe besides the nature of
it, and as many eyes.

Which eyes are the seauen spirits of God: That is, the gifts of the

Apostles, and that miraculous gift of speakinge on a subdaine *vwith other*
*tongues, Act.2.3.&c.*

With which power not onely the Apostles did singularly excell, but
others also afterwardes that did embrace the faith. Neither are they
onely sent into all the earth to conferre vpon the Elect the sauinge
knowledge of saluation; but that Christ might search into all thinges
that are done in his Church, yea that are done any where els in the
world. How great impudencie therefore is it, to thrust vpon the
Church a visible head, seeinge the Lambe is furnished with so many
eyes, and doth not carry them as idle about him, but sendeth them out
diligently into all the earth?

7. *He came and tooke the booke out of the right hand of him that sate
on the Throne:* There is a double consideracion of Christ, one as hee
is eternall God fittinge vpon the Throne together with the Father,
Chapter 4. 3. Another as he is Mediatour seruinge or attendinge on
the Throne, and readie & addressed to vndertake those thinges which
make for the saluation of his. The like consideracion there is of the
Spirit, who as he is eternall God, is a partner in the Throne compas-
singe it about, Chapter 4.3.
But as he sanctifyeth the Church with created gifts, is the *seauen
Spirits before the Throne, seauen burninge Lampes, seauen hornes and seauen
eyes.*

8. *Hauinge each of them harpes and golden vialls:* Heare is the gra-

the Lambes takinge and vnsealinge the Booke. They bringe there-
fore instruments fitt for such a worke, *Harpes and vialls*, to witt, prai-
ses and thanksgiuinges. For the *vialls full of odours* are the hartes of
the Saintes, which the Spirit hath filled with a burninge desire of cal-

prayers is the very giuinge of thankes. Nowe heare is an allusion to
the manner of the Temple, where the Leuits praised God with musi-
call instruments, and the Priestes had Potts and cuppes sett before the
Altar, full of odours, Zach. 14. 20.

10. *And hast made vs vnto our God Kinges:* Certayne Copies reade them, and this whole verse in the third person: But *Aretas* and the Vulgar Latine,in the first person. Wee haue interpreted these wordes before. But why doe they remember this benefitt as a cause of takinge the Booke?Because it is belonginge to Christs Kingly power to preuayle with God , and to fetch away those thinges from him, which there was no power to come by before. Wherefore they singe, that they are made Kinges vnto God : As if they should say that they are not onely Kinges, in that they haue vanquished death, sinne, and the Diuell , but specially because they haue God at hand to serue theire turne for any commoditie they want,and withholdinge nothinge from them,which may any way be profitable for them. This is that kingly power, most magnificent indeede, and allwayes to bee magnified. Nowe in that they say that they shall raigne vpon the earth, it is manifest from hence as wee said right nowe vpon the 8.verse, that this company belonges to the militant Church that raigneth vpon the earth. For what should the Saintes in heauen that haue obtayned heauenly glorie,reioyce in an earthly dominion ?

11. *And I heard round about the Throne and the Beasts:* Heare is the thanksgiuinge of the Angels, who doe magnifye God apart from the Church, as who haue another reason for it then men that are redeemed by the bloud of Christ: For these are restored beinge fallen, those are sustayned and kept from fallinge. And therefore they are placed without the circuite of the Throne and of the Elders, vnto which notwithstandinge they are next adioyned,gardinge the Church on euery side, partly that they may watch for the saluacion thereof, partly also that they may reioice with it for the prosperitie thereof. Hence it is that in the second place theire gratulatinge is recorded, as if they did more & more euery day perceiue by meanes of the Church, the incomprehensible mysterie of the redemption , into which they doe prie with so great and greedie desire; 1.Pet.1.12.

twenty Elders, followe the conduct of the beasts , as it is wont to bee
done in the Church ; where the people speaketh to God, not so much
in theire owne wordes, as in the wordes of the Minister, and doe giue
themselues wholy to bee guided at his commaund , as touchinge Re-
ligion, and the manner of worshippinge God, as wee haue obserued,
Chap. 4. 9. 10. &c.

## The 6. Chapter.

### The Logicall Resolution of it.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' with ornate leaf and vine motifs in a square frame.</image-desc>

*So much of the worthines of the Prophecy. The euents followe, which are first Seales, after that Trumpetts, last of all Violes. For the whole Prophecy that remaineth is distinguished into three notable termes of time, which containe in them the principall changes that are to fall out in the world, euen untill the comming of Christ, euery one of which is againe diuided into seauen moments the members of those 3. Termes, so that the whole Period following doth alwayes arise out of the last Article of the Period that goeth before. As touching the Seales, there is a certaine preparation in each of them, and then a Type of things to come. Nowe the Preparation is partly common whereby the Lambe doth open each of them in order, partly proper to the foure first, which besides the opening of them hath an inuitement to come and see by one of the foure Beasts. The Types in this Chapter are fixe, for there are so many seales opened in it) the White Horse vers. 2. The Redd vers. 4. The Black vers. 5. The Pale vers. 8. The Crye of the Soules vers. 9.10.11. And a mighty earth quake unto the ende of the Chapter.*

## T H E  E X P O S I T I O N.

*After that I beheld vvhen the Lambe opened the first of the seales.* Nowe
doth the H. Ghost sett vpon the euents them selues, which shall enfor-
me vs as touching the interchangeable courses of the world, so farre
as it shall concerne the Church, and those such as are of any moment
and that to the last consummation of all things. A great matter, and
exceeding necessary to be knowne, but such as no mortall eye though
neuer so sharpe-sighted, cā peirce into it. And therefore the same God
to whome in the beginning I made my prayer, doe I nowe againe call
vpon for his helpe, hauing by his grace alone made some good pro-
ceedinge thus farre. That he woud enable me to finish happily those
things, that remaine who hath geuen me power fo to begin, as is I
trust agreeing with his Truth. Thou their fore most Holy and most
Wise Lambe of God who onely haist meritted to take and to vnseale
the Booke, and that not to keepe those secretts to thy selfe alone, but
to cōmunicate them vnto the Church, so faire as might be behoofeful
for it. Grant I beseech thee forthy goodnes, sake, to me thy most
vnworthy seruant that I clearely perceiuing those things, which these
hidden and close kept seales containe, may in a holy manner lay the
same open vnto the world, to the edification of the Church, the ruine
of Antichrist, and the glory of thine owne name, which is to be mag-
nified vnto all ages, Amen. In that we distinguish the euents into three
Rankes, we haue the Spirit himselfe, for our Author to followe in so
doing, who doth annex the Trompets to the seales, and the violes to
the Trōpets so that alwayes the first of that which followeth, ariseth
out of the last of that which goeth before. They therefore doe cast
darke mistes before their owne eyes, who doe thrust the seales, the
Trompets, the violes, the seauen Candlesticks also, all into one, so as
euery one of each ouder doe cleaue one to another mutually in an
equall degree, as if the Father and his sonnes were equall, & did runt
out the same race of yeares together. Moreouer seeing the seales are
as it were pledges of things to come the Trompetts are euills that
rush vpon the world with a great noise, the violes such euils, as come

fifth Booke against Heresies, and Eusebius out of Ireneus, in the third

and ready course, not hindered with any perplexcities hard to be gone

the declaring of the word and then wee shall see the matter it selfe, &
the argrement of it.

The first preparation is of the Lambe opening the first seale. For
this Lambe is the word of the Father, who furnisheth vs with the
vnderstanding of Gods will, whatsoeuer it is wee knowe thereof.
Nowe the Euents are called Seales, both because they containe a most
hidden mistery, kept from the vnderstanding of the profane multitude
of men; Isa. 8. 16. As also because these first documents, should bee
as it were pledges of those that should come after. Not that wee
vnderstande them to bee bare foresignifications, and vaine promi-
sses and threatnings, which doe foretell and denounce good things
and euill, onely in word, the executiõ whereof is elswhere recorded in
this Booke, (for that is no where to bee found) but that they bee such
kind of Signes, which doe carry at once with them selues their execu-
tion, and yeeld a found pledge of things to come. Hee unsealeth the
Seales in order, one after another, not all together with one and the
same labour, both because the nature of the things to be done did so
require, and the whole Prophecye was not to be uttered out at once,
but to be broached by litle and litle, that it might be able to Minister
to the Church as it were a daily pittance for her releife.

The second preparation is of one of the foure Beasts, calling Iohn
to come and see. Nowe this first Beast is the Lyon, Chapt. 4. 7. The
Beasts are the Gouernours of the Churches, as hath bene obserued in
the aforesaid place, whose labour God doth vse, to instruct others.
These doe call to see and marke, not onely because it is their office to
admonish the Church of things that should fall out, whether they be
good or bad, but especially because the matters which should befall
in the next place, should be notable through their faithfulnes and dili-
gence. Nowe the Lyon speaketh first, because they who should enter

the listes first of all, should be of like virtue and successe, no lesse prevailing in that which they entend, then Lyons that followe their preye. The voice is as it were of Thunder, piercing, and striking farre of, so as it might be heard by many, and a farre of; Come saith he, and see, speaking vnto Iohn who nowe bare the person of the faithfull people, who should likewise be stirred vp to obserue these meruailous euents. The which is also common to the three Seales following, that this being once said, may bee vnderstood in the rest.

2. *I looke therefore, and behold a vvhite Horse.* The first Type is a white Horse, and his Rider with a Bowe, and a Crowne. As touching the Horse, it is a warlike, and a swift Beast, to which God doth worthily both here, and elsewhere compare his owne actions, because they will breake through with great courage, and swiftnes, whatsoeuer men shall endeuour to the contrary, *Zach. 6.* The white colour is ioyfull and festiuall, vsuall in any notable solemnity, as in the Triumph of Dioclesian and Maximian. After that, (saith *Pompon. Lætus*) the charret of the triumphers followed, made of Gold & pretious stones. Which foure horses drewe that stroue in whitenes with the snowe. But there is a rider attributed both to this and to the other horses, that wee may knowe that they doe not range abroad at randome as they list, but are guided, and gouerned with the raines of Gods prouidence. Nowe of what kinde this rider is, it may easily be coniectured by the analogy of the 8. verse. For there he is by name designed, who sitteth vpon the pale Horse, whose name is Death; the name then of this, (who is so goodly, and pleasant to see to) may be life or Truth. Nowe in that hee is furnished with a bowe and a Crowne, and hee cometh forth conquering, and that hee might conquere, by them is signified, that an onsett shalbe geuen a farre of, and that a famous victory is to bee obtained from thence, such as should not vanish away with the present successe, but should flourish alike in a future happines. For A bowe is such a kinde of weapon, as with which the enemies are striken, both a loofe, and at hand; The Crowne is an ensigne of victory, so that all things are ioyfull and prosperous, both in the Horse, and in the Rider: so standeth the Interpretation of the wordes, vnto which the History doth so meruailously agree, that no picture can more happily resemble his Patterne, then the Type of this Seale doth resemble the state of those times. Certainly nowe the truth did triumph besett about the head with a Crowne, and the Emperours lay ouerthrowne with the bowe, who yet seemed to bee farre out of the reach of priuate men. Yea by meanes of one Apology onely darted out, the enemies were so repressed euen in the most re-mote Cuntries, that they could doe nothing with all their assaultes against the truth. The same Iustine did by his most learned writings, stoppe the mouthes both of the Iewes and of the Grecians, so that the victory of the Truth was on all sides renowned. This time therfore being the next immediatly from Iohn, becomming famous through Apologies, and the ioyfull fruite of the Persecution suppressed, is the voice of the Lyon, that is, of the first Beast, as also that pleasant festi-uity, which the truth kept sitting on her white Horse with a Bowe and a Crowne.

3. *And when hee had opened the second Seale :* So much for the first Seale. The second followeth, which as touching the Lambe that ope-neth it, hath no newe matter in it ; as for the Beast that is an other, namely an Oxe, which had the second place, Chapt.4.7. Nowe this Beast is as wee knowe borne to labour, not to bee compared to the Lyon in the glory, of conquering, yet much more noble through the praise of enduring toile, and trouble. Neither is the voice here, so terrible, and so shrill, as was the voice of the Lyon thundring before, but ordinary, and vsuall, whence it is that he reporteth that hee heard the second Beast, saying, and yet it was such as had his force to excite men to geue heed to the euent.

time of the warres, wherewith the whole world should bee shaken,

fightings and battells betwene the Heathens, whereby some nations
should rush vpon the destruction of others. Wherefore here is no
entreating of the persecution of the Church, but of the tempestuous

being a great sword geuen to the Rider. The which thing came so
to passe, after that Antonius Pius had ended his life. For his sonne

<header>OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chap.6.</header>

thus. And hurt not the wine and the oile. The meaning is, yet see thou hurtest not the wine and the oile, after the Hebrue manner, the copulative being putt for the disjunctive. These Words oile and wine can not bee referred to those things which went before. As if hee should say, let such a measure of wheate bee sold for a Denarius, and let three such measures of barly bee sold for a denary, likewise let oile and wine be sold for a denary. For the words oile and wine are in the fourth case following the words, hurt not, or as Iunius turnes it in this place deale not vniustly with them. But they are not put in the nominative case going before a verbe, as the words for measure and measures are. Wherefore all releife for maintaining of life should not bee taken away, but necessaries onely should bee diminished. The oile and the wine, which serue for delight, should bee preserved without harme, because it seemed good to God to punish the meaner sort first, the Princes and peeres being reserued as dainties and kept from the famine for the plague. For whome hunger could not wast, because of their wealth and abondance, those the pestilence should feede on and those should it consume with a swift death, as we may see in the next Seale. So much for the words. The event here decyphered is not so plainly recorded, by the History writers as were to be wished, seeing that they doe cull out the more exellent matters, as for those that be common and vulgar, they passe by them easily, for the most part, seing this famine doth cheifely consist in the scarcity, of corne onely, not in the dearth of all victualls. And yet God would haue some footsteps of it to be extant, as much as should be enough to saue the credit of this prophecy. Vnto Antonius Verus commodus his sonne succeeded during the time of whose empire the world had some breathing from outward calamities through Gods mercy, and that for this cause as I suppose, because it had plague, and mischeife enough onely by hauing so wicked an Emperour, Pertinax and Iulianus succede him, both of them hauing a short raigne, & for that cause being the lesse mischeivous. At length Severus cometh to the Empire, who was a cruell Author of a most grieuous butchery of Christians, whether it were of his owne accord, or by the compulsion of others. At that time the third Beast cryed out mainly, admonishing the faithfull, that God would bee revenged of their wicked loathing of spirituall food, with sending a great penury of foode for this present life.

For Tertullian whome by right you may call a man, as being one
that excelled in witt, acutenes, learning, who hath as many arguments
almost as words in his writings, who in a very testy moode did reuolt
vnto montanisme, and so by this infirmity of his, did likewise shewe,
that nothing incident to the nature of a man was disagreeable vnto
him. This Tertullian (I say) wrote a most learned Apology against
the Gentiles, and sent it to the cheife Gouernours of Rome; out of
which as Francis Zephyrus writeth, they might at least priuily and
couertly take knowledge of the common cause of the Christians,
seeing it was not lawfull to doe it openly. And hee did not thinke it
fitt to speake vnto the Princes onely, of the Romane Empire, and
that generallonely, but also by name call vpon Scapula, the deputy
of Carthage, if so be that he might perhaps mollifie his sauage minde
He laboureth to teach him what was the true cause of the publike cal-
lamities to wit, that the wicked world by persecuting of the truth
did pull vppon it selfe those unfruitfull seasons, and grounds, so that
after the seedetimes the haruesttimes were lost, and inuadations by
showers, and horrible tempests did spoile all things for so hee saith,
yet must wee needs be greiued, that there is no citty that shall carry
away, scotfree the shedding of our bloud, euen as also it befell under
Hilarian the Gouernour, when as touching the corne floores of our
burialls, they had cryed, let there be no corne floores, they were indeed
no floores to those that owned them, for they did not carry their
haruests in thether. Which words doe plainly enough teach, that the
barrennes was very great in those times, when as there were no har-
uests, and therfore as it seemeth those cornefloures of theirs were of
old granted to the Christians, in which they might bury, their dead,
seeing that in regard of the great barrennes, they were of no use to lay
vp corne in. And why should wee not acknowledge a blacke Horse
here as the truth is, when as the Sunne had almost quite lost his light
in the assembly at Vtica, and that not by an extraordinary Eclipse, but
being sett in his full height and exaltation, as the same Tertullian
witnesseth writing to Scapula. Neither did this dearth of corne onely
vexe the wicked Gentiles, but it did likewise trouble the Christians
also, seeing God will haue commodities to be common to the profane
with the godly, and discommodities to be common to his people with
the wicked, that by this equall copartnership, all men might haue

8. *And behold a pale Horse*. The fourth Type is a pale Horse, whose
Rider is described by his name, his companion, and the busines com-
mitted to him. The colour of the Horse in the Greeke properly signi-
fieth greene as the grasse, sometimes it is that dead colour of herbes
that waxe dry whence it is taken sometimes for palenes, which is the
hue of any withering & fading thing, as feare is called pale, because it
maketh men pale; and so Constans the Father of Constantine the
great was called Chlorus because of his palenes, as Zonarus saith in
the life of Dioclesian. This diseased colour doth very well become
this Horse, on whose backe Death it selfe sitteth; The rider is decla-
red in the next words, where hee that sitteth, is used for, to him that
sitteth, the first case for the third, which kinde of speaking is after the
Hebrue as hath bene observed, Chap. 2. 26. Though least any should
thinke it to bee incongruous, and so through his owne ignorance
should impute a barbarisme to the Holy writer, there bee examples
enough in other tongues of this, taken from the most elegant Authors
that are. Livye speakes so, Those saith he that were skillfull in matters
of Religion, and in the common lawe, did denye that when two ordi-
nary consulls of that yeare, the one had died by sword, the other by
disease, the consul that was put into either of their roomes could call
a Councell. Where the first case is putt for the seconde, so Sallust
writeth. Therfore Kings in the beginning, for that was the first na-
me of an Empire vpon the earth thei did diuersely some of them exer-
cise their witt, some their bodye. Many such speeches are noted by
learned men, by whome it is also obserued that this is a manner of
writing most familiar vnto the Grecians. First there is a name geuen
to this Rider, to wit, Death. By proportion whereof names may bee
also geuen to the former riders, so that hee that sitteth on the white
horse may bee called, Truth, on the Red warre, on the black famine.
The which I geve notice of, because I see some to faine nothing fittly,
the Deuell and other Riders I knowe not whome. Nowe this Rider
is called Death in a peculiar and principall regard, both because the
Stroke of this Seale should bring destruction more swiftly then any
other, as also because it should annoye men with many kindes of
deaths. The third scourge of God is wont to bee Pestilence, as in
Ezechiel, they should fall by sword, famine, pestilence, Chapt. 6. 11.
Which yet is not here made a Captaine of a bande, but is onely pressed

Commonly translated into Latin *Infernus*, but it were fitter to be *Sepulchrum*, the Graue, which the Greeke word also signifieth, and so ought it to bee understood in this place, especially seing many Saints should dye amōg the rest of whome it were wicked to thinke that they were deuoured of the Hell of the damned. Afterwards power is geuen to this Rider, and together with it, is it circumscribed in his bounds; & power was geuē them, where some coppies doe reade changing the order of the words, and power was geuen him ouer the fourth part of the earth to kill; The vulgar Latin, ouer the fourth part of the earth reads, ouer foure parts of the earth, by this meanes the whole world being subdued, under their Tyranny against the consent of all the Greeke Coppies. But it is a hainous crime to thinke that nowe after the *Trent* decree, the Latin translation is not framed out of the most perfect Coppies. And yet a commodious sense might bee drawne out of the words so read, that the foure parts of the Earth should note out the multitude of the Cuntries, and regions wherein this destruction did assaile men, euen as also the fourth part of the earth noteth out the multitude of men, who should perish in this utter decay. The power is determined in that fourefold kinde of destroying, which Death sitting on the Horse useth as her ministers. The first band hath wants and battailes for their leaders, whose weapon is a sword. The second army is lead by want of victualls. The third is Pestilence, for that is meant by the words (by Death) the name of the generall being geuen to it, because it takes men away with a most quicke and dispatching death and setts before our eyes a most expresse Image of Death, as also it is alwayes wont to be the attendāt waiting on famine; & in the mother tongues of many nations it is called mortality. As for the wild Beasts, if they be properly taken, *I remember not that I haue read any notable dammage brought by them at this time , although it is no sleight coniecture , that they did much harme in the Easterne and Southern cuntryes.* In some latter ages when Famine & Pestilence did also waxe great and greiuous, men were afraid of dogges, least that seing they had bene used to feed vppon carkases of dead men cast out, they should afterwards fall vppon liuing men to make meate of them ; wherevppon they betake them selues to the killing of dogges, *Euseb. Book 9. 8.* Neither could it be, but that when meate failed the wild beasts in the feilds, and men grewe lesse able to defend them selues , many were deuoured by the wild beasts. But if we referre this to cruel men of sauage tyrants, there was neuer any in memory of man so great flockes of wild beasts, that did in euery place rende and teare men in pieces. For when *Gallienus* was Emperour, who alone did enioy all the Empire after that *Valerian* was taken captiue, there arose so many Tyrants, that tooke to them selues the name of the Emperour, as had neuer bene in so long a succession of Emperours from *Cæsars* time, who was dictator to that very daye. There are thirty reported by *Trebellius* to haue bene at one time whereof some in one place of the world, some in another did inuade the Empire, among whome also certaine women made a mockery of the *Romane* authority. Howe great a Butchery of men must there needs bee, when so many wild beasts did at once striue about the Empire. Thus then wee haue the three Seales, each of them notable by their owne scourges, the two former by singuler ones, the 3. that was last by all kind of punishments, with which the world was plagued because it had so wickedly despised and molested the truth. For when as more mild chastisements could doe no good with obdurate mindes, all the armies almost of Death are sett in araye against them , euen as the Euent hath also proued most fully. And yet these euils are not proper to this Age alone, that they should agree to no other, but they are the usuall punishments of such as despise Pietye, *Leuit. 26. Ezech. 6. 11. &c.* And so afterwards wee may see that after *Galienus* his raigne, the plague & famine did cõsume all things while *Maximinus* raigned in the East, *Euseb. <margin>9. *And vvhen he had opened the fifth Seale, I favve soules vnder the Altar.*</margin>
There is no Beast belonging to the first Seale , by whose voice Iohn is inuited to see. Neither is that done but euen for this cause, because this should passe awaye closely , there being no publike and solemne crye made by which to stirre vp men to obserue the euent, as there was in the former ; neither indeed doth the Historye relate,that any man vndertooke any such labour , in which regard such an office might bee worthily geuen him. Besides this Seale consists partly in reporting of things past, partly in recording an euent to come that is of such a nature as is wont to slippe by almost without perceiuerance. Cheifely seing we are so disposed that things aduerse and trouble some sticke faster in our minds, then things that be prosperous. Wherefore seing the Seales are conformable to the euents, it is no meruaile, that here is no type propounded as to the which there was no euent to answere it.

I favve soules vnder the Altar. The fifth Seale are the Soules lying vnder the Altar in this verse , requiring vengeance vppon their enemies,verf. 10. And carrying away an answere,verf. 11. Which three members doe belong to the three times , past, present, and to come. *The soules lying vnder the Altar* , doe most elegantly declare by that which followeth that which went before , to wit, what was the state of the Church during the time of the former Seales , and with howe great cruelty of men it was vexed. Wee haue indeed heard of the Truth ouercomming,we haue also had it reported that warre, famine and pestilence with their adherents did seaze vppon and destroy all things, but there was no mention as yet made , howe it fared in the meane time with the worshippers of Christ ; though their combate might haue bene coniectured by the victory of truth and by those calamities which did pester the world , it might bee conceaued,that there was great wrong offered to the Godly for which their enemies were so sharply punished. But nowe the matter is made manifest by this complaint of the Martyrs that were slaine , that is to say, that an infinite deale of the bloud of men adoring the Sonne of God was shed from the time wherein Iohn wrote,vntill the Empire of Galienus was ended,

But the words are as yet to be illustrated, and to be deliuered from the cauills of the aduerſaries. Whence then is this ſpeech fetched, that the ſoules of the Martyrs ſhould lye vnder the Altar? Doubtleſſe from the reaſon which *Dauid* often vſed, as *Pſal*. 27.5. For he will hide me in the time of trouble in his Tabernacle, in the ſecrett place of his Tent will he couer me, and will ſett me on a rocke. So againe, thou ſhalt hide them in the ſecrett place of thy preſence from the pride of man, thou ſhalt keepe them cloſe in thy Tabernacle, from the ſtrife of tongues, *Pſal*. 31.20. Nowe It is well knowe, that the Tabernacle both in the parts of it, and in the whole, was a ſhadowiſh figure of Chriſt. Wherefore to bee hidden in the Tabernacle is to haue a receptable, & a refuge pitched in Chriſt alone, as with whome onely we are couered, and fenced againſt all afſaults of the aduerſaries. Hence it is manifeſt why the Soules are ſaid to be vnder the altar, namely, that from thence we might firſt vnderſtande that all the Saluation euen of Martyrs is placed onely in the death of Chriſt, vnder which the Holy Champions lying hid as vnder a buckler, may ſafely and without terrour appeare before God; and

that they haue need of this couering of the Sonne of God as without
which they are not able to stande in the fight of Gods Maiesty.

And then that wee might knowe, that all the sonnes of God
ought to be made conformable to the Image of their first borne bro-
ther Rom. 8. 29. And ought to goe into heauen the same way, which
he went before vs, that is, by being made through suffering of afflicti-
ons sacrifices and oblations, and by being killed with many sorrowes.
In regard whereof Paul saith that he did fulfill by his flesh that which
was wanting in the afflictions of Christ for his bodye, Coloss. 1. 24.

Nowe these wants he speakes of are conformities, not satisfactions
either of dignity or of meritt. For whatsoever remaineth as yet to be
suffered by any of the saints, that is after a sort waiting to the afflicti-
ons of Christ, who esteemeth all our calamities to be his owne. These
things are common to all the faithfull, who haue all their place alike
vnder the Altar, but yet they belong chiefely to the Martyrs, whose
sufferings are more notable then of any other, for which cause this
hiding place is given to them. Seing then to lye vnder the Altar is to
be taken in this sense after the manner of speaking used in the Scrip-
tures, howe impiously doth the Jesuite wrest these things to that idola-
trous rite which the Papists, use in dedicating Temples? For so it is
their manner to bury the bodyes or the Reliques of Martyrs under the
Altars that are in those Churches, which they consecrate to them, and
then to call that Church by the name of that Martyr, whose reliques
are buried there; as if there were more regard to be had of the reli-
ques vnder the Altar, thē of him whome they wil haue to be sacrificed
vpon the Altar. What should the Holy Ghost haue respect here to this
custome, by which so exceeding great iniury is offered both vnto
Christ, as also to his Holy Martyrs? To Christ, because he is spoiled of
his honour, and thrust downe beneath his Seruants. To the Martyrs,
in that they are made the Spoilers of his glory, for defence whereof
they haue spilld their bloud. Neither doe the Jesuits thinke it enough
to abuse these words to the patronage of their Idolatry, unlesse they
doe also plucke vp & spoile that which was well sett downe by others.

For it was said that there was one encounter more remaining for them. And indeed it might easily be vnderstood, that the ende which should be putt to these publike slaughters, was not nowe farre of, seing all degrees of men did incline with so great kindnes to fauour the truth. Nowe this Seale hath both something proper vnto it, which we haue in the rest of this Chapter, as also something that is common, which is handled in the 7. Chapter. That is the last combate of the Seales, the first member whereof containeth an amplification of an heauy Tragedy, and of all the former calamities, vers. 12. 13. 14. The second containeth a ioyfull shutting vp of the same with a subduing and ouerthrow of the enemies and a happy composing of all troubles, vers. 15. 16. 17. 14. *And Heauen departed avvay.* Heauen doth euery where in this Booke, signifie the vniuersall Church, that is of the purest note, both because that reall heauen shalbe at last the habitacion which is prepared for it, as also because in the meane time that is so represented by this, that it can haue no more expresse image then this is vppon earth. Nowe this similitude of a Booke folded together, is taken from the auncient custome whereby Bookes were not compacted into leaues but were wound about like litle wheeles, wherevppon they were called volumes.

readily they fell and yeelded.

14. *And Heauen departed avvay.* Heauen doth euery where in this
Booke, signifie the vniuersall Church, that is of the purest note,
both because that reall heauen shalbe at last the habitacion
which is prepared for it, as also because in the meane time that is so
represented by this,that it can haue no more expresse image then this
is vppon earth. These things therfore doe teach,that the Calamity did
not stay it selfe in the Pastours alone, but that the whole face of the
Church was couered ouer with so blacke darknes, that it did scarce
appeare any where. Let Eusebius be per used Booke 8. 1. Where he
bewaileth the miserable desolation thereof borrowing words to la-
ment with all from the lamentations of Ieremy, Chap.2.1.2. Also out
of the Psal.89.39.&c. But yet this desolation should be onely like the
folding of a scroll together; A Booke is not defaced,when it is rolled
together, but remaines as great, as is was before, it is in deed made
lesse easy to be seene, being thrust vp into a farre more narrowe roo-
me,so nothing should be diminished from the soundnes and integrity
of the Church,howsoeuer her glory might seeme to be extinguished.
Nowe this similitude of a Booke folded together, is taken from the
auncient custome whereby Bookes were not compacted into leaues
but were wound about like litle wheeles, whereupon they were cal-
led volumes.

In the same sense is it said, Hebr. 1. 12. *Thou shalt folde them
like a garment*, that is, thou shalt deface all their beauty, and make
them like to a garment wrapped vp whose elegancy, and comelines
can not bee beheld. In the Hebrue it is, *Thou shalt change them*,
Psal.102.27. Which the Septuagint translate significantly, *thou shalt*

# *The 7. Chapter.*

## The Logicall Resolution.

*Hetherto we haue spoken of that which is proper to the sixt Seale. That which is common followeth, to wit, a certaine generall portraiture of the whole Church, that should be vnto the last ende thereof. The which thing is distinguished into two times. The first time is that, wherein the true worshippers are defined in their certaine number, Who are called by a speciall name, such as bee sealed; the occasion of whose sealing are the foure Angells, that be readye to shewe rigour without regard of any person, standing for this purpose at the foure corners of the earth, that they might stoppe the passage of all meanes for saluation vers. 1. And then the Minister vsed in sealing them is spoken of, who exempteth the elect from the multitude of those that perish, comming from the East withfull power, and no lesse couragiously executing his office that is imposed on him, by forbidding with a great voice, that they should goe on in their course, till hee had sealed vp a certaine number of men that were to bee excepted, vers. 2. 3. Nowe howe great the number is of those which are sealed, is declared in generall vers. 4. In speciall out of what Tribes, and howe many out of each Tribe, vers. 5. 6. 7. 8. And this time belongs cheifely to the Trompets. The second time is that, wherein an indefinite, & and innumerable mul-*

## THE EXPOSITION.

After that I favve foure Angells. This whole Chapter belongs to the fixt Seale, wherein a newe common Type is propounded of things that are to bee done hereafter. The former was common to all the three Periodes, Chapt. 4. This doth onely comprehend the two latter, namely the Trompetts and the Violes. For the Holy Ghost loueth to sett certaine common portraitures of matters before our eyes euer and anon, for perspicuities sake, and for the solace of the Saints, both that things might by this meanes be made more euident, as also that the issue being beheld a farre of, might refresh our mindes oppressed with greife. Nowe seing that after that last Act of the former calamities, which was spoken of in the ende of the former Chapter, the seauenth Seale should bring in troubles of a diverse kind, before hee commeth to declare them, he placeth this Table as it were in open viewe, in which we diligẽtly beholding the Image of the Holy Church

This purpoſe of the Holy Ghoſt being wel weighed in minde, will deliuer vs from that great Confuſion, whereby the Interpreters are wont to iumble all things together, and by that meanes to make the moſt wiſe diſtributer of times, the author of an incombrãce whereout a man can not ridd himſelfe, which if any where els, is eſpecially auoided in this Booke, wherein it ſhalbe made manifeſt, that the Holy Ghoſt is not one that loueth or breedeth, diſorders & confuſion. <margin>Foure Angells.</margin>
Theſe foure Angells are not thoſe that ſhall come in the laſt time, that ſhalbe a litle before the ende of the world; For the endevour of theſe Angels to repreſſe the winde, goeth ſomewhat before the ſealing it ſelfe, as the next words doe make plaine. Nowe theſe that are ſealed muſt raigne for a thouſand yeares vppõ the earth and thoſe not coming neere the ende by many Ages. As we wil ſhewe God aſsiſting at the 20. Chapt. the 4. verſe. But it greiueth me to contend ſo often with this Ieſuiticall monſter, to be ſhort then if euery verſe almoſt of this Booke confute not this fonde deuiſe, let it haue what autority it can come by. Beſides theſe are not good Angels, ſeeing that which they goe about to doe, tendeth to the deſtructiõ of ſoules rather than Bodies. Certainly the Prohibition doth not wholy take away from them power to hurt, but reſtraineth them onely for a time, till the Sealing was finiſhed, which it is plaine to haue bene done, before that the Trompetts ſound. Wherefore they ruſh in together with the Trompets, being in readines to bring in euill and being onely hindered by the ſtay of the Sealing, aſſoone as this were once finiſhed, they would eagerly flye vppon that from which they kept them ſelues backe againſt their wills. Therfore they doe cauſe thoſe foure euills, which are denounced by the foure Trompetts, and they are the diſmal and pernicious workers of ſo heauy an Euent. *Holding the foure vvinds of the earth.* We haue seene the Angels and their standings, their Enterprise, is to take away the winde from the earth; The foure winds of the earth saith Iohn, whereas yet there is but one winde in nature, but that one is diuerse according to the regions whence it bloweth. Nowe this is not a winde properly taken; seeing no such calamity as this hapned at any time, though there haue nowe passed many ages, since this Prophecye was made. And yet if it were a proper one , howe should not the stopping of it hurt aswell those that are sealed as the Reprobate, seeing they dwell together one with an other? I vnderstand therfore by winde, the force and power of the Holy Ghost, which Christ compareth to the winde, Ioh. 3. 8. *The vvinde (faith he) blowveth vvhether it vvill, so is euery one borne of the Holy Ghost.* For as of old that confused Chaos, and that seed of this world of ours, could not otherwise consist but by being quickened & refreshed by the Spirit, which moued it selfe aboue the waters, Gen. 1. 2. So neither doth this earth the sea? these trees here spoken of, feele any vital efficacy in themselves, unlesse that sanctifying winde doe sitt vppon them, out of whose breathing they may drawe their life and soule. It is not indeed in the power of the Creature, to represse the force of the heauenly Spirit, yet seeing they hinder the truth, which is the instrumēt whereby it is conuayed, it may worthily be said that the passages and pores are shutt vp, by which it should breath to our commodity.

*That the vvinde should not blowve vppon the earth, &c.* Nowe they are nombred vp, from whome the Angels would haue shutt vp the wind. That is to say from the Earth, the Sea the Trees. nowe he describes the Minister, by whome the Sealing is made; whome both the consideration of the time, and all the circumstances doe proue to be Constantine the great. This is he that succeeded in the Empire, after that the Lambe had thrust out Dioclesian, and the rest of those Idolatrous Tyrants. Nowe he ascended from the East being one that came forth from the Easterne parts to take the Empire vpon him. For when he was a yong man, he was a fouldier in pay in Syria vnder Dioclesian, but after that his virtue and valour had gott him so much enuye, that he was often putt in danger of his life by priuye cōspiracy & trechery; he was compelled to gett himselfe away by flight as swiftly as he could from the East and to goe with speed into Brittany vnto his Father. So saith Eusebius, on the life of Constāt. Orat. 1. He procured his safety by flight. Zonaras saith that he was geuen to Galerius for an Hostage to whome when he sawe that he grewe hatefull through enuye, and when he sawe himselfe of purpose exposed to danger in the warre with the Sarmatians, and was againe comaunded for the same purpose to fight with a Lyon, both which dangers he escaped happily, at lentgh he saith that he fledd away to his Father, and did with all auoide the danger by this meanes, and did enjoy his Fathers Empire, the cheife seate whereof he afterwards placed at Bizantium. Therefore whether we respect his first returne out of the East, or we understande, those Proclamation as touching the worship of the true God by Christ, which after he was stablished in his Empire, did fly abroad from thēce through all the Romane world, the History doth very well agree with the predictiō, but the former of these doth seeme to come nearer to the meaning of the Holy Ghost, because of those things that followe.

*Hauing the Seale of the liuing God.* That is, both himselfe being endued with the true knowledge of God, and hauing cheife authority to propagate it to others, whome while he prouoked to embrace the truth by his owne example, and earnest care, he is said to feale them with the Seale of the liuing God, and to make them Gods peculiar people set at liberty from seruing the Deuill. He is said to crye with a great voice, being one that aduanced the truth by his Edicts which he sett forth, and so remooued farr away to his uttermost all that which did hinder the enlarging thereof. For we shall see that such a kinde of a rouing progresse as it were of the Church hath continued from the death of Constantine. For in the first times, the purest part thereof seemeth to haue bene in Afrike, as it were in the tribe of Iuda. Which was then most free of all the parts of the world, from the heresy of Arius, though Aegypt that borders vppon it had hatched it forth, and an infinite deale of filthy corruption had in the meane time ouerflowed the rest of the world. Nowe this integrity endured from the time of Constantine till the inuasion of the Vandals. Then Reuben, & Gad succeeded. For when the Barbarians ouerwhelmed the whole East and South, the whole hope that was left, and the face of the Church did liue and flourish in the East. But when the Saracens did at length lay this vineyard also wast, our Britany, and the north coast cuntries, that looke toward the west, did flourish out as it were Ascher, and Nephtalim, when as two thousand Monks of Bangor, and more, refused to beare the Romish yoke. For which cause the Britanes did endure that greiuous persecution, which Austen the monke sent from Rome stirred vp against them. The Age following brought in Manasses, partly Eastern, partly westerne, when as both Leo Isaurus, & Charles the great with ioint endeuours, though somewhat disioined in places and times, did condemne the worship of Images by Synodes, which they called together. The times next to these were most miserable, whe~ as Antichrist had nowe come to his highest toppe of Authority, and power. Nowe did the truth so lye troden vnder foote almost euery where, that the Church could not be conspicuous as hauing any certaine settling, but those who were sealed did lurke and lie confusedly, and scatteringly as it were Simeon and Leui knowne to God alone, but altogether remote from the eyes of the world. In after Ages the seale went ouer to Issachar, and Zabulon, namely to the Northcoast part, that is to a people bending towards the Summer Sunrise. For there are famous conuersions reade of about this time, of the men of Poland, Saxony, Sueuia, Norway, &c. The exceeding great admiration of Gods goodnes in reſtoring his Church ſhould drawe forth a crying and ſpeaking loud from the Saints for very ioye, as who could not ſatiſſfye them ſelues in expreſsing this infinite mercy of God by an ordinary manner of ſpeaking. We and our fathers haue ſeene this thing performed with our eyes. There is no man that hath taſted of true pietye, but he giueth thankes to God from his heart,for the reſtoring of the light of the truth in theſe laſt times. And though that Antichriſt of Rome doe ſtorme and gnaſh his teeth at it, we ceaſe not to magnifie the great name of god freely and cheerfully , ſo that the whole world ringeth with the voices of the Saints. And why ſhould we not like to cõquerors crye out with gladſome hearts ſeeing we haue palmes in our hands,and we haue the neckes of our enemies ſubdued vnder our feete by the grace of God? God graunt,that we may alwayes magnifie him with ſuch praiſes as his ſo great kindnes deſerueth at our hands leaſt by our ſmal account that we make of ſo infinite grace of his we doe pull vpon our ſelues ſome rufull calamity, wherewith the ioy of our triumph ſhould be turned into our ſorowe ſhame,and confuſion.

**11.** *And all the Angels ſtood.* See Chapt. 5. 11. The auncient gladſomenes of the Church ſhall come about againe, at which the Angels ſhal reioice,both they them ſelues making a concent together with the ioyfull acclamation of the Saints, & as alſo praiſing God by them ſelues for their ſakes.

**12.** *And povver, and might.* That is , let the praiſe of his power and might bee geuen him , for God ſhould ſhewe forth marvailous power in deliuering his Church. The Saints indeed doe beare palmes, but the victory is obtained by the power of God alone. Howe indulgent is our God, who will haue it to be his labour in deſtroying the enemies,and our triumph.

But in that place the abolishing of the Ceremonies is vnderstoode, as the which they shal require no more to worship God with al. Here we are pilgrimes as yet from the Lord vppon earth, vvhere vve haue need of meanes to helpe vs to vvorship him, of vvhich there shalbe no vfe at all in Heauen.

16. *They shall not hunger.* There shall nothing be wanting vnto them, neither shall any calamitye afflict them, vvhich is signified by hunger and thirst. Moreover all the causes of calamities shall be driuen farre away, the Sunne shall not scorch them, neither shall there be any burning heate & drought, that shall bring in a scarcity; the whole frame of the Creatures shall conspire to promote the felicity of the holy people. Here is a tast geuē of those things in a fewe words, which are declared afterwards more largely.

17. *Because the lambe vvho is in the midst of the Throne doth feed them.* Nowe is the cause of the former felicity related, to the seuerall parts whereof it is agreeably distributed, so as those words he shal feed thē, answere to that, they shall not hunger, those words he shall leade them to the liuely fountaines of waters, respect that thirst, which he said should be no longer endured. Those words God shall wipe away all teares, haue respect to the heate of the Sunne, which he promiseth shalbe no more troublesome vnto them afterwards.

*From their eyes.* That is, the teares, which trickle downe from their eyes. Montanus reads from out of their eyes, that is, the teares which doe as it were seate them selues in their eyes, as if God would leaue no power of weeping by drying vp their eyes. Isay saith, the Teare from all faces, Chapt. 25. 8. Thus then is the Common Type during the Trompetts and Violes, that is, euen to the last consummation of the world. About the beginning and proceeding of the Trompetts the nomber of the Elect should be sealed, about the end of them there should bee a more joyfull & plentifull multitude more freely and openly profesing the truth, which afterwards increasing daily vnder the Violes, should at length haue their brethren of the Iewes ioined vnto them, when as there should be at length a full happines, so great as can be looked for vppon earth, which shalbe neuer interrupted againe with any such times of trouble, as doe commonly fall out nowe, till Christ himselfe shall come to Iudgement. This common Type is to bee explaned by each member of it in the rest of this

## THE EXPOSITION.

*And vvhen he had opened the ſeauenth Seale.* So much of the Sixth Seale the Seauenth followeth, whose effect that ariſeth out of the opening of it is called a ſilence, which is ſometimes vſed for any ceaſing of a matter. As, why doe ye hold your peace in bringing back the King, that is, ſtand ſtill, and doe not beſtirre your ſelues, 2.Sam.10. 11. Oftentimes it is oppoſed to a tumult, whence we reade of the vvaues of the Zea that are ſtill, Pfal. 107. 29. Of which kinde is this ſilence here, that was made in heauen, that is, in the Church vppon earth, which is often called by Chriſt the kingdome of Heauen. The ſpace of ſilẽce is as it were halfe an houre, that is, very litle, that ſhould almoſt ende as ſoone as it ſhould begin. By which we are taught, that the Church, ſhould afterwards enioye a happy reſt for ſome ſmall ſpace of time after that the opẽ enemies thereof ſhould be thruſt out, and that healthfull Angell Conſtantine the great ſhould ariſe out of the Eaſt. For this ſilence is ioined next vnto that ſubduing of thoſe cruel enemies, wherewith the ſixt Chapter was concluded. For the common Type to which the ſeauenth Chapter belonged doth nothing at all breake of the order of things. And indeed ſuch an happy tran-

For first the Emperours themselves did scarce hold concord for three yeares together, & then straight after they were reconciled together, did Licinius assault the Christians with open force, and endeuour their vtter destruction. To this was added that ciuill warre, which burned out betwene the Bishops themselves, that were the Gouernours of the Church, who being free from all feare of the common enemy, did rush one vppon an other with the darts of reprochful words, as if they were cloyed with their peace, assoone as they had but tasted the sweetnes thereof euen at the tongues ende. To this was added that ciuill warre, which burned out betwene the *Bishops* them selues, that were the Gouernours of the *Church*, who being free from all feare of the com-mon enemy, did rush one vppon an other with the darts of reprochful words, as if they were cloyed with their peace, assoone as they had but tasted the sweetnes thereof euen at the tongues ende. See *Aurel. Victor.* of the *Cesars* part. 2. *Euseb. Lib. 10. 8. 9.* And vppon the life of *Constant*, *Book. 1.* At the ende, and in the beginning of the first.
