*And he staid before the Altar*; The Greeke is, at the Altar, Moun-
tanus, on the Altar, all in one meaning. It wilbe manifest afterwards,
Chapt. 11. 1. That the Church about this time did remooue into the
Temple, and hidd it selfe with in the secret places thereof: wherefore
hee is here worthily said to stand before the Altar, seeing he was the
principall of those, who being escaped out of the corruptions of the
world, went aside into the hiding place with in the Temple. But yet
he stoode not in this place as one of the commõ sort of the faithfull,
but in the araye of the high Priest, hauing a golden Censer, and many
odours geuen vnto him, that he might offer them with the prayers of
the Saints. Howe can these things agree to Constantine, maye some
say? Namely, as being a Type of the high Priest Iesus Christ, whose
person to beare is not nowe proper to any certaine kinde of men, but
common to all the faithfull, all whome Christ hath made Priests, not
secõdary, but cheife. But why should not he especially carry the Image
of a Priest, in whome the shadowing out of the Regall dignity did
cheifely shine forth? Well doth he speake of himselfe being in an as-
sembly of the Bishops. And I saith he, am here present as being one of
your company. For I would not denye my selfe to bee your fellow-
seruant, it being that wherein I doe cheifely reioice, Socrates Booke 1.
Chapt. 7.

*Hauing a golden Censer.* The Greeke word that doth properly sig-
nifie incense, is here taken for the censer it selfe, wherein it is offered,
as is manifest out of the fifth verse, where the Cẽser is filled out of the
fire of the Altar, nowe the Golden Censer was a vessel vsed in the holy
of holies, Hebr. 9. 4. & belonged onely to the high Priest.

*And there vvere odours geuen him.* This Angell therefore is not
Christ, who doth not take odours from another, elsewhere, but he him
selfe being a most rich, and abundant treasure of all graces, doth geue
liberally to euery one as much as is needfull. These odours are that
ample both power and desire of making peace, which was the ende
of the Priest hood, and of burning odours before God. For which
cause the Lord is said to smell a sweet fauour, when he accepteth of a
Sacrifice, Genes. 8. 21.

*With the Prayers of the Saints.* The Greeke hath the word prayers

geuen to any thing:is made of the same thing to which it is geuen.

Hee commeth nowe to the secondary effect, which onely dam-

tempest seemeth to rage more greiuously against the grasse then the Trees. For the third part onely of these is sett on fire but the whole grasse is burnt vp; but this whole grasse belongs onely to that third part, euen as the third part of Trees are al the Trees of the East, so that it fareth not a whit better with the Trees, then with the grasse. These things doe shewe vs, that all belonging to the Christian Religion, both high and lowe who kept in these Regions, and were not truly founded and built vpon Christ, were to be miserably smitten with this tempest, that they should make this wrack of their saluation. It may be you wil say, they were ordained to destruction & so damned, before & so it is tru indeed in regard of Gods con-saile yet it often falleth out, that reprobate men doe flatter them selues for a time with a false hope, & doe professe some outward deuoutnes with great shewe of forwardnes, which afterward time conuinceth to haue bene, but meere hypocrisy, and a vaine vizzard of holines. So these trees and grasse thus burnt vp, should suffer a losse of all their piety, by dashing them selues against the rocks of so great impiety that was among the Bishops. And indeed howe could it be otherwise, but that all they in whose hearts the truth had not taken deepe rooting, should either be carried away into errour, or which is worse, should despise all Religion, should reuolt from Christ, and hate those that worship him, as whome they should see to minde and labour this one thing, euen to stirre vp strife, contentions, and hurly burlies. Worthily doth Constantine in an Epistle, to the Synod gathered in Tyrus, vpbraid the Bishops, that they did nothing els but sowe discord and hatred, and such things as tended to the destruction of mankinde *Socrat. Book. 1. 34.* But there is no need of witnesses in a matter that is not doubtfull, rather is Gods great mercy to be magnified, which preserued a fewe safe from this boistrous strome.

This is a great Starre, not an obſcure and cloudy one, but of a notable greatnes. It fel from heauen, by reuolting from the true Church by hereſy, or ſome other impiety. It burneth as a lampe, becauſe the fire thereof is flaming; and ſhewing it ſelfe forth, openly breaking out into the publike viewe, not glowing onely with an hidden kinde of feruency, as the Mountaine burned a litle before; whoſe flame though ſhould not be long laſting, but for want of mat-ter to feed it with, like the flame of a lampe, it ſhould go out. It falleth into the Riuers and Fountaines, namely vppon thoſe, from whome as from Fountaines the doctrine ſhould flowe forth vnto others, ſuch as are the Biſhops the diſpenſers of the worde whoſe ſundry reſpect gets them ſundry names. Euen nowe they were ſhips trãſporting the traf-fick of the word hether and thether, nowe becauſe they doe feede and preſerue that whole Sea of Doctrine with their continuall flowing, and increaſe that which is abiding in the multitude, they are worthily compared to flouds and Fountaines. The Starre falleth vpon theſe, while perhaps the people remaineth more ſincere, which cã not con-ceiue of ſo great ſuttilties. The Name of the Starre is wormewood, not that it was so called commonly , but because it should shewe it selfe to bee some such thing by the effect. Nowe wormewood sometimes signifies the bitternes of affliction, as behold I will feede my people with wormewood, *Ierem. 9. 15.* That is, I will afflict them with most greiuous punishments. Sometimes it signifieth the deadly poison of hereticall wickednes, as, take heed least there be in any of you a roote bringing forth gall or wormewood, that is least your minde be a seminary of any Idolatrye, or of a cursed life as the most learned men *Tremellius* and *Iunius* doe interprete the place, *Deut. 29. 18.* Both of these *as it semeth*, are to be ioined here together, that so the bitternes of calamity should be mingled with naughty & corrupt doctrine. Nowe to come to the application , this third Angell blewe his Trumpet about eleuen yeares after the former. When as *Constantius* to whose share the Easterne Empire fell, straight after the death of his father , was cast downe from heauen into the *Arian* heresy through the fraud of a certaine Preist, whome he tooke into his familiar acquaintance. The impiety indeed was be gotten before by *Arius* , and had gotten some patrons, as we haue shewed before, but *Arius* did straightway dessemble a recantation, by the same cunning tricke *Eusebius* & *Theognis* recouered their chaires. Neither durst any man be any whitt trouble some in an open fort while *Constantine* was aliue; this madding gadbee did indeed vexe the minds of many and compelled them to stirre vp what troubles they could against those of the Sound beleife but they had another matter in pretence and shewe besides these were lesser starres. But *Constantius* was a great Starre flaming like a lampe, bringing forth the matter into the open light out of the lurking holes thereof, and striuing to amplifye it with exceeding great heate of spirit. The like account is to be had of *Valens* the Emperour, who followed after *Iulian* and *Iouinian*.

And yet the orthodoxe men endured all these things, and many things more at the hands of Macedonius of Constantinople, and of other of his companions, who were rather hellish furies, then Bishops, as Socrates reporteth, Booke 2. 27. This plague did a long time most miserable torment and vexe that third part, both by it selfe alone, as also by that unluckie brood of the Macedonians, & some such other cursed offspring, & yet after that Valens was dead, this flame, also died whose nourishmẽt was spent as of a lampe which hath no more oile supplied vnto it. And that not without cauſe but for this pur-poſe as it ſeemeth, becauſe the former euills proceeded from thoſe that were of the houſehold of faith in profeſsion,and therfore it was needefull not onely that it ſhould be declared what was done,but that the Authors alſo ſhould be knowne,to which the firſt effect did chei-fely belōg.Nowe this calamity ſhould come wholy from the enemye, and from men that are ſtrangers from the Church, touching whome it was not neceſſary to record any fall of thiers. We interpret Sunne, Moone and Starres as before,to bee, the cheife ornaments of the more pure, and true Church; ſo that the Sunne are the Scriptures thēſelues,the fountaines of light,the Moone, the doctrine fetched from thence, which is ſometime compared to water,ſometime to light in a diuerſe reſpect. The Starres are the mini-ſters,the daye,ioye and gladnes which are in the Church ariſing from the enioying of this Sunne, the night the more rufull ſtate thereof whether it be by reaſon of affliction,or of ſome darkenes and obſcu-rity, that is caſt vppon the truth, or of both, whence it is, that there ſhalbe no night, in the full felicity of the Church, *Chapt. 21. 29.* Neither are the Miniſters Starres, becauſe they are ſeruants of the night,but becauſe they driue away darkenes in others,thē ſelues being meane while inlightened throughly with the light of the Sunne. The meaning therefore is, that a moſt greiuous calamity ſhall inuade the third part of the world, which ſhalbe common no leſſe to the falſe then to the true Church; as the Hiſtory witneſſeth that it came to paſſe. ## The 9. Chapter.

### The Logicall Resolution of it.

*Such was the common proheme, as we haue said in the last verse of the former Chapter. A secondary one, the opening of the bottomlesse pit, a smoke ascending out of the pitt, darkening the Sunne, vers. 2. And the procreation of Locusts, whose description afterwards, is first of their power like to Scorpions, vers. 3. Against whome it is, vers. 4. Howe long it lasteth, vers. 5. Howe great it is, both by the degree of the torment which should not bee vnto death, but onely vnto a butcherly torturing of men, vers. 5. As also by the esteeming of death as a lighter matter, vers. 6. After that a description is added of those Locusts, both of what kinde they are by them selues, and that partly summarily that they are like to Warlike horses verse, 7. Partly member after member in respect of their heads and faces in the same verse, their haire and teeth, vers. 8. Their breastes and wings, vers. 9. Their Tailes and the continuance of their power to hurt men, verse 10. Then lastly of what kinde they are in respect of their kinge Abaddon, vers. 11. So much for the fifth Trompet. ## THE EXPOSITION.

1. Then the fifth Angell blevve the Trumpet, and I ſavve a Starre. The firſt effect of the fifth Trompet is the fal of the Starre as we haue ſaid in the Reſolution. Which Starre is not any good Angell. These are neuer ſaid to fall from heauen to earth, which is alwayes taken in the worſe part in this Booke, but to deſcend, as Chapt. 10. 1. and 18. 1. and 20. 1. Moreover this Starre is the Angell of the bottomleſſe pit, of whome verſ. 11. Who is called a deſtroyer, not onely becauſe he ſhall deſtroy others, but alſo becauſe he himſelfe ſhal goe into deſtruction, Chapt. 17. 8. Who came forth of the ſame bottomleſſe pitt from whence he wrought deſtruction for others; in the ſame place. It is true indeed that the holy Angel hath the key of the bottomleſſe pit, Chapter 20. 1. But that is a key of ſhutting vp the pitt onely after the Diuel was thruſt into it, this on the contrary hath onely power of opening; Neither is it a found point that the key is neuer cōmitted to any other but to frends. For what other thing is a key but a power ouer any thing; which we knowe to be geuen to vncleane Spirits, whence the Diuel is called the Prince of the world, Ioh. 14. 30. The Prince of the power in the aire, Ephef. 2. 2. The Prince of the darkenes of this world, Ephef. 6. 12.

2. *And he opened the bottomlesse pitt ; and there arose the smoke of the pitt ;* So much for the first effect; Those that be secondary, spring each out of other in a certaine order. Nowe the smoke is heresy in doctrine , and superstition in worship. For what other thing can steame out of the pitt of Hell? Before this time indeed it breathed out a hideous steame by many holes and pores as it were, but nowe hell gates being opened by these mens helpe, it began to come leaping out in abundance. The Sunne and aire are darkened, when errours preuaile, and the light of the truth is extinguished. Rome, and no where els in the world, so that whosoever should cutt
himselfe of from the Church of Rome, did exile himselfe from all
Christian Religion, as *Adrian* speaketh in an Epistle to the *Spaniards*, it
was no meruaile if the sunne was taken away out of al Churches euery
where by meanes of this darkenes. But yet this blacke night grewe yet
a great deale thicker with smoke, whẽ as at length the Holy Scriptu-
res were quite swept away behind the doore, & al good learning was
banished away, & Schoole diuinity was onely esteemed, and the Filthy
decrees & dyrty decretalls carried al the swaye. Then the Egyptian
darkenes, was no darkenes to this, which ouerwhelmed the whole
West. The Easterne smoke sent out by *Mahomet* was so grosse euen
from the beginning of it, that it might haue bene groped with hãds.
He ioined his *Alfurta* his seruice Booke, a horrible heape of all blas-
phemies vnto the three parts of holy Scripture, as he diuides them, the
lawe of *Moses*, the Psalmes of *Dauid*, & the Gospell. And as if the men
of the East had not receaued mischeife enough by the dotages of *Ma-*
*homet*, *Heraclius* the Emperour poured in also amõg them the errour
of the *Monothelites*. So thẽ about these times any man may see abun-
dãce of smoke breaking forth out of the pit whẽ it was once opened.

   3. *Nowe out of the smoke came Locusts.* Another secondary effect,
was the procreating of Locusts; that is, of men, who in their multitude
& nature doe most fittly resemble them. The words can not be vnder-
stood of certaine true poisonfull creatures, whose originall doth not
require to haue a man departing from the truth to beget them, such as
we haue shewed the Starre to be that fell from heauen, neither doe
true Locusts arise out of the smoke of Errours, but the broode must be
of the same kinde, that the damme is of. Wherefore out of this igno-
rance, & most grosse errours doe the *Saracens* that worship *Mahomet*
come forth in the East, a Company that flyeth by troupes, to robbe-
ryes, & that liueth not so much by their owne as by other mens goods.
A nation made to eate vp, & to deuoure, other mens estates, which in
a very fewe yeares wasted the whole East, and after that drained vp
the West, and our Europe miserably. The Westerne Locusts are the
Monkes, Fryars, a huge company of Religious orders, Cardinalls, with

4. *And it vvas commaunded them, that they should not hurt the grasse of the earth.* These words shewe ouer whome the power was geuen them. First al the grasse is simply excepted, and then also in part euery greene thing and the trees, onely those men who are not sealed are geuen ouer vnto their lawlesse lust. As for the grasse, which may bee translated as the old Interpreter doth and called haye cheifely seing greene followeth immediatly, it is dried grasse cutt from the earth, which seeing it is the company of the wicked as wee often shewed, the gras that is cutt from thence shalbe men that are separated by God from the company of the wicked by certaine manifest notes. The locusts should not hurt these men, not because they wanted either wil or endeuour, but because they should loose their labour in seeking their destruction, whome the Lord should defend with a mighty arme against their assault. Euen as we reade it came to passe in the East when Constantine Pogonatus was Emperour, about the yeare 674. Nor euery greene thing nor euery tree, but onely men vvho, &c. The meaning is, that soome good deale of greene things, and some trees were to be exempted from this vexation by the Locusts, all the rest being left to their cruelty to seaze vppon, who had not the signe of God on their foreheads. In the former Chapter, the seuenth verse, the third part of the Trees was burnt vp, and all the greene grasse, namely of that third part, because all that grasse and those trees were of the flocke ordained to destruction. But unlesse some trees had bene accounted to be in the number of the Elect, the foure Angels aboue should not haue bene forbidden, and made to staye their fury, no not for one moment, Chapt. 7. 1. Here are a fewe therfore exempted, as the natiue force of the words declareth sufficiently; the wordes indeed doe beare that interpretation, which the most learned <term>Th. Beza</term> bringeth, neither any greene thing, but onely men. For the universall signe All, is sometimes taken for any; as Chap. 7. 1. Neither vppon all trees, that is, any where the <term>Complutense</term> readeth vppon any tree; and Chapt. 21. 21. Euery thing that is uncleane, that is, any thing. The particles also (saue onely) may be reade by waye of Opposition, but onely, as Chapt. 21. 21. But onely those that were written. But here I doe thinke that we ought rather to translate according to the proper signification of the words by waye of exception, saue the men onely, which had not, &c. The difference is, that an exceptiō is alwayes of a thing that is of the same kinde, the opposition may be of any thing that is diuerse. So this placeth euery greene thing, and euery tree in the number of those who are sealed; That giueth this sealing to some certaine trees & to some greene thing onely, counting all the rest but as shrubs in no roome of those that are to be saued, which is more fitting to that which before

5. *And to them it vvas commanded, that they should not kill, &c.* Nowe we shall vnderstand howe great this power is, by the degree of torment, the continuance of it, and the comparing it with death. But howe can this agree to the Saracenes who spilled so much Christian bloud. These things seeme to be spokē not simply, but by comparison. If the slaughter which these men made be compared with that was to be made in the next Trompet. The Saracenes may seeme to pricke, & to torture, and not to kill. At their first Originall, the Christian profession was not so hatefull neither was there any neede to make any great slaughter, when as the nations, which they sett vppon did in a manner of their owne accord geue vp the bucklers and strike hands of fellowship with them in their impiety. In times that followed after the victory was gotten with so much the more cruelty, and greiuous trouble, by howe much fierce the fight and resistance was on the contrary side. But the Holy Ghost hath of purpose chosen that kinde of speaking, which might excellently agree to both the troupes of Locusts. nombred for ſo many yeares, that fiue moneths ſhould be æquivalent

for a yeare*, and according to the conſtant cuſtome of this Booke, as
we ſhall ſhewe afterwards godwilling, yet what is this ſo ſmall and
narrowe a ſpace, to theſe ſo longe, and laſting tyrannies? Wherefore
*Bullinger*, and others of our writers, doe thinke that this nomber is

cheifely the *Locuſts* are wont to be in their ſtrenth, in ſteede of the

which opinion ſeemeth to me to be likely, if the exceeding great accu-
ratenes of the computations which is vſed in other places of this
Booke, did not require ſome certaine and definite matter in this place
alſo.

The Iesuites doe of sett purpose, as I thinke, like the fishes called cuttells cast inke after them, that so they might lurke the more safely when all matters are confused, and troubled, these fellowes will haue so many moneths ordinary moneths vnderstood as are set downe, as if that denouncing of woe had bene in vaine, which the Angell that flewe through the middest of heauen did sound out before the three latter Trumpetts. Did he not therby fore shewe that the plagues to come should bee more greiuous then those which were past. Nowe what more or more greiuous shall this Trumpett containe then the former, if the Locusts, in whome all the force of it lieth, haue neither any power to kill, and that which they haue should be of for so short a time? It was a great destruction which the former Trumpetts did bring in, full also of terrour, and that not passing away in a moment, nay not in many yeares as we haue shewed. But if this calamity should be so contracted, it should neither be equall to the former euills in the greiuoufnes of the vexation, and it should be much lighter by reason of the shortnes of the greife. But I will not staye in confuting the trifling conceits of the Iesuites. It is most equall, that they who hammer out figures at their pleasure where there are none, should like blinde bettles be able to see none where there are some in deed. The matter may perhaps the better bee cleared, if wee doe obserue certaine positions, which the words them selues doe helpe vs with. Of which this is the first; that here is nothing to doe with whole Kingdomes, & the Kings them selues, but onely with the Locusts, and their great power. Which we se to breake forth as it were by certaine degrees. First they come forth of the Smoke, the smoke came out of the pitt when it was opened, the pitt is not opened before the key was geuen; neither is the key geuen, assoone as the Starre fal, but after some longe time: Out of which it must needs be, that the Angell of the Pitt, is much more auncient then his hellish broode. For who can require a childe, to be equall in time to his Parent? That therfore which is proper to the locusts is not to be cast vpon the Kingdome it selfe, and the Kings, as whose age is not from hence to be cõsidered but onely the sommer as it were and cheife vigour of that ouerflowing sinke of mischeife; I say the sommer of it, because neither the first Original of the Locusts, nor their last end seemeth to be defined in this space. For it must needs be that they must haue a beginning to bee borne in, before they haue

The Turkes not induring to haue their kindnes so litle or nothing to be regarded by the Romanes, disquieted the whole East vntill a nevve assault of the Scythians stroke a feare into them, and made them to bethinke them selues rather howe to defende them selues, then to prouoke others ; to which point when they were brought, they entreated and obtained peace at the hands of Iohn Duca,the Emperour of Rome, who then liued at Nice, because Bizantium was of old taken by the Latines. Which thing fell out in the yeare 1223. Niceph. Gregoras Book. 2. Rom. Histor. For so it pleased God the highest Gouernour of all things that the Turks should first torment men like Locusts & Scorpions, ere they made slaughter vpon slaughter without al indifferent respect of person, age, or Sexe, like feirce, and enraged Lyons. And therfore their Assaults they made till the yeare 1300. are worthily called by the History-Writers, robberies rather, then iust warres; For during this time, all they did was rather vppon a minde to rauen and prey, then vppon any hope to possesse those places, which they sett vppon. I haue related these matters with more words then ordinary, but it is because I desire to make this prophecy more lightsome and cleare, vvhich to doe I care not what labour I putt my selfe vnto. The other kinde of Locusts, are our westerne Religious ones, vvho came not to their ripenes vvhile the Saracenes vvere in their vigour. There were indeed svvarmes of these drones before, but as yet they were not come to their hott Sommer time. <header>OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chap.9.</header>

Saracẽs are famous in all Histories, the warlike chiualry of the Popish bande, is not perhaps so well marked by all men, and yet it is as euident, and notable, yf we shall examine the matter throughly : What Souldiers did Innocent the 3. muster for the rooting out of the Albingenses ? Besides Dominicus who was a deadly proclaimer, and heralde of this warre, who became a litle after one of the foure Captaines of the begging Fryars mustered an Armye of the Crucigeri, by the helpe of whome as of Horses running to battell, he hoped to ouerthrowe and quite to destroye the Hereticks, as they call them ; This order indeed had their beginning some time before, but whẽ as it had bene with in a short while after, almost brought to an vtter decay Innocentius the third restored it againe, that they might doe him seruice in this warre ; so as these pestilent company that had bene at the point of death was fetched backe from Hell at his commaundment, and by his autority they gott power to rage, and more noisomely them euer to trouble the world a fresh Polyd. Verg. of the Inuent. Book.7.Chap.3. Neither did the Pope whose manner it was to make hurly burlies, and to sett Kings together by the eares (as probus Tullensis sheweth in the meeting at Herbipolis vnder Honorius the fourth) vse any other bellowes after that time to stirre vp the fire of contentions : Yea as often as the Pope himselfe was to wage warre, (for the Pope holds of Mars as being a iolly warlike fellowe, and not without cause seeing he hath such warlike subiects as the Locusts are) full armies of the crosse bearing fryars was alwayes at hand to fight in their Kings quarrell. Worthily did Hildegard foretell that these hypocrites should be sowers of discord, who doe reioice in nothing so much as in the contention, and bickering of other men.

> *And they had as it vvere crovvnes on their heads.*

The first property was generall, nowe he persecutes the matter member by member. These Crownes on their heads like gold, is that polling or shauing of the heade, which was wont to be of old in great account with men, euẽ as if it had bene a diademe of Gold. It is called a Crowne, because the top of the head when it is shauen, seemeth to shewe it selfe in the midest like a Crowne. What reckoning was made of it in old time, Bellarmine sheweth out of Hierome in one of his Epistles to Augustine which is the fixe and twentieth Epistle of those that are written to Augustine. I beseech your Crowne to salute in my name my Lord.

Alipius, and my Lord Euodius. And Augustine in his 147. Epistle to
Proculian the Bishop; your men doe adiure vs by our crowne, and our
men doe adiure you by your Crowne. Methinks I should heare that in
Homer I liad α: Yea by this scepter doe I sweare. Both kinds of locusts
are notably knowne by these Crownes. Herodotes reporteth in his
Thalia that the Arabiens are shauen euen as Bacchus was wont to be
shauen; nowe they are polled so as they make a rounde circle beneath
when they shewe their Temples. But the shauing of monkes, and all
Religious orders is most famous, Polydor Vergil speaking of the Be-
nedictines saith they are shauen with a razor from the Crowne of the
heade beneath the middes of the skull; the haire is cutt of belowe into
the likenes of a litle circle; it compasseth the whole heade about the
eares and the Temples like a crowne, whence it is that that the toppe
of the heade when it is shauen is called a Crowne, Book. 7. Chapt. 2.
See howe fittly he interprets Herodotus, though thinking of no such
matter, but onely lead therto by the agreement of the matter it selfe.
For that which he saith, they are shauẽ into a round beneath, this man
translates it elegantly, the haire is cutt of belowe in forme of a litle
circle. It was indeed a matter forbidden of old to the Iewes. Thou
shalt not cutt round the corners of thy head and that as it seemeth be-
cause of the Arabians who were their neighbours, & were shauẽ after
this fashiõ, least they should in any thing be like the Idolaters, Leu. 19.
27. But it was meete that these Monkes, who differ in name onely
from the wicked nations, should agree with them in the likenes of
shauing their heads. The Gold of this Crowne, that is, the authority &
dignity of this manner of shauing, we may see by that that they made
their obtestations by their shauen crownes, as we sawe right nowe in
the Epistles of Ierome, and Augustine. If this superstition while it was
in the tender yeares of it, was in such request, what a stately and Ma-
iesticall thing was it trowe ye after that it came to the full ripenes?
Ribera will haue the Greeke word that signifies a Crowne to bee here
put for a helmet, according to the custome of the Greek tongue,
butt he is deceaued. Another word indeed very neere it, Stephane is
vsed sometimes in that signification in Homer, but the other worde
which is here Stephanos, is neuer so vsed, as we may learne out of Plu-
tarch. Sympos. 8. Problem. 6. The Latines saith he, call Stephanos a
Crowne, from the Crowne of the head, as Homer likened, a helmet to

Stephane; fo Hefychius defcribes *Stephane* to be a kinde of helmet, that

*And their faces vvas like the faces of men.* They made indeed a plea-
fant, alluring fhewe, and ful of humanity but fuch as had no truth, nor
fincerity vnderneath it: What crafty knaues were all the rout of
thefe Religious Orders in this part? whome did they not exceed in
their cogged vrbanity, but wel did *Hildegard* prophecy of them. *They*
*fhalbe curteous faith fhe, but yet great flatterers, perfidious traytors,*
Holy hypocrits, we haue no need of witneffes in fo cleare a matter.
Thofe inhumane *Arabians* alfo, howe could they haue gottē fo many
countries in a fhort time vnder their power, vnleffe they had allured
them by their fained humanity to a voluntary reuolting. When bloody
cruelty fheweth it felfe openly, men had rather die by fighting, then by
miferable feruitude.

8. *And they had haire, as the haire of vvomen.* Haire is giuen women
for a couering faith the Apostle 1.Cor.11.15. This haire that groweth
fo rankly teacheth vs, that the Locufts fhould be hidden vnder the
names of women, as it were vnder long haire; and that they fhould
glory exceedingly in this ornament, as counting it to be a very high
honour to them felues. What is more expreffe? It is well knowne,
that the *Arabians* were called *Agarenes* of *Agar Sarais* maide, and
that this name is often giuen them in *Zonaras, Necetas, Gregoras,* and
other Greeke writers, who were of necessity to make mentiō of their
Acts, and it was no name geuen them by way of reproch, as *Sabellicus*
writeth *Ennead* 8. Book 6. Fol. 177. But it was alfo theer moft aun-
cient name, & moft glorious in their owne opinion, 1.Chron.5.10.19
and 27. 31. And long before the booke of Chronicles was written,
Pfal.83.7. Whence it may alfo appeare that is was an honorable name
and fuch as they would haue them felues cheifely called by. For els
howe fhould they be diftinguifhed from the *Ifhmaelits* that had the
fame Originall, but that they inhabiting towards the fouth of *Iewrye*
did bragge more of their fathers name, thefe dwelling Eaft and fout-
heaft ward, and being more nye the *Iewes*, boafted more of their mo-
thers name. And this name did at length ouercome the other in glory
it being more famous among the forraine writers and it becomming
at laft the aunceftors name vnto the *Ifhmaelites* themfelues in fteed of
the former. But whence then came the *Saracenes*? Of *Sara* herfelfe

as it seemeth. For after that their offspring from Agar seemed to bee some what more base, thē was fitting for their Estate, that was growne more mighty (for by the ouerthrowe which they gaue the Iewes, both their hart and their wealth waxed great,) they cast of the handmaide & went in to the name of the Mistresse, and so would be called afterwards Saracens.

For so *Ierome* writeth vpon *Eze. 25.* The Scripture by *Madianites*, vnderstandeth, *Agarenes*, who we now called *Saracenes*, taking to thē selues the name of *Sara* falsely, that they might seeme to be begottē of her that was a free woman, & the Mistresse, whence he saith often in other places that this is an vntoward name, because it had bene per-uersely challengded by these men to them selues. Which things doe conuince that this name can not well be deriued of the Arabick word *Sarak*, which signifies in that tongue theeues and Robbers. For what one man, much lesse a whole nation would take such a reprochfull name to them selues? And there was no reason why *Ierome* that was so neere, to their first arising both in time and place, being one that was skillfull in the Tongues, & curious in such things as these, should enuy them this name, & call it a peruerted name, which might indeed most fitly and worthily be geuen them comming from this roote. If I may be suffered to giue my coniecture. I thinke it to be a name com-pounded of *Sara*, and another word putt to it, *Kedar*, whose first letter after the manner of the *Hebrues* commeth into the composition as if it had bene written, *Sarah quedar*, by contraction *Sara* and in *Chaldee*, *Sarak* or *Sarag*. Which is as of they should call them selues, the *Saracens*, to distinguish them selues from the *Sarean Israelites*. Not that they would faine them selues to be borne of *Sara*, but feing the maides children belonged to the mistresses, *Gen. 16.2.* Why might not the children take the name of the mistresse to them selues, aswell as of the maide? This indeed might haue had some shewe if they had bene borne in the house, but when as they were borne out of the family, & that so many Ages after, they doe impudently in putting on this name; I haue bene more large in relating these things that I might search out the truth of a matter that was doubtfull; if perhaps my la-bour might be profitable herein. The summe of all is this, that the Arabians did geue them selues this name taken from women for the honour of there Nation.

Out of which we see with what haire the Friars are adorned ; And not these alone , but the whole rout of Romanists also , who account not to haue Iesus Christ fauourable vnto them any otherwise then as they can gett Mary to winne them some Fauour at his handes,by making request for them. But it wil be need-lesse to goe cite witnesses for that which they them selues doe of their owne accord confesse at this day. But (you will faye) howe is it that I attribute long haire to the Fryars nowe , whome right nowe called shauelings , and Pollards ? To be shauen and to boast of the names of women are not contrary , and that this is signified by this allegorye , and not any proper haire of their head , I suppose it to be manifest enough , so aboue Chapt. 4. The foure and twenty Elders are said to sitt vppon Thrones with crownes aboue vpon their heads who yet afterwards fall downe on their face , and cast downe their crownes at the voice of the Beasts ,that doe continually geue glory to God,which wil not seeme to hang together if we take the words properly, and not figuratively. Christ also in the Parable,by one man that was not clothed vvith his marriage garment , and therfore vvas cast out into vtter darkenes , inferreth that many are called,but fewe are chosen , when as the proper application would conclude the contrary that many are called, and fewe are reiected, Matth. 22. 13. 14. But indifferent readers vvill easily by their owne helpe ridd them selues & others of such doubts.

*And their Teeth vvere as of Lyons.* The experienced Cruelty of both kind of Locusts hath abundantly proued this truth to the world, that they haue Lions teeth, when as the Saracens did robbe and spoile with fire and sword,the Friars did deuoure widowes houses vnder a shewe of prayers and deuotion.

Greeke that Angell of that bottomleſſe pitt, make a great force in
ſpeaking, as is wont to be in matters that be certaine, & wel knowne.
Yet we haue had no other mention of this Angell of the Pitt in ex-
preſſe words vnleſſe that ſhould be he, to whome the Key of this Pitt
was geuen, verſ. 1. And ſo indeed it muſt needs be. For what ſhould be
rather the Angell of the Pitt, then he that hath the Key geuen him to
open the pitt, and to ſende out a ſmoke? By which argument we haue
proued that the Starre which fell, was an euill Angel. This King of
the Saracenes is Mahumet, or the Mahumetan Calipha, whome they
obeyed and the King of the Religious Locuſts is the Pope. For Boni-
<margin>☛</margin> face the fifth made theſe Monkes to be of his Clergy, whereby it
appeared plainly, whoſe creatures they were, as we ſaid on the 3. verſ.
So Innocent the 3. that it might appeare plainly, that the Tailes of the
Locuſts, that is the begging Friars acknowledge no other King but
the Pope, decreed in the Laterane Councell, Can. 13. That no man
from thence forth ſhould inuent any newe Religion, but that who-
ſoeuer would conuert to any Religion, he ſhould aſſume one of thoſe
which were before allowed of. Which is not ſo to be vnderſtood, as
if he did ſimply forbidd newe Religions, but that no newe order
ſhould be thenceforth ordained, without the approbatiō of the Apo-
ſtolike Sea, as it is Chap. of the Relig. Domin. And this decree was
renewed by Gregory the tenth in the Councell at Lyons, Chapt.
about the diuerſity of Religions. By which decrees that was made
neceſſary, which before was free as Bellarmine confeſſeth Booke 2.
touching Monkes, Chapt. 4. Nowe what is this els but to be a King?
Namely, to haue power to binde men, with the chaines of Lawes, and
to impoſe a neceſsity of doing things which of them ſelues were free
before. Wherefore the Papiſts are ſelfe condemned by their owne
iudgement, neither neede we any other arguments. Nowe this King
is ſett downe by name and that two wayes, for he is called in Hebrue
Abaddon, in Greeke Apollyon, after ſuch a manner as is com-
monly vſed by the Hebricians, who putt the participle for the ſubſtan-
tiue; And indeed that Aduerſary Antichriſt is called the Sonne of

<header>Chap.9. A REVELATION,</header>

Abba Father, that there should be a consent of Gentiles aswel as Iewes in the worship of one true God. The Hebrue word indeed agreeth to the Saracens, because they come neere to the Hebrues in a kind of affinity, and are neighbours to them in their countries; but the Greeke word Apollyon, after the manner of the Scriptures noteth out the rest of the nations whatsoever, which haue their offspring elsewhere then from the Hebrues. In howe neere an acquaintance therefore are the Pope of Rome and this Mahumetan Kinge ioined together, though they make a shewe of fighting one against another enemye-like? The Holy Ghost doth worthily geue them both one name, who doe one & the same thing though under a contrary shewe. Thus then we haue a most plentifull description of the Locusts, so that no man can nowe iustly make doubt, either who should be the Angel of the bottomlesse pit, or which is his hellish armye? Did not Bellarmine therefore egregiously abuse and deceaue both him selfe and his Auditors, who in a certaine oration which he made in the Schooles, dragges in all these things by the head and shoulders, that they might make against the Lutherãs? Did he once respect the time, wherein this pernicious company should ouerrune the world? For certainly that is the time which did next of all ensue after that destructiõ which the Vandalls brought upon the third part of the Christian world. And what other Locusts were there extant then, but these vvhich I haue spoken of? Where els shall Bellarmine finde, they hauing this Patronage by vvomans name, a Captaine, that is both a destroyer: & destroyed, and the rest of those ensignes, then among that flocke, vvhich he is one himselfe, and that nowe vvhile it is languishing, and ready to breath the last? But that the matter may be yet made more cleare if it may be; I haue a good minde to adde to all that hath bene said in steede of a conclusion; the prophecye of Hildegard the Abbatesse, both because I haue often made mention of it, as also because I thinke it is not easily come by, and it doth serue to giue much light to the matter in hand. That worthy man Iohn Foxe our Cuntryman of blessed memory, hath sett this same downe in his Booke of the Acts, and monuments of the Church, and that in our English tongue into vvhich he turned it out of the Latin Coppy which he had by him written in parchment in old Characters. I will turne it againe into Latin out of his translation, and thus it goeth.

In those dayes there shall rise vp a sort of Blockish fellowes proude , couetous , perfidious , and crafty , that shall eate vp the sinnes of the common people , carrying a certaine shewe of foolish superstition vnder a fained couerture of beggery : preferring themselues before all other men by reason of a counterfait Religion; Men of an arrogant disposition , and fained Religion , Voide of all shame,or feare of God,hauing valour and vigours to be deuisers and plotters of strange villaines ; but all prudent men, and faithfull Christians will wish a plague of God to light vppon this pestilent order, of men who will shunne labour,& geue themselues wholy to idlenes, rather chusing to gett their liuing by flattery , and beggery , and that will bend them selues with al their might euery way they can,peruersely to resist the teachers of the Truth,and they will hinder them.and for this ende they will curry with noblemen that they may assist them in this purpose ; They shall also deceaue the Nobles and drawe them into errour , that they may furnish them with all necessaries, yea with all the delights and pleasures of this world. the vncleane Spirits are shutt vp into certaine places, as it were into a prison.

The which though seemeth not to bee common to them al, but peculiar to some certaine of them. For howe should all of them bee tyed vnto certaine determinate places when as it is free for some of them to compasse about all the earth, Job 1. 7. When as the Ancients and Cheifetanes among them doe walke about like roaring Lyons, seeking whome they may deuoure, 1.Pet.5.6. They haue also power in the aire, & there is a Spirit, that doth nowe worke effectually in the childrē of disobedience, Ephes. 2.2. & there are some that be the Princes of the world yea the Gods of this world, blinding the minds of vnbeleeuers, Ephes. 6.12. 2. Cor. 4.4. What can they doe these things when they are absent? Therfore certaine of them onely seeme to bee cast into certaine places, as it were into prisons, others seeme to haue more free scope to friske vp and downe. And yet the impiety of Magicians is nothing helped from hence who thinke that they can binde the diuells necessarily to abide within a circle, in a smooth stone, Iron. brasse, a glasse, a mans naile, or some such matter. For God hath reserued this power to him selfe alone, and to his holy Angells, whome he vseth oftentimes for his instruments in this matter, as for men he hath geuen them no such power as this in any place. Nowe these Angells are not the Deuils onely, but they be also men, who are vnder their Government, and at their command for whome to be called Angells we haue seene it to be an ordinary matter.

For the Deuills armye is made of men; as it is manifest out of the twentieth Chapter of this Booke, vers. 7. Where this same matter is againe entreated of, Satan went out to deceaue the Nations, and togather them to battell, nowe the Captaines are of the same kinde with their Souldiers.

Wherefore seeing the order of matters in this Booke hath brought vs to the thousand three hundreth yeare, it is not to be doubted but that that these Angells bee the Turkes, and to this opinion doe the most of the Interpreters consent. They are said to be foure, because there were foure principall families of the Turkes. spill more bloud, than any other enemies that were spoken of before.
A great nomber was slaine by the Saracenes, and the Antichrist of
Rome is wholy embrued in the bloud of the Saints, as we shall see
Chapt. 17. 4. 6. But the slaughters that should be made by those are
none to these which the Turks should make, and therfore they come
not into any account. The rage of this sauage enemy is limited with
the bounds of the third part, as we haue seene it already accomplished
in the East, partly in Asia, partly in Europe, whereuppon it is not to be
feared, that it should be much more enlarged. And certainly it is staid
by force of the same prohibition, whereby the waues of the raging

The things that be Reuealed are either such as are to be sealed up, or to be communicated. Those haue the voice of the Angell for their principall cause, the seauen Thunders for their Instrumentall cause vers. 3. # THE EXPOSITION.

1. Then I saw another Angell. We referre these things in the Analysis to the solace of the Church against the euills of the former Trompetts, specially the sixth. Which is added vnto it very seasonably. For who is there, who would not languish away almost with the tediousnes of such long lasting troubles, hearing of nothing els in the Church throughout a long rowe of yeares and Ages but stormy tempests of Haile, burning mountaines, the darkening of the sunne, Troupes of Locusts, and Serpents spitting out flames of fire, with which an infinite nomber of men should be miserably consumed and burnt vp? Nowe therfore after that the Church hath bene as it were tossed vp & downe in the deepes a longe time, and in exceeding manner and the lande hauē is shewed them, wherein they should at length haue some rest and respite from these euills; and not so onely, but a prosperous gale of winde also bloweth vpō them in the meane time, which might make them to ridd way the better in their voyage. For which purpose an Angel of most great power descendeth downe from Heauen, of a diuerse nature from those Angells, who blewe the former Trumpets, or of which any mention had bene made elsewhere before. For they were Seruāts, this is the Lord Christ himselfe, as whose apparel, countenance voice, and his whole araye is more maiesticall then can suite with a creature. Neither doth this hinder it that he hath such a strange forme, and so vnlike to his true humanity. Seing it is cleare out of the first Chapter, that he doth in speciall manner take to himselſe such a resemblance, as might most fittly serue to explane and to confirme the things that are propounded to come : Therfore this description, he is

*And he putt his right foote vppon the Sea.* This thicke Sea of the

them out of the rabble of Clergy men, and then he lead them vnto the

feete taken out of the Laitye, were Ludouick of Bauaria the Empe-

with all their might defend the truth, when once they had come to the

3. *And he cryed vvith a loud voice.* Hetherto we haue had the deſcription of the Angell. Nowe the principall cauſe of ſealing vp matters is ſet downe,to wit, the crying of the Angel,like to the lowing of a Lyon. For ſo the word here called roaring, doth properly ſignifye the lowing of Oxen and ſuch beaſts ; Lyons roaring is called by three other names in Greeke. And yet the word properly ſignifying to roare is geuen ſometimes to Oxen, and this word of belowing is ſometimes geuen to Aſſes and Camels,as Heſychius teacheth. But the Angel here is ſaid to bellowe,not becauſe he ſhould mutter for feare, & durſt not put out his voice, for with all it is ſaid he cryed with a loud voice,but to ſhewe that the meekenes, & patience of an oxe was nowe to be mingled with the fortitude of a Lyon. And ſo indeed did Chriſt cry out at this time valiantly being as it were reuiued in his members,and yet this Crye was onely like the bellowing of an Oxe, neither did it much terrifye any man as yet. Thoſe Chriſtian worthies who firſt of al ſprung vp did make pittiful complaint & outcrye with their voices while they contended for the truth, againſt lies, but yet they were faine to endure the greiuous yoke of bondage, which they were notable to ſhake, with all their ſtruggling to the contrary.

*The ſeauen Thunders ſpake.* Which like an Eccho anſwered this bellowing. Nowe theſe Thunders are thoſe ſeauen Angells as I ſuppoſe of which there is mention made afterwards, Chapt. 14. 6. &c. Certainly the time agreeth,as we wil ſhewe on that place,beſides their function may very well be likened to Thunder, which did refound whē this bellowing noiſe was made. For they taking their beginning from hence,did ſo warre, and make ſuch a loud noiſe, that they who deſpiſed the bellowing of the Angel l, began at length to be horribly afraid at this Thunder,nowe it is worthy the obſeruing that the thunders ſpeake not but at the crying of the Angel,enen as the Eccho hath not a voice of it owne, but giueth backe the voice onely which it receaued; euen ſo theſe reſtorers of the truth howeſoeuer they ſhould bee condemned of the word for bringing in nouelties, yet they held nothing which them ſelues were not taught of God.

*That there should be no more time.* I translate the word here called Time , and call it delay of time, thus , that there should no more delaye of time. But they are to be referred rather to the shortnes of time should be to the consummation ; For other wise here should be no speciall consolation, but such as should be no lesse common to all ages. 8. *Goe and take the litle Booke.* Another thing that is to be communicated is the gift of Prophecy restored againe vnto the Church. For this newe commaundement sheweth what should be done by the Ministers of the word, that should liue in the times of this sixth Trumpett.

As for Iohn himselfe, hee for his part seemeth to bee prepared enough before to perceaue the matters in this Reuelation, both by the things vvhich he sawe and heard, as also by the inspiration of the Holy Ghost, wherewith he was extraordinarily indued. And if there vvere onely some transition propounded here, that so matters might bee taught more clearely, hee would haue vsed the same in their due place elsewhere in this Treatise. Wherefore I doubt not, but that Iohn is here propounded for a Type of the Ministers of that time, as he doth commonly elsewhere stande in the Roome of the faithfull. As hee therefore should take the Booke from the Angell, and after he had eaten it vp, should againe doe the worke of a Prophet, so there should bee faithfull Ministers raised vp about these times, who should preach the truth vnto the world. complained of long agoe, Chapt. 15. 16. Also Ezechiel 3. 3. And
so in a word haue all done that haue runne in this race, but especially
these newe Champions of this time that I speake of. And indeed the
word was so much the sweeter vnto them, with howe much more
hearty hunger they came vnto it, after it had bene stolen away from
the world for certaine Ages, and was nowe first of all restored againe
through the mercy of God, contrariwise the office of preaching it,
was so much the more bitter, by howe much more grosse the blind-
nes was wherein men were drowned, who must needs be found to be
the more obstinate, and mischeiuous, against the faithfull preachers
and professors of the word, because they had bene so long inured to
and nousled in their wicked opinions and practises. The State of that
time could not bee declared more breifely, and yet in more liuely
manner.

10. Then I tooke the Booke. Although Iohn heare howe great
trouble this meate should bring yet hee willingly obeyeth the Angell,
and deuoureth the Booke, as he was commaunded. The desire after
the heauenly word of God was more stronge and forcible with him,
then any respect of irkesomnes, or of gripes at heart that were like
to arise out of the bitternes of it. And this kinde of fortitude was
singular in the learned men of that Age, that we spake of before; it
could not be, but they knewe well enough, what dangers and troubles
they should raise vp against them selues by defending of the Truth
yet for all that they were not a whitt lesse painfull, and couragious in
seeking and setting out the truth, but contemned all the bitternes of
any dāger whatsoever, in respect of that sweetenes, which they tooke
in and sucked out of the ioye of the Holy Ghost. By whose worthy
example, all the Ministers of the word are to be prouoked, to goe for-
ward in the discharge of their holy function boldly and stoutly, and
neuer to forsake, or to balke it for any troubles they can meete with
all. It is not any strange thing to finde that bitter in experience, which
when it was first but ouerly tasted with the tippe as it were of the
tongue, seemed to be sweete. Let euery Prophet therefore meditate
troughly of this instruction, and hide it in his heart, least perhaps
when hee lights into euills which he neuer before made reckoning
of, he faint and giue ouer all at length not being able to hold out to
the ende, in regard of his owne great infirmity.

11. *Thou must Prophecy againe.* Nowe hee sheweth in a fewe words, to what purpose the former signe was vsed, namely that wee might vnderstand that the gift of Prophecye, should bee restored againe to the Church. The preparation whereunto was the taking and eating vp of the Booke, and that is, the desire after all good learning, wherewith men were inflamed, which gaue great hope that more plentifull light would breake forth euery daye more and more. But the opinion of those men is fonde, who will gather out of these words that *Iohn* is to be looked for together with *Enoch* and *Elias* to come againe at the ende of the world.

These things belong not to the last daye, but to the *sixth Trumpett*, which wee shall demonstrate afterwards to be nowe past and gone. As for *Iohn* hee is onely brought in as a Type not described by any office that he should take vppon him, & discharge in his owne person in the last Age of the World.

*they should rise againe being raised up by the Spirit, first uppon*

# THE EXPOSITION.

Vers. 1. *Then vvas there giuen me a reede.* After the preparation
that was made, whereof we haue heard in the former Chapter, na-
mely, that in the first time that the truth begã to spring againe afresh,
& when as many exellent men did geue themselues diligently to the
studye of good learning, whose feruent desire thereunto was so great,
that for two hundred yeares together after the yeare one thousand &
three hundreth, they seemed to eate up Bookes ; I saye, after this præ-
paration, at length about the ende of the sixth Trumpett, the matter
was brought to this passe as is here in these words sett downe, to wit,
a more full Prophecye, and a more plentifull knowledge shined forth
both of the times that were past, as also of those that were present;
learned men sawe by that Booke which they receaued frõ the Angel,
that the Church had bene nowe for many Ages in very great afflicti-
on, so that it could not be seene clearely of the world, as also that it
was at this present time meruailously vexed by Antichrist. For this
Prophecye is a repeating of matters long since past, and recorded as
Moses did Prophetically write of the first beginning of the World;
which name of a Prophecy, how much doth it amplifie the dignity of
this Historye? But to the matter, this Prophecy (I saye) that doth thus
call to minde the time past, doth containe the whole space of the for-
mer Trumpetts, euen as it is manifest by the determining of the time,
in the next and third verses.

For the two and fourty moneths, wherein the Church should con-
uerse in the Temple, if we nomber them backward doe not onely
containe that houre, daye, moneth and yeare of the sixth Trumpett

whereof we heard, Chapt.9.15. But also besides the fiue moneths of the fifth Trumpet, in the same Chapt. vers. 5. And those foure times repeated, and yet so as there are yet remaining ouer and besides all these, nine moneths aboue the number, which whether else can they be referred, but to those foure first Trumpets of the eighth Chapter. But perhaps you will say, these two and forty moneths take their beginning at the ende of that houre, daye, Moneth, & yeare, of the foure Angells, Chapt.9.15. And so both these spaces of time should belong iointly to the sixth Trumpet, which indeed can by no meanes be so. For the whole sixth Trumpet is wofull vnto the wicked, in which regard it is called the second woe, Chapt.9.12. and 11.15. But if the times should be disposed after this manner, it contains but a litle misery for them, who should Triumph with all manner of ioye, for the space of two and forty moneths, when as the Godly should be afflicted all the while. What great discommodity should the sixth Trumpet bring them, if after that short trouble of one yeare a moneth, a daye, and a houre, they should haue thrice as long a felicity and more.

It is most certaine therfore that this prophecye doth reach, backwards to the first beginning of the Trumpets, but yet it is sett in this place, because the whole race of this time could not be seene throughly before that is was brought to the issue and ende thereof. And nowe indeed about this time did God raise vp learned men, namely *Philippus Bergomensis*, *Francis Guicciardin*, *Martin Luther*, *Iohn Carion*, *Philip Melancton*, *Gaspar Peucerus*, *Henry Bullinger*, *Iohn Sleidā*, *Iohn Functius*, and others. Who compiling the Histories of the times past, did set before vs the outward estate of the Church in their writings as in a mappe. And indeed this Prophecye was nowe at last to be added of necessity.

For a man would and that not without cause enquire, what was become of the true Church, when the haile smote the third part of the grasse, the burning mountaine turned the Sea into bloud, the Locusts, and the rest of those feends ruffled it so? In declaring all these troubles, there was a meruailous silence kept touching the Church. Nowe therefore the Holy Ghost teacheth by the helpe of this reuiued Prophecy, what manner of estate it was in during this time, least otherwise she onely should bee passed ouer for whose sake alone this Booke was written.

This Chapter therfore is to be ioined with the Seauenth,where the Prophecye touching the Saints ended. That Sealing there,and this Temple measuring here belongs to the same time, and it is one & the same matter that is handled in both places , saue that that belongs to the Citizens seuerally one by one , this belongs to them all iointly,and certaine of the principall members.

Novve as touching the vvords. The Reede that was geuen,is a power that was granted to knowe the truth, whereby the Saints might measure the length and breadth of the true and lawfull worship,least that in so great a confusion , they should stray from a iust proportion , in that it was like vnto a rodd , it teacheth vs, that the truth was to bee greatly helped,& vnder propped with the autority of Princes. For a Rodd is oftentimes putt for an ensigne of honour , namely that staffe which Kings carry in their hands,by which name also that bundell of rodds is called,which was wont to be carred before the Magistrats. It signifieth also an instrument wherewith power is executed , as in the Poet, Circe the witch worketh all her inchantments with a Rood, Mercury with a litle wand proper to Ambassadors. This sheweth then that the Temple was to be measured by the helpe of some Prince or great man,as we heard in the seauenth Chapter,where Constantine the great was the instrument whome God vsed in sealing his seruants. For while he tooke care for the peace of the Church , and defended the truth with all his endeuour , hee prouided a safe refuge for the Saints to preserue them in from the contagion of the times.

*And the Angell stood by.* These words are wanting in Aretas, whereupon it is that he makes the Reede to commaunde him to arise and mete.But the helpe of Angels ioined elswhere with the Ministers, where the like busines is in hande, doth seeme also to require, that nothing should be done but in the presence of the Angel;see Ezech.40.3 And afterwards,Apoc.21.16.Wherefore Th.Beza hath done well to make this place perfet out of the Complutense Edition.

*Mete the Temple.* The true Christian Church is shadowed out by the Type of the old Temple : each part whereof was most accurately decyphered and measured out of old by the commaundment of God himselfe ; And that to this ende , that men might knowe that this house is framed by God, and is not made by mans might or cunning, and that therfore they should not take vppon them any power to

After that the Temple which was enlarged by *Salomon*, and by the

Temple then that is onely measured, doth declare that the Church
was to be brought into great straits, to be limitted with smal bounds,
and to be altogether remooued from the eyes of men. For the Holy
place did not lie open to the people, but the Preists alone did minister
there, such as all true Christians are reckoned to be in this place, as
aboue, *Chapt. 1. 6.*

When *Constantine* therfore came to the Kingdome, the Church
began to hide it selfe in secret, by departing aside from the veiwe of
the world into a certaine secret sanctuarye. To which purpose that
sealing *Chapt. 7.* serued. By which some fewe were seuered and sett
apart from a great many, by some priuy marke. And it must not be
meruailed at, that this setting and going apart was to be seene in the
middest of such a glorious peace and in the time of so great a desire
to aduance the Christian profession as then was. For when as some
kindled contentions, others gaped after honours many were with
child, and deliuered of monstrous heresies, all men gaue them,
selues to heape vp superstitions, was it an easy matter, to preserue any
thing intire sincer and sound, while matters were at this passe? But the
obscurenes of the true Saints grewe euery daye more and more, the
more those foure plagues grewe. And this doth *Rome* it selfe at vna-
wares confesse. For dost thou enquire, where our Church was before
*Luthers* time? Thou therfore are ignorant of it. But to answere thy
question, knowe that where thou ô *Romish Church* was not, there
was ours, namely in the hidden sanctuary of our God, wheether it fled
together with all the Saints from thy Contagion. But seeing thou

boastest that thou art the Citty sett vppon an Hill , which was neuer hidd,but alwayes flourished with a perpetuall, & glorious succession, apparant in the world,acknowledge with al that thou art not the true Church,seeing thou foundest no place in that secret couert.

*And them that vvorship therein.* The word to Mete, is common and belonging to the cōtinued quantity, but here it signifieth by a Synechdoche to nomber,as if he should saye, reckon those fewe in the nomber of my seruants,who doe worship me truly in secret. So in the sealing of the Elect the nomber was certaine, Chapt. 7. Which is the same thing that is declared here in other words, when he bidds him measure those that worship. Nowe all the faithfull are said to worship in the Altar, because they place all their hope, and affiance in Christs death alone ; which kinde of sacrifices belonge not onely to the Tribe of Leui ; but aswell to euery truly godly one. And this is that onely, which distinguisheth a true Christian from one that is false and counterfeit. But it may be thought worthily, that the most in these times, did not so worship God vppon the Altar,when as it is clearely euident by their writings,that many who ought to giue light vnto others, with all manner of good knowledge,did attribute too much to the works of their owne chusing and deuising,and to their owne holines.

2. *But the Court vvhich is vvithout.* So reade Aretas and Complutensis, but certaine Coppies reade: *That is vvith in the Temple, Namely, the court of the Preists*, wherein was the Altar of the whole burnt offrings, of which he spake right nowe, which is wont to bee contained oftentimes vnder the name of the Temple.And this reading is not to be lightly reiected. For Iohn is not bidden to mete this Court, but onely the Altar of this Court. And perhaps it agreeth better with that followeth,if that inward Court be cast out of doores,then if that should be cast out,which was alreadye without before. But both tend to one, that it is to be had in reckoning at all, whatsoever is more then those three things abovesaid,the Temple,the Altar,and the worshippers.

*For the court is geuen to the Gentiles.* That is,to the Christians that are so in name onely, and not this onely, but the Holy Citty also, the which they should tread vnder foote, not by spoiling and sacking it in hostile manner, but by frequenting it continually vnder a pretence to worship God, as it is in the first of Esay,12. of two & forty moneths. These things doe teach plainly, what should be the state of the false Church in the time of those Ages wherein the true should lie hid. First it should exceed no lesse in nomber and multitude, then the people that dwelt in Ierusalem of old & that were wont to conuerse in the outmost court, did exceede the nomber of those, that bare office in the Temple. And it can hardly be expressed howe great difference was betwene them? The Company of inhabitants, of those that did flocke daily to the Temple, was huge, but howe fewe were the Preists, that were with in meane while, to that innumerable multitude that was without? The same proportion should there be of fained Christians, to the true and kindly Cittizens. Secondly, it should haue the counterfaite worshippers, dwelling as neere as could be vnto the Temple. For they should possesse Ierusalem, and the whole Court should be theirs, nowe howe neere was the court ioined to the Temple? Howe dooth it compasse it round about, <margin>Ezek. 40. 5.</margin> Howe neere a society is this? Who durst haue condemned the Court as being profane, vnlesse the Angel him selfe had bidden a man so to doe? And indeed the euent did answere to this Prophecy altogether. For in those first times, when the foure Trumpets did blowe, what was one Athanasius to so great assemblies of Bishops as then were? And afterwards, what was Basil the great, or Gregory Nazianzene, to the whole East almost? If a man would looke to nomber, who would not haue contemned one or two, in comparison of so great a rabble? But if a man would respect holines, were they not all Bishops? Did they not all desire to bee thought to be valiant Champions for the truth? Howe easy a thinge was it then to be deceaued, either with their nõber, or their neerenes to the true Church? The same bragging of the Holy Citty and the outmost court may we also see in these last Ages, to be vsed against the Temple. For thus they babble, and let their clappers runne. What is not the Church of Rome scattered farre and wide thorough the whole world. Haue the heresies of the Lutherans euer passed ouer Sea. Haue they euer seene either Asia, or Affrike, or Egypt, or Greece. Who can doubt whether the Church of Rome be the Holy Catholike Church, which can nomber her Bishops, by a most certaine succession from Peter himselfe. But let Rome boast nowe of her multitude, the more it doth nowe flourish as it hath for a long time done with a great nomber of Professours,

the more neere a kin is it to the crouds of people,that tread Ieruſalem vnder foote, and the more vnlike is it to this poore handfull, that lurketh with in the Temple ; we ſee the patterne of a whoriſh Church in this place, that is furniſhed as much as can be with multitude, and neerenes to the true Church. If theſe things be enough to get the victory withall, thou haſt gott the daye (o Rome) with thy troupes of cittizens,& thy exceeding great neerenes to the Temple that is ioined withall.

But let them looke to it, who are lead by the noſe,as it were, with the name of the Catholike Church,howe eaſily they may be cooffened by this whore, which takes poſſeſsion of the Holy Cittye, and of the outmoſt Court, that is ſo neere the Temple ; let them in the name of God weighe the matter in good earneſt and diligently, and let them not ſuffer them ſelues to be gulled with her vaine bragges. Let them thinke, that all thoſe ſeeme indeed to be in the Temple, who are with in the very outmoſt compaſſe of the walls, at leaſt while they looke vppon them a loofe of, but let them once come neerer, and they ſhall ſee moſt clearely,that they whome they ſuppoſed, to conuerſe in the innermoſt, and moſt ſecret places of the Temple, are kept out of the Holy place, with wals of braſſe. And yet the matter is not nowe ſo hard to be iudged of, as it was longe agoe, while the Church wanted all publike liberty of Gods worſhip.

Onely doe but reade the writings of our men, and thy eyes ſhalbe inlightened thorough Gods grace,to ſee the truth clearely; maiſt thou not worthily ſuſpect the fraudulent dealing of the Popiſh Doctors & rulers, who doe forbid thee all medling with our Books, and all Society with men of our Religion. But doe thou ſtriue, the more to knowe the truth, which thou ſhalt ſee to be thus hated of thy leaders and teachers, as who are priuye to the filthines of their Religion ?

*Tvvo and forty moneths.* This is the time in which the true Spouſe ſhould lie hid, and the falſe ſhould ſwaye all and dominere. But howe great is the obſcurity and difficulty of this point ? And no meruaile,ſeing there is ſo great blindnes in the minde of man. Thou therfore who haſt receaued theſe things to declare them to thy Seruants, be preſent with me, that I may thorough thy conduct ſet my feete in ſafe and ſure places.

Secondly, ſeeing this computation can not be of common moneths, we muſt needs number theſe moneths according to the cu-ſtome of the other Scriptures. For all things are expreſſed in this Booke of the Reuelation after the manner of the old Types. Nowe what is this manner? Shall each moneth note out ſeauen yeares as the weekes in Daniel doe? It is quite deſtitute of all exemple and reaſon to equall the moneths to the weekes. Neither will the words beare it by any meanes. For the Angell teacheth vs, that euery one of the dayes are to be numbred one by one, whereupon he doth note out this ſpace indifferently, ſometimes by the forty two moneths, otherwiſe by a thouſand two hundred dayes, as in the next verſe, & Chapt. 12. 6. But that manner of accounting, by which the moneths are reduced to weekes, and the number of two hundred ninety foure yeares is made vp, doth not number the fourth part of the dayes; we therefore iudge that the yeares are to be reckoned vp one by one, and that ſo many are to be ſet downe, as there are dayes in theſe moneths, which agreeth perfectly with the cuſtome of Daniels weekes. Thirdly, we muſt ob-ſerue, that theſe are no Iulian yeares for theſe two and forty moneths onely doe make a thouſand, two hundred and threeſcoore yeares. To conclude, he doth hereby teach vs,that the moneths are not to

mournefulle state (stripped of all their glorious and glistring shewe,

and mourne at funeralls vsually.

But whence commeth it, that they should be thus dolefully arayed,
in that Triumphing time, that the Church liued in vnder Constantine
the great? Certainly howsoeuer the glory of peace, honours, digni-
ties, and wealth was great, wherewith he did enrich and adorne the
Churches,in most magnificent manner,yet as touching true pietye,all
began then to waxe worse & worse. The heauen departed away vnder

when the cruel enemies sword was hacking vppon necks and backs

Vers. 6. *These haue power to shut heauen.* He passeth over to another power of these, which is mighty and admirable, wherewith they doe likewise equall the greatest of all the Prophets. Elias is famous, at whose prayers God did so shut vp heauen, that the earth was not made wett with any showre in three yeares and sixe moneths, 1. Kings, 18. 1. Luc. 4. 25. But we reade of no such things acted by these Prophets. It is true indeed if we take the words properly, but if we transferre them to spirituall matters, according as the rest haue bene, that we haue spoken of, howe great agreement shall wee finde? That drought came three yeares and sixe moneths at the prayers of Elias.

So the time of the power giuen to these Prophets, should be for so many great yeares and moneths. For 42. moneths, or a thousand two hundred & sixty dayes, doe make this space of yeares and of moneths. But they be great ones as I haue said, and haue nowe sufficiently proued, not such commō ones, as those of Elias were, each of them being three hundred & threescore ordinary yeares, and the halfe yeare being a hundred and fourescore.

Howe great a drought and penurye of spirituall dewe, was there all this time, for want whereof piety withered away euery where in the world? But they that bring all strictly to the letter, and will haue these three yeares and a halfe vnderstood of common yeares, doe they likewise dreame of such a restraint of raine as indeed they must needs? Certainly they make Antichrist Kingdome ill fauoured hunger starued, and euery wayes miserable and wretched, altogether contrary to that excesse & riot, wherewith the holy Ghost saith he shall run ouer. Neither should Antichrist bee at leasure to carry Weapons about, to subdue the Nations withall, but he should rather leade his droues of oxen and cattell, to water them where he can, as we reade that Ahab did of old. But it is no meruaile, that they fall into many such absurdities as these, who had rather followe their owne opinions that they haue once concieted then the truth it selfe.

*In the streets of the great Cittye.*  This great Citty is all that place of Iurisdiction, whereof Rome is the mother-Cittye, in which sense the tenth part of the Citty is said to fall, beneath vers. 13. a streete is some part of the Romish Iurisdiction, wherein this spectacle is sett forth to be beheld, the ioy whereof spreads it selfe through the whole Empire.  Nowe this great Citty it selfe, together with her mother Citty is described in the rest of the verse, and that by two expresse names, and by a notable marke that is ioined together with them , least any man perhaps should be mistaken in the Cittye, and for the more heed taking also, we are admonished that these names are not to bee taken properly, but spiritually, that is , after the manner of a riddle, Trope , allegory. The enemies sawe this and stormed at it, especially the Pope did as it became him, take it most heinously, who was credibly thought to sollicite Cesar that he would make that edict of his voide againe,

13. *And there vvas a great earth quake.* Aretas, Complutensis, & some other reades, *in that some daye.* It is very ordinary for an earth quake to signifie a chāge of the estate of matters, as we haue obserued, Chapt. 6. 12. And indeed there followed a great change by meanes of this Decree through out all Europe. The men of Austria doe earnestly require of Ferdinandus their King that the same thing might be graunted vnto them that was graunted to their fellowes that were of the Augustana Confession. The Bauarians doe importunately request as much of Albertus their Prince. Which Princes when they sawe it was scarce safe to be vtterly crosse against this so feruent a desire of mē, they doe both of them grant their subiects somewhat that they petitioned for, though sore against their wills. The like things were done in many other places, whereupon a man might see newe reuoltings euery day to be made from the Popish Kingdome.

*And the tenth part of the Citty fell.* The Citty in this place is the whole Kingdome of Popery, which began for the greatest part thereof, to bee diminished after that the Germans had thus reuolted. I doubt not but the Pope himselfe will confesse of his owne accord, that he forfeited the tenth part of his Cittye and more by this fall; but together with this ruine and earthquake, *there were seauen thousand heads of men slaine.* Nowe that is translated heads of men, is names of men in the Greeke, & that is put for the men them selues, as Chapter 3. 4. But it is a very significant manner of speaking, teaching vs that God doth not strike men after the māner of those that play with swords winking but that he doth set them downe certainly and by name, whome he will haue beaten with his rodds. ## The Resolution of the rest of
### The 11. Chapter.

*And thus much of the sixth Trumpett, and of the se-*
*cond Period of times. The last followeth, which is*
*declared by the seuenth Trumpett, which is expla-*
*ned first summarily in the rest of this Chapter, and*
*afterwards point by point. The summary exposition*
*doth celebrate the Kingdome of Christ, partly by word, partly by*
*signe, both of the Presidents of the Chistian Assemblies,*
*verse 15. As also of the foure and twenty Elders, whose gesturne*
*is sett downe vers. 16. And then their speech, vers. 17. And this*
*doth illustrate the glory of this Kingdome by the fury of the enemies,*
*by the Wrath of God manifested in vanquishing them, and conclude*
*by the Retribution, which should be both to the good & bad, vers. 18.*
*Lastly the signe is, the Temple that was opened, the Arke that was*
*seene, and the lightenings that were sent forth, vers. 19.*

## THE EXPOSITION

*Verf. 14. The second vvoe is past.* Here vve haue a Transition made from the second more greiuous Trumpet of the three lattermost, to the last of all. Nowe in that he saith that the second woe was past, it is not to be so vnderstood, as if there were nothing at all thereof remaining at this time, but this is meant, that the force thereof is onely empaired, and much weakened which should also more and more waxe out of heart euery daye, till it should be at length altogether abolished. For those foure Angells of the ninth Chapter, whome we haue shewed to be the Turkes, vvere not quite destroyed at the first blast of the seauenth Trumpet, but hastening onely tovvards their destruction. In like manner they came vpon the Locusts not staying till there vvas not one Locust remaining, but rushing in vppon them as they began to come to their old and vvithering Age, Chapter 9.12.

*And behold the third vvoe.* Why is the last Trumpet called a woe, vvhich shall bring full reformation to the Church. It is so called in respect of the vvicked, vvhose ende doth novve approch, together vvith a full paiment for all their sinnes, both vvith such punishments as are begun here vppon earth as also vvith eternall punishments in Hell. It is said he should come soone, because of that small delaye, of time that should come betvvene that rising of the Prophets againe, vvhich he spake of before, and the last Trumpets blast. As also because the last calamity of the vvicked should be dispatched in a short time, and should not linger so long, as the former Trumpets did, but should flye rather vvith svvift winges.

*Then the seauenth Angell blevve vvith his Trumpet, &c.* Namely in the yeare 1558; As the euents doe make it plaine, for then vvere the great voices geuen forth in heauen, that is, great ioye arose in the reformed Church; for that is the meaning of Heauen, as vve haue said often before, neither are these voices such terrible ones as are ioined vvith the Thunder and lightenings that follovve after in the ende of this Chapter, and are meant elsvvhere, but they are voices of ioye and thanksgiuing as the matter of them shevveth in the vvords next follo-
