Whose these voices are it is gathered out of that that followeth vppon the voices in the next verse, namely, that the Elders fell vppon their faces, which they had heard those voices, which they are wont to doe at the hearing of the voices of the foure Beasts, Chapt. 4. 9. 10. They are therefore the Gouernours of the Churches who goe before their flocks stirring them vp, and shewing them the waye to magnifie the Lord for some notable benefit, which this seauenth Trumpets blast brought vnto them. They shewe what kinde of benefit this is, when they saye, *the Kingdomes of the world are become subiect to our Lord, and his Christ, &c.* But what meaneth this? Doth Christ raigne nowe first of all. Certainly hee hath alwayes raigned, euen in the midst of his enemies. But nowe is his Kingdome to be especially extolled with praises, when as he doth make his Maiesty to be visible after a sort in the Kings them selues, by so framing and fashioning their hearts, that they are glad to cast downe, their crownes & Scepters before his feete, and doe geue them selues wholy to seeke the aduancing of his glorye. And yet this is no strange thing neither. He raigned thus in auncient times by meanes of *Constantine*, & other Godly Emperours. In these last ages also those renowmed Princes of *Germany* had restored this Kingdome, erewhile before this; To whome *Gustauus* the King of *Sueueland*, and *Christianus* the King of *Denmarke* may be added, who in the yeare 1558. put downe *Antichristian* impiety, and set vp the Gospell in the roome of it. I answere that this is not the meaning of this Prophecye, that nowe the Kingdomes become Christian first of all, but onely that there should be a great addition made, at the first blast of this Trumpet; for then doe we cheifely say that a man raigneth, when we see the bounds of his Kingdome to be enlarged; And yet ouer and besides this, this is a peculiar prerogatiue of this time, that this Kingdome of Christ, that began from this time to be great and manifest, should neuer be obscured so againe as the former Kingdomes were, which came to an vtter ruine in processe of time. For so it is said and he shall raigne for euermore. The first entrance therfore of this Trumpet should be famous by this increase of newe Kingdomes, euen as it came to passe in our Kingdome of *England*. all the Saints to goe into , seeing nowe all the mysteries of saluation
were made so plaine, familiar and manifest vnto euery one as they
were of old to the learned , whose whole studye was spent in them.
And who is there but one that is altogether enuious and vnthankeful,
who will not acknowledge, that most rich and aboundant encrease
that hath accrued to the truth, in these last times from the yeare 1558
wherein the seuenth Trumpet blewe.

The doctrine of the truth hath bene illustrated with more heardes, hath bene more also exactly and distinctly knowne and deliuered, then was to be seene in many Ages that haue bene in times past. And I doe not speake this for ostentation sake, but to magnifye the goodnes of God, and to demonstrate the truth of this Prophecye. Certainly God hath begun to destroye the couering in his mountaine that couered all people, *and the vaile that vvas spread vppon all nations, as he promised, Esay 25. 7.* He hath begun it ( I saye ) because it shalbe taken away more fully, when it shalbe taken from the Iewes also.

*And there vvere lightenings.* This is the third part of the signe, which teacheth what should followe of the opening of the Tēple. Great euils should rush into the world from out of the Church, when it should be thus increased & enriched with such great abundance of diuine knowledge, the world waxeth leane when that waxeth fat & well liking, and the more bright and glorious a sunshine the Church hath the more doe the eyes of the world waxe sore, and full of paine. Wherevppon it wisheth the subuersion of the Church & doth endeauour to effect it as much as it can, but all the profit that cometh by the labour it taketh, is to pull downe vppon it selfe lightenings, and all the euills that are here spoken of. But this is onely a compendious shadowing out of these matters beforehand, the expresse portraiture shalbe seene afterwards.

# The 12. Chapter.

## The logicall Resolution.

WE *haue spoken summarily of the seauenth Trumpet: the members thereof are a recognizing, and reuiew-*
*ing of the time past in three Chapters, 12. 13. 14. And *of the* Dragon *that raiseth it,* vers. 3. 4. ## THE EXPOSITION.

1. *And there appeared a great signe in heauen.* Whereas we intimated shortly in the Analysis, that the three next Chapters doe belong iontly to the continued History of the time past , some man may perhaps meruaile, why the Holy Ghost should doe the same thing twice, and repeate the former Historye , which seemeth to haue bene sufficiently laid open in the Chapters before, of which we haue spoken, but cheifely why he should doe this in this place , after the seauenth Trumpets blast, when as the ende of all things was shortly after to come,as we haue heard out of the tenth Chapter.

The causes of both these things are most iust. For there is no man that beholdeth the parts of a building disioined,& scattered one from the other here and there , that can scarce take any due information in his minde touching the whole frame , much lesse can he perceiue the elegancy thereof which would be seene when all the parts are ioined together,and when each part is sett in his proper place,& compacted one with the other in a comely order among them selues . The former handling of this Historye, was a certaine preparation & fitting of the parts as they were distinguished one from the other , but this perpetuall narration compacteth all into one, & setteth the whole building before our eyes , that we might see to what perfection that singular

<meta>catchword: frame</meta>

frame doth at length come. Nowe it is referued for this time, because there could not be a full vnderstanding of these things before the last Trumpet. The euents came forth by litle and litle, and point by point, to the knowledge of which the world attained seuerally & by leasure-like, as when hangings are vnfolded but nowe when al things were at last accomplished, it was a fit time to see the whole garment displaid at large, and to make vp the whole frame of the building together & at once; but we are especially taught by this repetition, that there was such a History of al these matters to be compiled vnder this last Trumpet, as is framed typically in these three Chapters. The which thinge came to passe about the yeare 1560. when certaine learned & skillfull men made that worthy worke of the Centuries at Maidenbrough. In which thirteene Centuries, whatsoever is to be had scatteringly in the auncient Ecclesiasticall or political writers, as touching matters done from Christs birth to the yeare 1300. is framed into one bodye, and like a house that is built vp and hath all the parts of it compacted together fitly among them selues, is set vnder one viewe. Our Cuntry-man John Foxe, & John Sleidan tooke a torch-light from these mens writings, and by the helpe thereof continued the History to the yeare 1555. Namely, to that time, that went some two or three yeares before the seuenth Trumpets blast.

Because of this, that is, by force of that restoring of the Church and of that commandment, Chapt. 10. 10. 11. The former times are called to mind vnder the last Trumpet, because all things should be nowe at length opened most plentifully through the lightsome labours of learned men, which thing was neuer done before. The like industrye of learned men that liued about the ende of the sixth Trumpet, begat that continued History of the times foregoing, whereof we haue spoken in the former Chapter; but that was somewhat more generall and more obscure, such as the condition of that time would suffer, but this is most full, and copious, because there was nowe greater knowledge of matters attained, then euer before this These things are to be obserued as touching the order of this Prophecye, to the entent that we might the more easily perceaue, that these things are not shuffled into an vnmeete place as some suppose, but that they are referued most wisely & conueniently to be brought in this manner vnder this last Trumpet, as being their naturall and proper seate. And yet notwithstanding

Elswhere this clothing is made of white and pure linnen, but the comely hewe of no latter time did come neere this excellent glory of the Sunne. 2. *And vvhen she vvas vvith child, she cryed.* The fourth property of the Church is her Child-birth ; the words are *hauing in her vvombe*, as Matth. 1. 18. Aretas and the vulgar read the next words thus, *She cryeth trauailing being pained to bring forth.* That is, in bringing forth, or that she might bring forth, which kinde of Composition is not vnlike to that which the Grecians vse elsewhere, faire to see to, valiant to fight, for in shewe, and in fight. The Church had an exceding great torment for a long time, as it were, the paines of a vvoman in trauaile. Nowe she desired with all her heart to be deliuered at length from that most distressed estate, wherein she laye vnder the most cruel heathenish Emperours.

And she knewe she should enjoye the thing she desired, if she could at length bring forth some certaine man, that might take the gouernment vppon him, and haue the rule of all thing in his power. For the woman was not barren and vnfruitfull before this time, but prosperous in hauing great store of Children, yet was there one sonne wanting, who might defende her frō the iniuries of her enemies, whome while she trauaileth with, and seeketh for a Champion to fight in her quarrell, she endured greiuous paines, before she could obtaine that which she wished after.

3. *And there appeared another vvonder.* So much for the description of the woman, that that remaineth of her estate is to be seene by the description of her enemy, namely the Dragon; which consists partly of such things as are inherent in him in this verse, partly of his effects in the next. Those things are his red colour, his hornes, heads, diademes, before all which the place is sett wherein the Dragon was seene, namely in heauē, but not that that is properly so called. For what should the Dragon, that is, the Diuel doe in that heauēly pallace from whence he is for euer banished? It is in that heauen then which is on earth. Nowe this Dragon is not onely the Diuel in his owne person, but such men also as are the instruments of his furye, especially the Emperours of Rome; who did most greiuously persecute Christ in his members from the time that Iohn wrote, as Traian, Hadrian, Antonius Pius, Verus, Commodus, Seuerus, Decius and at last Dioclesian

But it vvas enough for the Holy Ghost to describe the enemy by some certaine property; And indeed there could be none more cleare then this amplenes of his Iurisdiction and Territories, & this so remarkeable a course that he tooke in deuiding the Prouinces. Novve he vveareth the crovvnes vppon his heads, not on his hornes, because the supreme soueranity did reside at Rome, vnto vvhich the rest of the Prouinces submitted their authoritye, as acknovvledging it to be receaued there from.

4. *Whose Taile drevve.* Hauing novve shewed vvhat kinde of nature and properties the Dragon hath, he novve cometh to shewe howe he carrieth himselfe towards the Church. And he mentioneth a double effect and vvorke of his; One against the Starres; another against the womã. As for those, he threvve dovvne many of them from their heavenly profession vvith the cruelty of his persecutions, vvho ought to haue bene the lights of the vvorld, to direct others in the darkenes of errours and vvickednes. For this is to cast the Starres of heaven to the earth; Euseb.Book.6.Chapt.41. See more of this before Chapt.6.13.

and power he had to cutt of this hope. And certainly as soone as the Dragon Maximinus sawe Alexander the sonne of Mammea to bee somewhat wel inclined towards the Christiãs, so that he was thought to haue bene instructed in the principles of their Religiõ, he deuoured him straightwayes. That Dragon Decius also swallowed vp the two Phillips, the father & the Sonne, though he himselfe was shortly after swallowed vp in a quagmire or a moorish place. But the matter is most clearly apparant in Constantine, at whome the Holy Ghost did principally point the finger as it were. When Diocletian and Galerius with whome this man liued in the East when he was yonge, perceaued that he had a singular towardlines by reasõ of his virtuous dispositiõ, they left nothing vnattempted to cut him of in secret. So saith Euseb. vppon his life Book. 1.

Pomponius Lætus tells vs, that he was sent with an host of men against the Sarmatians, which were a most fierce and sauage kinde of people, accustomed to kill and flaye men; from whome when he had carried away, not his deaths-blowe, but the victorye, quite besides that which Galerius thought of and looked for, he saith, that he fought with a Lyon in the Theatre by his setting on with a pretence as if hee desired to haue him exercise and shewe his valour. But questionlesse Galerius fought to destroy the yong man at vnawares, as Euristheus serued Hercules of old. And this was not the ende of the snares that were laid to deuoure him. Maximian Herculius that red Dragon indeed, had almost quite eaten him vp by meanes of such ambushments as he laid for him afterwards. Constantine escaped many other priuye assaults and treacheries not by any foresight of his owne or of others that descryed the dangers for him, but by the helpe of God, who reuealed them vnto him; as Euseb. saith Book the 1. on the life of Constant. <header>Chap.12. A REVELATION,</header>

*And her child vvas taken vp to God.* Howe was he taken vp? Whether is it meant, that *Constantine* was taken vp into heauen, when he was taken away out of the world by death? Or rather was he thus taken vp, by meanes of that high earthly honour, which God bestowed vpon him, when he had deliuered him out of the snares, and from the conspiracies of his enemies? This latter sense seemeth to be made good by the euent, rather then the other; specially seing. *Magistrats are called Gods*, by proportion whereof, *the throne of the highest dignity vppon earth*, may by right be called, *the Throne of God himselfe*. In the former Chapter, also we heard, howe the two Prophets that reuiued, & recouered their former honour, *are said to ascende vp into heauen, vers. 12.* Neither is it like, that he whose power was so great ouer the nations, should haue both his birth and his death ioined together, without mentioning any notable fact of his, wherein he should approue this power of his, that he had formerly receaued. To be taken vp to God then, is to be placed in the highest Toppe of dignity among men, that is, to be made Emperour. Nowe he is said to be taken vp, because the Kingdome was not so much fought for by him, as it was cast vpon him, when he thought of no such matter. He fled from the snares of his enemies, by getting himselfe away vnto his Father, whome he findeth departing out of this life assoone as he came. And when he was once dead he tooke possessiō of all that power of his Father, as being heire vnto it, vnder the shadowe whereof he desired to lie couered, while his Father liued. Shortly after he is fought out, and much longed after, by the feruent desires of the people of *Rome*, whome the intolerable yoke of the tyranny of *Maxentius* did oppresse, they come and persuade with him, yea they beseech him that he would not thus lie lurking in a litle corner of the world, but would take vppon him the gouernment of the whole world which was nowe offered him. The heauenly signe, & voice that bad him to doubt nothing of the victory, was added hereto at the same time, to helpe them in their motion, and to encourage him to hearken to it.

Howe great a force was here and that sent from God, that takes vp, & aduanceth a man to the highest honour in the world? He would willingly doubtlesse haue rested him selfe in those boundes which his Father left him of *France* and *Britanny*, wherein he kept him selfe quiet the fiue first yeares, vnlesse he had bene rapt vp from heauen to

6. And the vvoman fledd. This is another Euent in respect of the woman ; who fled away presently after the birth of her manly sonne; And this flight of hers is declared by the place whither she betooke her selfe , by that estate which she liued in there , and by the space of time, which she continued there. All which things are explaned a litle more largely afterwards from the 13. verse. Where the continued prophecy of this flight is sett downe together ; These things are here breifely spoken of , as in their proper place , to the ende we might vnderstand the more easily to what time this flight doth truly belõge. The place is the wildernes , that is , the Temple that was measured, Chapt. 11. 1. Where while the poore handfull of the Elect lurked, there was a meere solitary wildernes in respect of that place, where that Innumerable company liued, that possessed the holy Citty, & the outmost Court.

And yet this desert is that place that was prepared for her by God, as we haue seene by that so exact measuring of the Temple, that was vsed; For God cared for her, and prouided her an hiding place, howe-soeuer he suffered her to want her publike solemnitye. The condition of the Church while she thus lurked is such , that she was fed by the helpe of certaine men. But who are these ? Euen those two Prophets of whome we heard in the former Chapter, vers. 3. And that power which was geuen them to prophecye, was this office of feeding the woman. For as God did of old feed the Israelites, in the wildernes by raining downe Manna from heauen , so he prepared meate for the woman , when she was in this desert. Yea and more then, that he would haue enioined the rauens to take that office vppon them of feeding her , as we sawe he did for Elias sake , rather then he would haue suffered her to perish with famine. This is that time therfore wherein those that ouercame did feede vppon that hidden Manna , as we shewed vppon the Epistle to the Church of Pergamus , Chapter 2. 17.

The space of time wherein she should liue thus in obscurity , and want her publike liberty, is that space of a thousand two hundred and threescore dayes , the same wherein those two witnesses should Prophecye clothed in sackcloth, Chapt. 11. 3. 7. *And there vvas a battell in heauen.* Hetherto of the Persecution,
which lasted all the time, while there was no man that for this whole

heauen, as it is aboue, verf. 3.

In the combate each Prince doth putt forth all his power by their

descry them of what quality they be. Constantine therefore that faith-

shewed before at the 6. Chapter 15. That Christ began this warre
against the Dragon, when he cast Dioclesian & Maximinus Herculius
downe from the toppe of their Empire, by a pretence of a voluntary
yeelding.

That which is called heaven and earth, was called the Temple and the Court in the former Chapter. The Church laye hidden in that, the Gentiles, dominired in this, namely that people, who tooke to them selues the name of the Church, because they were so neere vnto it bodily, and yet were but as heathens in Gods account. The Dragon then that was cast out is thrust downe into this earth, and into this Court together with his Angels, hauing power geuen him to vexe the whore , who did before that of a long time exercise all his crueltye against the true Spouse.

10. Then I heard a loud voice saying. Here we haue the Song of Triumph which the Saints sing out, wherein they magnifie God for this great benefit; which is first declared by those things wherein the benefitt it selfe consists in this verse; and then it is illustrated by the causes thereof vers. 11. And the effects, vers. 12. The benefit it selfe in respect of men, is saluation and strength, because nowe were those tyrāts ouer throwne, who endevoured to satisfy their malicious hearts with the destruction of Christians in respect of God, it is the glory of his Kingdome, and of Christs Kingdome and power. For then is his power truly seene aloft, when he doth destroy and put downe his enemies utterly. His Kingdome also is after a sort visibly seene, when he setteth up godly Princes to governe his Church, hēce also is Christs power made glorious as which before when it was so troden under feete by the enemies, and did not shewe it selfe in taking vengeance on them as they deserued, seemed to be weake or rather none at all. But Christ did nowe declare abundantly when he tooke this Kingdome into his hands, that his former winking at his enemies, and suffering them to goe away scotfree, proceeded not from any want of power in himselfe, but onely from a willing forbearance of them, for such a time as seemed good vnto him.

In respect of the Diuel this benefit was the iust guerdon of his impietye, which he principally shewed in accusing the godly in the sight of God continually. Nowe we must obserue that the Seruants are called by the same names that the Prince himselfe is called by, because they had both of them a like will and desire to doe mischeife, though the Princes power were greater.

But of this hurly burly, which the Deuill brought vppon the Earth
and the Sea, when he was cast downe from heauen, we haue spoken at

open that more largely in those things that followe in this selfe same
Chapter, which is here touched in one word.

<margin>As vvho knovveth he hath but a short time.</margin>
The word here in the
Greeke put for time, signifieth ofte opportunity, which agreeth better
perhaps in this place. For there was a great deale of time as yet to
come, which yet should be but a litle time after a thousand yeares ; as
it is Chapt. 20. 3. Where the Holy Ghost seemeth to haue vsed another
word of purpose that doth more properly note out a space of time.
But nowe the Deuill being tumbled downe into his house of correc-
tion as it were, which was before in his iurisdiction, should haue but a
litle opportunity. To doe that mischeife he desired to doe. Diuelish
enuy doth reioice more to poure out poyson vppon the Saints, than to
torment men vppon no necessity, who were already sold ouer and
enthralled fast enough vnto himselfe. He would willingly spare this
labour, and he would rather be doing with those, whome he seeth to
his greife pulld out of his iawes. Besides the word (knowing) may be
an argument to proue this matter, the moments of times that are to
come are without doubt vnknowne to the Diuell, aboue the rest the
last day of all, which euen the sonne himselfe was ignorant of, but he
could not be ignorant of his present opportunity. This seemeth ther-
fore to be the cause of his furye, that being nowe cast out of heauen,
he must nowe needs poure out his rage against his owne cittizens,
whereas yet he did more desire to hurt the Elect ; But these he could
not touch, being expulsed out of their company; and seeing this large
feild as he counted it for his rage to course it in, was nowe barred
from him, he accounted of all the rest but as a pinfold in comparison
of that.

13. *And vvhen the Dragon savve.* Hether-to of the things that
were done in heauen, where the sixth Seale endeth. Nowe we come to
the stratagemes of the Dragon when he was cast vppon the earth;
which belonge to the same time with the Trumpets. Nowe first of all
he raised vp a persecution against the woman, which begat the manly
Sonne.

Nowe that is called persecution properly, when one party suffereth force and wronge,and is not able to defend him selfe against the injuries of his enemye. But what should the womā need to feare any such matter as this , seeing the Diuell was nowe cast out of heauen? Can the heauens be hurt any whitt by the lowest parts of the earth? But Heauen here is not distinguished from earth in distance of places, but in the holines of faith and manners. Yet howe cometh it to passe that the Church should suffer persecution , as if it were destitute of a defender , which did right nowe bring forth her male child , and had *Michael* for her most valiant Champion? The truth is this , that these wrongs befell the woman from the Dragon , because the cheife care of the Emperours was to driue out the open and outward enemies from the Church,which when they had once attained,they cared lesse for other matters ; neither did they consider, at least so diligently as it was meete,that the Dragon had many other wayes to doe mischeife, which they them selues did at vnawares ,make a more easye way vnto him by their helpe, so farre of were they, from opposing them selues valiantly against his enterprises.Hence it was therefore that the Dragon did first of all sowe a priuy heart-burning among the Bishops ; Which being sprung vp together with *Constantine*,before the Trumpetts began to blowe, gaue a dolefull presage of the euill to come,as we haue noted on the 2.verse of the 8.Chapter. For this sparke did shortly after growe vnto a flame, but cheifely after the controuersy began about the essence of the Sonne of God. In all which troublesome contentions, the truth had the worst alwayes. But the greatest heate of persecution burnt out, when *Constantius*, *Iulian* and *Valens* raged against those of the sincere faith after the manner of open enemies.

Certainly *Constantius* and *Valens* differed nothing from the most cruell Tyrants that had bene, but onely in their bare name and profession. They were called *Christian* Princes, but they exercised the sauage cruelty of the Heathens vnder that name. The Dragon therefore would grant the woman no time of Truce,but when he was cast out of Heauen, he vexed the woman straight-after by other meanes. This persecution is that which we haue spoken of in the expounding of the first, second, and third Trumpetts, Chapt.8. But see howe profitable this short repetion is , which enformeth vs as touching

14. *But the vvoman had tvvo vvings geuen her.* Here we see by what waye the woman escaped that assault, which the Dragō made against her which was no other but assoone as euer she could to prouide for her safety by flying & so getting her selfe away from those troubles. Therefore while the assemblies of the faithfull were filled with superstitions, the Bishops were bickering together through hatred & contentions, while Constantius and Valens made hauocke of all with fire and sword, the truth that had bene preserued in the primitiue Church, fled quite awaye, (for she had bene preparing her selfe to trucke in some sort nowe of a long time) & the naturall beauty of a true Churches face was not any where to be seene.

For the furdering of her swiftnes in flying awaye, she hath two wings geuen her, yea and those of a great Eagle. God when he departed from his temple of old time, went leasurely, and by litle and litle,

But the woman who did retire somewhat slowly before this time, doth not gett her away so slowly and pace by pace nowe, but vanished away in one moment as it were. And yet she fledd not away because she feared the blody cruelty of Constantius or Valens, or any other such Tyrant (for she learnt this lesson longe since, to despise sword, fire, rackinge, or any other most extreme torments.) But when she sawe that Christ was oppugned vnder a face of the Christian Religion, and that not the bodies onely of Christians, but their minds also were fought for to destructiō, she held this to be a matter by no meanes to be endured. She flieth away then through an hatred which she had conceiued, of this indignity that was offered her, euen she whome no other danger could dismaye. For she was euer wont to be more horribly afraid of heresy, then of bodily torments, & more to tremble at wicked and obstinate errours, then at any bloudy butcherings;

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*For a time, and times, and halfe a time.* Theſe words if they be fett alone by them ſelues , can not be vnderſtood , ſeeing time here ſtands for nombèr , and there is an infinite ſort of nombers , that may be deuided into three or more whole nombers and into halfe a nomber. But the words are made plaine by thoſe things that haue bene formerly ſpoken. For the ſame ſpace is meant here which was noted out before , by the thouſand tvvo hundred and threeſcore dayes, verſ. 6. Or by the tvvo and fourty moneths , Chapter 11. verſ. 2. Out of which it is manifeſt what is meant , by *time, times, and halfe a time.*

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For the time of dayes are three hundred threeſcore dayes, times are twice ſo many, namely ſeauen hundred, and twenty. Halfe a time is a hundred and foureſcore. So the time of moneths is twelue moneths, times foure and twentye , halfe a time, ſixe,he alludeth to that of Daniel, Chapter 7. verſ. 25. But it is not the ſame ſpace there meant. For there is ſpeach had of the people of the Iewes,here of the Church of the Gentiles ; as the whole drift of this Prophecy declareth. But perhaps Iohn intimateth by this alluſion that a definite number is to be found elſwhere , from whence that place of Daniel might be explaned. But I may not digreſſe to that matter at this time. Onely let vs remember that this flight of the woman is the ſame with the ſealing in the ſeauenth Chapter , and the lying hid in the Temple in the eleuenth.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Beſides let vs conſider that this ſame ſpace of time is ſundry wayes fett downe,according to the variety of the perſons. In reſpect of the Gentiles and the beaſt it is ſett downe alwayes by moneths , Chapter 11.verſ.2. and Chapter 13. 5. In regard of the Prophets it is ſet downe by dayes ; Chapter 11. 3. In reſpect of the woman both by dayes in the ſixth verſe of this Chapter,and by times in this verſe, and that becauſe all thoſe dayes ſhould not goe on with one equal tenour, but there ſhould fall out a threefold change in them ; to wit, that she ſhould flye awaye neerer hand,vnder the time then furder of and into more remote places vnder the times , but she ſhould flye homeward and approach neere againe in her returne, vnder the halfe time. The euent maketh this manifeſt , as it may be vnderſtood both by thoſe things that haue bene ſaid,& by thoſe which ſhalbe ſaid afterwards.

15. *And the Serpent caſt out of his mouth.* The ſecond perſecution of the woman whẽ ſhe was put to flight is laid downe in theſe words. For the Dragon held it not to be malice enough to chaſe her awaye into the wildernes, vnleſſe he could alſo quite aboliſh her remembrance. For which purpoſe he poured out the Barbarous nations vppon her like a floud that ouerrunneth all; that in what corner ſoeuer of the world ſhe lurked, ſhe might be ouerwhelmed with this inundation.

For as *Herode commaunded all the children in bethlem of tvvo yeere old and vnder to be ſlaine, that ſo that that one childe Ieſus, whome hee fought to deſtroy,might not eſcape,* ſo the Dragon, leaſt that this one woman ſhould remaine in ſafetye, made euery place to bee couered ouer with a moſt violent floud, where he ſuſpected that ſhe could lie hid. The Franci, the Alemanni, the Burgonions all being people of Germany, the Goths,the Vandalls,the Hunni, the Treballi,the Heruli, the Lombards, and ſuch other Northen nations as theſe, which were moſt obſcure before this time, ruſhed in vppon her about the yeare 400. the ſluces as it were being taken away throughout all Europe, and brought as it were a diluge of waters into a great part of Africa. And indeed it is meruailous, that the Church was not wholy drowned vp with theſe moſt deepe gulfes.

And ſo it had bene, vnleſſe this ſhippe had learned of old to floate aloft and ſo to ſcape drowning in that vniuerſall diluge of the whole world. But ſeeing it is nowe manifeſt, that the Dragon caſt out of his mouth ſo great ſtore of waters into Europe and Affricke after the woman it may likewise appeare moſt euidently, that the woman fled out of the Eaſt into theſe Regions. And indeed the Church was more peaceable here abouts,amideſt thoſe troubles which the Arians raiſed in the Eaſt about the word Coeſſentiall. But leaſt we ſhould imagine that ſhe liued any where happily, the Holy Ghoſt doth call our Europe a defert place and a wildernes in expreſſe words. For the woman going into the weſterne parts is ſaid to flye into a wildernes. For ſuperſtitions did ſo preuaile at that time,that there were no more frequent aſſemblies rightly planted in this part of the world, thẽ there are wont to be ſtore of habitations of men in a wildernes. Here and there was ſome more expreſſe footeſteppe to be ſeene,but it was very rare,as it is to meete with many men in the wildernes.

16. *But the Earth helped the woman.* Not this earth which we treade vpon, but the counterfaite, and earthly Religion, together with the professours thereof, as it signifieth euer before. This Church so called commonly in the world of what fashion soeuer it then was (while the true Church was not conuerfant in the eyes of men , but laye hidden in her lurking holes ) brought much helpe vnto the woman.

For these Barbarous nations , which did maintaine heathenish impietye in their owne cuntries, as in the which they had bene borne and brought vp ; after that they came into these cuntries, that were more full of humanity, they were content be of that Religion which they sawe to be receaued by the most there. The Vandals and the Gothes, seating them selues first about Thracia where the Pestilence of the Arian heresy had spoiled all, were conuerted to Christ in name, but in very deed to such a forged and counterfaite Christ as Arius had made. The rest of the Barbarous rout in Germany , Italy , Fraunce , Spaine, followed the Romans in all things. And this thing did much tame and mollifie their sauage minds; For while they gaue their names but euen to this Religion, & sufferd them selues to be enrolled among the professours thereof, they were not so malicious against the Christian people, as to seeke to roote them out vtterly; wherby it came to passe, that while their wrath was asswaged in fauour of their newe profession, and while they rested them selues in those cuntries , which they had possessed, this floud was at last swallowed vp, and the Serpents hope was notably deluded. The earthly Church did nowe once for all procure this good vnto the heauenly, but she meant to make her pay for it afterwards , by those infinite euills , which she was about to heape vppon her.

17. *Then the Dragon was vvroth.* Hetherto of the persecution, which when the Dragon sawe to be in vaine , yet he would not leaue of, but fetteth vppon another waye of mischeiuing her. He determines to assault the rest of her seed with warre. But why doth he raise vp warre against these , and persecution against the woman? Because that is persecution as we haue said , when the one side beareth the iniury, and doth not defende it selfe by force, such as the Estate of the woman was, as in her first beginning.

His malice would not suffer him to geue her any breathing, but assoone as he perceaued that his former endeuours were frustrate, he betakes himselfe to another project; rather coueting to make himselfe perpetually miserable with continuall labours and molestations, then that those fewe remnants of the Elect, should want any misery for any short time.

Therefore he first of all egged the Saracens forward to make defection from the Romans. And after that he made Mahumet their Captaine, and then he sent them into the whole world to ouerthrowe all. Who can declare and conceiue when it is declared what a world of mischeife sprung from them? There was perpetuall warre by meanes of them from the time that they came in for the whole space of feauen hundred yeares, vntill the Turkes a broode of vipers, worse then their Parent, did utterly destroye the Saracens their mother that begatt them.

This warre went farre and wide , such as neuer was elswhere. It reached from *Persis* in *Asia*, to the *Gades* that be two *Iles*, that part *Europe* from *Africa*; and from the *Garamantes* a people in *Lybia*, to *France*.

*Nowe* howe noisome and cruel a warre was this, that brought vn-der subjection; *Arabia, Syria, Mesopotamia, Persis, Egypt*, the *Iles* of the *Sea, Affrick, Spaine*, and all this in a fewe yeares? Certainly the *Christian* world was most pittifully distressed by meanes of it. Nay the *Diuell* did not spare his owne brood , so he might withall sweepe away that lurking seed of the world with a common calamity. This warre was intimated before , partly by the *Locusts* as we haue expounded them, *Chapter 9. to the 12. verse*, partly by the *Angells* of *Euphrates* that is the *Turks*, who haue euer since to this daye endeuoured to finish that destruction of the *Christians*, which the *Saracens* began, as we haue shewed, *Chapter 9. from the 13. verse*. And it must not seeme strange that so cruell a name as of warre is nowe geuen to this matter, which not long before was said to be done by a swarme of vermin-lyke *Locusts*.

There is one manner of shewe in a matter, when it is once finished, such as is described in this place, and another when it is in hande in doing and readye to be done ; of what nature that is which is there spoken of. Nowe then we see out of the persecution in the *East*, the inundation of the *Barbarians* in the *West* , and the *Saracens* warre common to both , with what mischeifes the *Dragon* plagued the world after he had lost heauen and howe iust cause there was to denounce a woe to the inhabitants of the *Earth*, as we heard in the *12. verse*.

And indeed this whole *Chapter* may be in steed of a commentary to teach vs howe the *Prince that ruleth in the aire, is a spirit vvorking in the Children of disobedience, Ephes. 2. 2.* And thus we haue the *History of the Dragon*; so farre as he assaulteth the *Church* with open force, which he doth in his owne person. The other parts of fraud and craft he playeth by his *Vicar* the *Beast* to whome he geuen them ouer, of which kinde of enemy we shall heare in the next *Chapter*. The whole *Prophecy* is of a thousand two hundred yeares, more or lesse, from *Iohn* the *Apostles* time, till the yeare a 1300. where the *Booke of the Centuries* also doe leaue of to entreate, which were

## *The 13. Chapter.*

### **The logicall Resolution.**

*Hetherto of the Combate with the Dragon, the encounter with the beast followeth, which beast is twofold, the first & the second. The description of that is from the beginning of the Chapter to the 11. vers. And first from the causes, that he arose out of the Sea, as also from the integral parts, his hornes, heades, and their ornaments, vers. 1. His whole shape, his feete & mouth, vers. 2. And then from the authority wherein he excelleth, which is threefold, that which he receaued first of al from the Dragō, vers. 2. That which was a litle after diminished, and then that which was recouered when the wound was healed againe, vers. 3. And this is more ample then that which he had at first, as is declared both by the honour which his worshippers geue him, vers. 4. And also by the power he had both of blaspheming, as also of making warre, v. 5. 6. 7. And lastly by the amplenes of his Empire, vers. 7. 8. All which things are shutt up with an Acclamatory conclusion, to geue the greater Caueat and comfort, vers. 9. 10. Such is the first Beast. The second declareth his offspring by his arising out of the Earth, as also by his likenes unto the Lambe and the Dragon, vers. 11. ## THE EXPOSITION.

*Then I sawe a Beast.* To the ende that the whole treatise following may be made more plaine, we are to cõsider summarily of two things, before we come to the explaning of the matters one by one, the first as touching the kinde of this Beast, or who and what this Beast is, the other touching the time wherein he riseth vp. For the first, this Beast is not the ciuill Empire of Rome, either heathenish or Christian corrupted with heresye. For if we respect the Heathen Emperours, these raigned, when Iohn wrote, but this Beast was not yet come, whose first arising he sawe in a Type. For there was none of those things past, whose Original was represented vnto him, but onely that which was to come, according to that, *I vvill shevve thee those things vvhich must be done here after*, Chapter 4. 1. But the Angell certifieth Iohn afterwards that this Beast was not yet come saying, *fiue are fallen, one is and another is not yet come,* Chapt. 17. 10. He that was not yet come is this Beast, as it is manifest out of the 12. verse of that Chapter. *The ten Kings are they vvhich haue not as yet receaued their Kingdome, but they shall receaue their povver as if they vvere Kings for one houre together vvith the Beast.* Besides this Beast receaued his throne and power from the Dragon, vers. 2. Who had before that persecuted the woman that is the Christian Church. But the Heathen Emperours receiued their

the arising of the Beast, not that he had not begũ to put forth his head
before, but because he began nowe first of al to be beheld and marked
by men.

Which had *seauen heads*. Such was his Arising. His integral parts are first his heads, which are as many as those of the Dragons, and the very same with them. For the seate and dignity of both is the same. *For these heads are the hilles, and the Kings, Chapt. 17. 9. He hath also ten Hornes, as the Dragon hath, and ten crownes, sett vppon his hornes, which Hornes, are ten Kings, Chapt. 17. 12.* Yet with a twofold difference from the Dragons Hornes. First in the Crownes, wherewith these are adorned, as which doe note out such Kings as haue all the rule in them selues and are not subiect to any other mans commande, such likewise as are not bound to yeeld account of their doings to any others, but haue such a gouernment, as is absolute, free, and Soueraigne.

The Hornes of the Dragon had no such ornament, but this belonged onely to the heads, as it is *Chapt. 12. 3.* Wherein commeth this difference? Namely from hence, in that the Heathen Emperours placed the fixed Seate of their Empire at Rome, which hath seauen heads; thereby making her to be the ladye and Empresse of all other places, and therfore they tooke away the Crownes from all other Kings, and Prouinces, and put them vppon the seauen heads or Hilles of Rome. But nowe matters should be carried with another manner of Port and pompe, after that Antichrist began once to shew himselfe. For the Maiesty of the Empire, should not reside at Rome, but should be seated in other Nations also, in respect whereof, the Diademes, which belonged to the Heads before, were nowe translated to the Hornes after an vnwonted manner.

Secondly they differ in time. *For the Hornes of the Beast vvere not sprung out as yet, vvhen Iohn vvrote, Chapt. 17. 12.* The Hornes of the Dragon vvere lift vp on high euen before *Iohn* vvas borne, and those spread abroad vvith many boughes as vve haue seene, *Chapt. 12. 3.* Therefore though they agree in number, yet they are not the same in all things alike; neither should a man doe vvell if he should goe about to apply those hornes to the Beastheads, which belong to the Dragōs. But vvhich then are these Hornes of the Beast? In this common Calamitye, she that was ere-while the Ladye of the Nations, and the Queene of the whole world, scaped not scottfree, but came to a more greiuous downefall, then any other citty almost, as being more oftē ouercome, spoiled, wasted, and brought vnder the lawlesse lust of the Barbarous people, then any other, and that for the space of an hundred, thirty, and two yeares. Verf. 4. *And they vvorfhipped the Dragon.* That is, men acknowledged, that the power of the Beaft was the greateft, & that worthily, becaufe of the auncient Majefty of Rome, which the heathen Emperours which are Dragons, did purchafe vnto it. For was not this to adore and worfhip the Dragon, to geue the higheft authority to his fucceffour for his fake? But nowe this was the firft foundation of the Pope of Romes primacy, beeaufe this City was of old the mother Citty of the Empire.

Hence it is that it is called euery where in Eusebius, and other Ecclefiafticall writers, the Cittye that raigneth, but the Councel of Chalcedon fheweth this moft euidently, Act. 16. For(faith it)
> *the Fathers did geue the Priuiledges that vvere agreeable to the feat of old Rome, becaufe of the Empire of this Citty. Thofe hundred and fifty Bifhops likewvife that vvere moft belovved of God, being moued by the fame intent, gaue equall Priuiledges to the Sea of nevve Rome, iudging reafonably, that the Citty that vvas honoured vvith the Empire, and the Senate, fhould enjoye equall Priuiledges vvith old Rome, and fhould carry a Maiefty in Ecclefiafticall bufineffes as vvell as that, and to be the fecond next after that, &c.*

The Empire therefore & the Senate begat the Primacy to old Rome, which while thofe firft Fathers graunt to this Citty becaufe of the heathen Emperours, who raigned there in times paft, those that followed afterwards did amplifie that dignity that was firft graunted vnto it, for the fame caufe, and did all of them caft them felues downe filthily before the Dragon, worfhipping him for being the Author of this honour. The Bifhop of Conftantinople ought to obtaine the like dignity by the same argument; but the Dragon did not fuffer him who made the Bifhop of Rome his onely heire of the whole primacye. Wherefore the Legats of the Bifhop of Rome withftood that decree of the Councell of Chalcedon; Neither would Gelafius the Pope, who allowed of the Chalcedon Synode in other things, confirme this one Canon of the Priuiledge of the Sea of Conftantinople. Nowe seing they attribute these and many such blasphemous things as these vnto them, who seeth not what he is whome all the reprobates of the earth doe worship, & adore with diuine honours? Not that all those who haue at any time adored the Beast, be reprobates. For it might be they should repent, & should be conuerted to the true God, but because all reprobates doe adore him. And let not any be foolishly suttle, and obiect, that there are many cuntries on earth, wherein the Pope of Romes name was neuer so much as heard; I doe not take the whole earth & all reprobates otherwise then the Holy Ghost doth; if the Papists haue any thing wherewith they may cut the throate of this vniuerfality, let them drawe their Weapons, & doe their worst to it. Nowe seing these things be so, let the Pope creake out and say, that it is altogether neceſſary to saluation to be subiect to the Pope of Rome; The Holy Ghost doth crye openly to the contrary, that all they doe wholly ieopard and cast away their saluation, that are subiect to the Pope of Rome; if so be that they depart out of this life with out repentance; Whether of these two trowe ye are to be beleeued. The Pope would haue it thought that he can not erre, but howe foolish a thing is it for a man to delay the triall hereof till that time when if he doe erre in beleeuing, there will be no time nor meanes granted to correct his errour.

This Beast is worshipped of all reprobats, with whome while thou conspirest in thy worship, who shall separate thee from the State of reprobates? He doth not therefore breake of unity, who departeth from the *Synagogue of Rome*, but he purchaseth vnauoidable destruction to himselfe, who cleaueth vnto it, without repentance. O you most cursed wretches, that are called Reconcilers to the *Sea of Rome*, whose whole endeuour is, to call back the People to *Romish doctrine* and subiection. Is it not enough for you to perish your selues, vnleſſe you doe increase your condemnation, by dragging others together with your selues into the same destruction? But let no godly man be offended, if he shall see Reprobates runne backe againe after their Beast; the Holy Ghost hath foretold that this load-stone will drawe this drosse vnto himselfe, and let him not meruaile hereafter, that all those, who are wicked and dissolute in their life are more prone to followe the Pope, then the Truth.

Of that *Lambe vvhich vvas slaine from the beginning of the vvorld*. *Aretas*

What lamentable Epistles doe *Stephanus* the 2. *Constantinus*, *Stephanus* 3. and *Adrian* the Popes, sende to *Pipinus* and *Charles the great* ? Howe full are they all of complaints, piteous lamentations , teares, and most vehement obtestations ? Doe but consider what inhumanity they doe charge their enemies with, & howe they doe sett forth the innocency of the Bishops.

Certainly you would thinke that they were wolues , and that these were Lambes, and that he had a heart of iron, who would not assay to deliuer these men that were thus in danger, out of their most cruell iawes if so be he could possibly. And yet the beast retained his old nature in the middst of this his distressed estate; and he spake bigge & terribly like a Dragon. Vers. 17. *And that no man can buye.* The force of this Marke is, that it may bee a token of liberty geuen to commerce and bargaine among men. What a great dammage then must they needs endure that want this badge , when they can neither conuerse nor haue any dealing with any man? That soueraigne obedience is due to the Pope, that it is not lavvfull for any man to commune vvith him, to vvhome the Pope is an enemy for some deeds of his, neither can he be in the Church, that forsaketh his Chaire.* For confirming of which matter the counterfeite Epistle of Clement is alledged, saying *vve must not stay in this case till one be excomunicate , but if this Clement be an enemye to any man for any of his ill deeds , doe not you stay till he saye vnto you, &c.* Doubtleffe his becks are to be obserued, that so we may depart away from those with whome we may coniecture that the Pope may be angry , and that without, any warning geuen thereof. What plainer prohibition can there be made to keepe men from bargaining with any of them who want the Marke? ## The 14. Chapter.

### The logicall Resoluing of it.

*We haue heard in the two former Chapters What things haue bene acted by the enemies of the Church we shal heare in this Chapter following as touching the valourous works of the Cittizens thereof, for here we are taught, What was the estate of the true Church from the time, that the battell was fought in heauen, and the Dragon was cast out uppon the earth, Chapt. 12. 9. as also wher the Beast began to arise out of the Sea, Chapt. 13. 1. Nowe this estate is double, the first while she kept with in her Tent, Where we haue the happy condition of the Saints declared unto us, by their Captaine that stands uppon Mount Sion, as also by their Souldiers, Who are both a definite and a choire company, vers. 1. After that by the ioye of the Spirit that is expressed in their newe songe vers. 2. 3. And lastly by their holines wherewith they are indued, vers. 4. 5. And this army of Saints is that seed of the woman scattered here & there in the World, with whome the Dragon made Warre, after that the woman vanished out of his sight by flying into the desart, Chap-ter 12. 13. *Vers. 1. Then I looked, and loe a Lambe stoode.* This Prophecy beginneth from the time that the Dragon being cast out vppon the earth, chased the woman into the wildernes, chapt. 12. 13. &c. Chapter.** The eleuenth Chapter did touch more shortly the state of the former times, dispatching as it were in one word the whole remainder of the Prophecy in the sufferings of the two witnesses, as

<margin>Vers. 3.</margin> *And they sung as it vvere a nevve song.* The newe song is the magnifying of God the Father by Iesus Christ, by whome the elect are made the sonnes of God. It is called *nevve*, not because men began nowe first of all to be, and to be counted the Sonnes of God, but because this grace is communicated to farre more in the true Christian Church, then euer before the comming of the Redemer, and so it is confirmed with more plentifull arguments. For which cause we are said, to haue receaued the Spirit of adoption, Rom. 8. 15. Not because we were the first that receaued it, but because we receaued it more fully then they that were before vs. Or els, there is a double song that hath bene from the beginning of the world, an old one, and a newe one. That magnified God, because we were made his Sonnes by creation as Adam was before the fall, this extolleth God with praises, because we are made his Sonnes by redemption.

*Vers. 7. Feare God,&c.* This was a most fit matter for this Angell to speake of at this time, when all reuerence towards God lay quite extinguished, saue onely such as the precepts of men did teach, according to that of the Prophet Esay. *This people dravveth neere vnto me vvith their mouth, and they honour me vvith their lippes,but their heart is remoued farre from me,and their feare tovvardes me, is that vvhich they haue bene taught by the precept of men,Chapt.29.13.* So when wicklefe came abroad into the world, men were commonly afraid and that with a bodily feare to transgresse mens commaundements, but the commaundements of God were securely contemned. If a man had bene absent from the Sacrilegious Masse if he had not murmured out certaine prayers vppon his beades or had not abstained from forbidden meates,on set dayes, or had not obserued such other foolish and wicked rites as these, he thought himselfe to be guilty of a greiuous finne; but if the same man had bene ignorant of God, and his Holy truth, if he should haue no confidence in Gods mercy by Christ, but should fly to Saints, as oft as any perplexity vrged him, if he should defile Gods Holy name in euery word almost that he spake and should violate all other dueties of true piety and honesty, he felt no sting at al in his Conscience. This Holy Angell therefore did not without good cause begin his preaching with these words, feare God, that so he might call men back from their false feare, to the sense and feare of the true God; Consider and waigh well the doctrine of Iohn wicklefe that was condemned in the Councell of Constance, and you shall see howe greatly he laboured to pull downe mens fooliries, and to teach men to followe after true godlines in good earnest.

They preached at the yeare 1404. and they shoke the foundation of the Romish Tyranny a litle more mightily then <term>wicklefe</term>, which the Holy Ghost intimated that it should so come to passe, making euery ensuing Angell to be a more fierce enemy then the former. <meta>catchword: The</meta>

*If any man shal adore the Beast.* He dealeth earnestly, & cutteth to the quicke. The summe of his speachs cōtained in this hypothetical propositiō. *If any man shal adore the Beast, he shal purchase to himselfe euerlasting destruction.* The former part of which is set downe in this verse, the latter part is declared in the two verses following. As touching adoratiō it is illustrated first by the double subiect thereof, the beast, & the imag. Simple & rude people adore the Beast, as who are carried away with the present lustre & glistering shewe of the things which they see. But the learned & witty sort of men adore the Image, as who looke farder of, & who doe therfore worship the present Beast because of that venerable antiquitye of succession, and that auncient Image, which was newly flourished ouer againe in this that is present. Both these shalbe alike in dāger of destruction unlesse they repent. Aboue ch. 13. 15. The adoring of the Image was common to all, but seing it is here distinguished in some respect from the adoring of the Beast, this seemeth to be that differēt respect which we haue made, that the learned sort worshipped the one, the unlearned the other. After that the mānner of adoring is opened, that it is done two wayes, by taking the marke either in their fore head, or in their hāde: The cōmōn sort of mē are signed in the foreheade, as who acknowledge their obedience by a bare professiō; The Princes, Peeres, the whole rout of the Churchmen, & the rest of that stampe, are signed in their hande, because they are to defend the Beast to the uttermost of their power. Why thē is the order changed, & why is the first, place geuen to the marke in the foreheade, which was set in the second before, as the which belonged to men of lesse estimation, chap. 13. 16. The reason is, that the condemnatiō of these champions that fight in the defence of the Beast, might be thereby declared to be greater, as if he should saye, euery one shalbe tormēted in fire & Brimstone, that shal take the Beasts marke, yea euen in the forehead, much shal he that shal take it in his hāde. But why is there no mention of the nōber of the name? Because this marke is proper to the Grecians, who should adore the Beast by their cōsent with the Latin Church; chap. 13. 17. Nowe this Angel was appointed for the westerne people, specially seing greece was before this time already ouerthrowne with the Turkish Tyranny. But obserue that this adoration is performed, not by falling down upō the earth; but by acknowledging his dominiō, & supremacy after which mānner they may adore the Beast, who neuer sawe him. *Vf. 10. He shal also drinke of the vvine of Gods vvrath.*

The cõsequent of the propoſition deſcribeth the deſtruction of thoſe
who doe adore the Beaſt, both by the kinde of the puniſhment in this
verſe, as alſo by the eternity thereof in the next. That is firſt propoun-
ded allegorically in the beginning of the verſe, thẽ it is explaned with
proper words in the other part of it. To drinke of the vvine of vvrath, ſee-
eth to be a Metaphore, made by a figure wherein there is a referẽce in
another ſenſe to that wine of fornicatiõ of which vſ. 8. Whereby was
ſignified the Idolatry with which men are no leſſe delighted, then with
the dainteſt wine. As mẽ therfore doe greatly rejoice in their ſinnes, ſo
ſhall God no leſſe rejoice in puniſhing them ; for he wil mingle vnto
them a Cup of the wine of his wrath; according to that, Deut. 28. 63.
Or the ſenſe of it may be takẽ from thẽ who put wicked men to death
with poiſoned Cuppes, as the athenians & other people did of old &
as the Turks vſe to doe at this daye. But what is this mingled wine?
The words in the Greeke ſeeme to be contrary to thẽſelues the word
put for wine ſignifying that which neuer was mingled, which in Latin
is called *merum*. To cleare this, a thing is ſaid to be mingled, which is
poured into him that is to drinke, though it be not alayed with water,
but that expoſitiõ ſeemeth to me to be more probable, which wil haue
diuerſe kinds of wines to be mingled together, which confuſion doth
much ſooner beget drunkennes, & doth worke greater diſturbance to
the whole Bodye; water mingled with vnmixt wine breakes the force
of ſuch wine; which tempering of water with wine cã not ſo wel ſerue
to ſignifie the exceeding ſeuerenes of the puniſhment which thing is
ſpoken of here, ſo then mingled wine ſignifieth iudgement vvithout
mercy to thẽ that repent not. *He ſhalbe tormented vvith fire & brimſtone.*
Theſe words doe note out the puniſhmẽt more properly, which is like
to be ſuch as that was of Sodomes longe agoe; A feareful ſpectacle
whereof doth ſtil abid in the world, in that aſhy earth, & ſtinking lake
which is called of it, *Aſphalites*; wherein we haue a viſible resemblãce
of the euerlaſting puniſhmẽt. This puniſhment ſhalbe inflicted in the
presence of the Angells, and the Lambe, that the torment may be the
more greiuous, by howe much more it is knowne to their enemies.

*Verſ. 11. And the ſmoke of their torment.* These words doe teach the
eternity of the puniſhmẽt; for the ſmoke of their torment ſhalbe euer-
laſting. Now ſmoke is here put for fire, whereof it is a token. It is here
vſed, to teach the worſhippers of the Beaſt, not onely that they are to
be tormẽted eternally, but alſo that their tormẽt ſhal neuer be hidden
from the Saints, who ſhal alwayes ſee the ſmoke thereof at leaſt.

In that he saith, that they shal neuer haue rest day nor night, thereby

aswell as euerlasting. The former part of the proposition is repeated 
againe in the ende to put more vehemency into the Speach; Where he 
onely mentioneth the Character of the Beasts name, because this en-
signe is commō not to them onely which are branded in the forehead, 
but to them also who are branded in the hand. Consider therefore 
diligently, ô ye Popish people, vvhat an horrible punishment vvaiteth for you, 
vnlesse you vvil make a revolt from the Pope of Rome. These stinging words 
of Martin Luther, came not from a man, and from a prouoked aduer-
sary, but they are such as the Holy Ghost put into his minde & mouth. 
You see he was a man sent out from the Tents of Christ himselfe. And 
thinke not that these Threatnings are dead and gone together with 
him, but rather let them be continually sounding in and about your 
eares, For they liue at this daye, and shall keepe their efficacy no lesse 
for euer then whē they were first spoken. By which they doe denounce 
euerlasting damnation to euery one, that doth still persist to worship 
that Romish Idoll. Yea so much the more greiuous punishment is 
prepared for Papists that liue obstinately in their Papish impiety at 
this daye, by howe much more manifestly the Abhominacions of that 
Sea haue bene discouered; Let euery one hearken that hath a care of 
eternall Saluation.
*Vers. 12. Here is the patience of Saints.* These are words of Con-
solation, which the Angel addeth to shutt vp his speach therewith as 
with a Concluding Epilogue; And yet they may be the words of Iohn,

It is a defectiue speach, for here is a triall of the patience of Saints,

nowe it should be manifest, who be indued with true patience, & who

ther, that they must needs be truly Godly, who could beare of his 
assault valiantly, and yet would not forsake their profession. Of which 
fury Germany is a witnesse, which by meanes hereof did wholy ouer-
flowe with the slaughters and bloud of the Godly; Chapter 11. 7.

And so it came to passe in the restored Church after the yeare 1545. that is after the Parliament at Aquine held against the men of Merindoll,and Cabriers,and after many other calamities endured in France,when as also there was a rumour noised abroad touching the close practises of Cæsar & the Pope against Religion, thē did many of the brethrē being terrified with the present dangers as also with those which were looked for , begin to prouide for their goods & life by dissembling their Religion. What are these things which are once sett downe to bee referred in common to this Angel also? Or rather, is it so that this Angel commeth not neere that degree of dignity which the former had but is rather one of a litle more inferiour ranke? So indeed he seemeth to be; seing it is not safe to ad any thing to those words that are inspired from God but vppon a most certaine reason. This Angell therfore is Thomas Cromwell, who liued in the dayes of Henry the 8. that most mighty King, and was a man of great renowme and place in our Kingdome, being the Earle of Essex, & Lord keeper of the priuy Seale; who came out of the Temple which is in heauen, being a sincere fauourer of pure Religion; He had a Sickle in his hand, being made the Kings deputy in all Ecclesiasticall matters, and it was a sharpe one, as which he set stoutly and deliueratly to his worke, and yet he had no crowne or Diademe to grace his head with all, as being a minister rather to put another mans power in vre, then any that wrought by his owne power and authority.

Vers. 18. And another Angell came out of the Altar. The second Angell is described by a triple property, that he commeth out from the Altar, that he hath povver ouer the fire, and that he exhorts his fellowe to cut downe the vine. As touching the first, he is said significantly to come out from the Altar. For so the Greeke expresseth it, not as Beza turneth it, *from the Altar*, which doth not sufficiently expresse the force of the speach. A man is said to come from a thing, ouer against which he was; but he is said to come from out of a thing within the compasse whereof he was shutt vp. But howe can he come forth from out of the Altar? This may be vnderstood out of the 9. vers. of the 6. Chapter. Where it is said: *I savve the soules of them vvho vvere slaine, lying vnder the Altar.* This kinde of speaking then teacheth vs, that this Angell is an Holy Martyr, such as they are who are vnder the Altar. Nowe they that lie vnder the Altar, must needs come forth out of the Altar, when they goe any whether. But seing there are many kinds of Martyrdome, for some are consumed vvith the svvord, some vvith the Haltar, some vvith vvild Beasts, some vvith fire, to the entent that it might be vnderstood what kinde of Martyr this is, it is added in the next words, *that he hath povver ouer the fire, that is, that he induring and ouercomming the torment of fire, vvhich is to haue povver ouer the fire*, did thus giue testimony to the Truth, Nowe in that in the third place,

## The 15. Chapter.

### The logicall Resoluing of it into the parts of it.

*Hetherto haue we heard of the things past which the seauenth Trompet recordeth vnto vs, so farre forth, as they should be more fully knowne vnder it, then euer before. The things to come followe, the common Type whereof is in this Chapter, and then the speciall execution of them is in the rest of the Booke. This Type doth first of all declare summarily, that there are seauen ministring Angells prepared to take vengeance of the Churches enemies, vers. 1. Also what should be the state of the Church conuersing among the Gentiles, till the Angell haue discharged their office. Whereof we haue a portraiture propounded both in the glassy Sea, mingled with fire, as also in the Conquerours, and Harpers, vers. 2. And in their Song, the Authors whereof are Moses and the Lambe, the argument is the praise of the omnipotency and Iustice of God, v. 3. And of his gathering together of all the Elect, vers. 4. After that he doth in speciall giue vs a more description, partly of the Angells, who are addressed to their office, as by the place whence they come forth, vers. 5. 6. By their apparell, vers. 6. And their instruments, namely Viols with which they are armed, vers. 7. Partly of the whole Church, both in respect of the Elect nations, to which the glory & presence of God shineth out, as also in respect of the rest, to whome it remaineth shut vp untill the determinate time.*

# THE EXPOSITION.

*After that I sawe another signe.* These are vsed in the Roome of a Transition, whereby this Prophecy wich followeth, is distinguished from that which hath bene right nowe explaned, in the three former Chapters. And nowe is the third and last Period remaining, diuided from the former by the kinde of the euents, which haue therefore a newe instrument of the Viols yet so as it agreeth with and is ioined to the former, as it is a part of the seauen-th Trumpet, as it may easily appeare by those things which haue bene said before. For the tabernacle in heauen is not opened before the seauenth Trumpett, Chapter 11. 15. 19. But the instruments of this worke, who haue the busines committed to them of pouring out the Viols, come out of the Temple that is opened in heauen, as it is beneath, vers. 5. 6. of this Chapter.

Besides the Angell foretold that the ende should come, when the seauenth Trumpet blewe; Chapter 10. 7. Nowe these seauen Viols bring the ende with them the instrumẽts whereof are said in this verse to haue the seauen last plagues, & therfore they are necessarily proper to the same Trumpet. But if the first Viol should answer to the first Trumpet, and so the rest that followe in order, so that each of them should belong to the same time to which the Trumpet belongs that is ioined with it, there were no reason why they should be called the last plagues. But it can not be so by any meanes, specially seeing the first Viol bringeth an euil uppon the men, who had the marke of the Beast set uppon them, Chapter 16. 1. 2. Which we haue seene to be the inuention not of the first Beast, but of the second, Chapter 13. 16. The birth day whereof fell into the fifth Trumpet. And yet by this reason the Character must needs goe before al the Trumpets, the first whereof should not so much set the marke vpon men, as it should vexe them who were marked with it before. And to the time til the two Prophets shal rise againe from the dead, chap. 11. 11. Which we haue shewed to haue hapned about the ende of the sixth Trumpett. I but (will some say) there is great likenes betwene the Trumpetts and the Viols. There is indeed (I answere) but such as tends onely to this, that we may knowe that men are punnished by the same degrees and footesteps by which they haue sinned. But they differ both in the time and in the kinde of the Punishment, seing the Violls are punishments onely, but the Trumpetts are Sinnes also. It is manifest therefore that this whole space of time from Iohn to the comming of the Lord is diuided into three Periods of time, & that each of those Periods is againe diuided into seauen members so as the first member of that Period which followeth, beginneth vnder the last member of the former, that is so, that as the seauen Trumpets haue their originall from out of the last Seale, so the Seauen Violes haue their offspring out of the last Trumpet. Which manner of distributing the time makes this prophecy to be easye vnto vs, and to goe currantly on to our vnderstanding, which otherwise would not be able to be vnfolded.

*In heauen.* That is, in the purer Church ; For as the Lord was wont of old to roare out of *Sion, and to putt forth his voice out of Ierusalem, Amos 1. 2.* So the euil with which al the Churches enemies should nowe vtterly perish, shal come forth out of his holy Church, in which he shal shewe himselfe a reuenger, when he shall punnish all the reprobats. Nowe this Signe is great and admirable, because of the change of things which would astonish a man with wondring at it, to see the Beast and the dragon ouercome and destroyed, and euerlasting Felicity gotten for the Church, as we shall see in the things that are to be opened seuerally.

*Seauen Angells.* According to the custome that was vsed in the former Periodes. Nowe these Angells are men that be citizens of the pure Church, as it appeareth by the place whence they come forth, & by their apparel, of which we shall see in their owne place. Theodore Beza expresseth it by a forcible kinde of speach, those Angells, but neither the Article is in the Greeke, neither were these either seene before, or once spoken of before that the Temple was opened.

Tabernacle should not loose the lawe, which lost the Arke, wherein
it was laid vp; specially seing the Arke was neuer placed in that Ta-
bernacle afterwards, 1. Sam. 4. 21. This therfore is no sufficient cause.
But these two seeme to be coupled together; that it might be shewed,
that this Temple is a pilgrime as yet in the world, and that the Angels
that come out from thence, are denizens of the Church militant. But
(wil some say) if they come out of the Temple, it may seeme that the
Church lieth hidd still in her lurking holes; by which argument wee
found out the time of the former prophecy Chapt. 14. 15. Those An-
gells indeed of the former Chapter came forth out of the Temple,
when it was shut vp, these here come out of the Temple when it is
opened. The Church doth indeed dwell alwayes in the Temple, for-
what other more commodious harbour can it haue? But this Temple
is not alwayes in one state. Sometimes it is shutt vp in the time of
mourning, and desolatenes, such as the condition thereof was, when
those reapers and vinecutters came out of it Sometimes it is open and
manifest, when a more joyfull and pleasant day shineth vppon it; And
thus happily it fared with it, after the victory was atcheiued against
the Beast, when those seauen Augels came out from thence.

Vers. 6. *Being clothed vvith pure and bright linnen.* The clothing
of the Angells doth more betoken joyfullnes, then that of the two
witnesses who were clothed in sack cloth, Chapter 11. 3. For there is
another manner of condition and shewe of these times. And yet these
garments be common to all the Elect, though they be fitter for some
times rather then other. For they be the garments of the Sonnes of
Aaron, Exod. 28. 42. But all the elect are made Priests. All the faithfull
dwell nowe in the Temple, the entrance into which was open to the
Leuits onely of old. The purity therfore of the Angells is signified by
this garment, which they obtaine by the onely imputation of Christs
righteousnes. Nowe least any man should despise this imputation as a
vile thing, and too base for a man to appeare clothed with in Gods
sight, as the blasphemous Popish Teachers persuade their people at
this daye, he saith that these garments are pure and bright; as wherein

Not because he had any such need, but onely to teach vs and to represent the Church of that time, which was very much adorned in this regard.

*Vers. 7. And one of the foure Beasts.* It doth not appeare by name which of these it is; especially seing one of the Beasts may be either words of order or of distribution. But it matters not which of them it is. That agreeth to them all, which belongs to each of them, all the foure virtues of whome being ioyned together set such an image before vs, as euery faithfull minister ought to resemble, as we haue obserued on the 7. verse of the 4. Chapter. Here the Holy Ghost purposeth to make vs knowe, that these seauen Angells drawe forth that out of the precepts and instructions of some Minister of the Holy Gospell, which they doe afterwards conuert and apply, to worke the destruction of the enemies of the Church, with all. Yet this minister is not to be thought to be any one singular man, but many who consent in one faith and doctrine; as Phillipp Melancthon, Martin Bucer, Peter Martyr, Henry Bullinger, Iohn Caluin, & the rest of the seruants of God, who flourished about that time.

Out of whose godly & learned writings, so many men haue drawne exellent and golden vnderstanding of holy things, so as they haue bene made able thereby, to encounter with Antichrist, and to dispatch thoroughly the remainder of that warre, which they began with so happy successe.

## The 16. Chapter.

### The logicall Resoluing of it.

*Hetherto we haue heard of the common Type the speciall execution doth nowe followe , Which is distinguished by the seuerall members thereof in this Chapter, and is handled more at large and by a continued order in the rest of the Chapters. That containeth both a commandement, vers.1. As also the parts thereof, both those which be common, the effecting of the Worke and the euent , and the particular ones also, the seauen distinct viols, that signifie, according to the manner of the former Periodes, those seauen notable discomfitures wherewith the enemies of Christ are to be destroyed, the first whereof is poured out uppon the Earth, vers. 2. The second uppon the Sea, vers. 3. The third uppon the Riuers, vers. 4. Whose secondary euent is a double testimony, the first of the Angell of the Waters, vers. 5. and 6. The second of the Angell comming out of the Altar, vers. 7. The fourth uppon the sunne, vers. 8. 9. The fifth uppon the Throne of the Beast, vers. 10. 11. The sixth uppon Euphrates, whereof there is also a double euent, the former, the drying up of the waters, vers. 12. The second, a preparation to a Warre, of which there are three principall Authors, and as many instruments, the froggs, vers. 13. 14. Then also a warning giuen to the Elect, vers. 15.*

## THE EXPOSITION.

Verf. 1. *Then I heard a great voice out of the Temple.* In this commanding voice, we are to consider from whence it came, to whome, and to what ende. It came out of the Temple, as it came also, Chapter 9. 13. *Out of the foure hornes of the Altar*, & sometimes it commeth out of the Throne, as afterwards, Chapter 19. 5. The difference is this, that the voice commeth out of the Throne when it proceeds as it were immediatly from God, out of the Temple, when any thing is obtaine by the prayers of the Saints; to whome the office of commanding is here geuen, that we might knowe, what force faithfull prayers haue, which should be as it were the first mouers, and the principall Agents in the matter that was to be done, they doe so boldly command the busines to be set vppon. And indeed it could not be, but that such men as God had inlightened with so great knowledge of his truth, should thus striue with all their might by prayers to God, that he would with all possible speed destroy Antichrist. Aretas reades not the words *out of the Temple*, but all our Coppies, as also the vulgar doe with one consent read it thus, and it is wont to be shewed in other places, whence the voice commeth. They to whome the voice commeth are the seauen Angels; But what need is there of this will some saye, seeing they were long since appointed, and furnished vnto this office with all necessaries; in the former Chapter? They stoode indeede at the barriers and lifts, prepared, and looking for their signe to make onsett; But there must come a speciall commandement vnto the generall, if a man desire to haue an authenticall commission to warrant

Neither is the earth that soile onely which we tread vppon,but first of
all men,and then not all men in generall, but the branded rogues of
Antichrist onely , as the euent doth shewe straightwaye , whereby it
came to passe that a botch was inflicted vppon the men that haue the
Marke of the Beast. In which sense the word Earth was oftentimes
vsed before, which we therfore doe retaine constātly throughout our
Exposition , that so we might see the better from thence howe the
whole prophesye agreeth with it selfe. The euent bringeth an euill and
noisome vlcer with it, that is , such an one as the Phisicions call a

virulency in it,that it will neuer suffer a scarre to be drawne together.

so called, the procuring causes whereof we see to be Metaphoricall.
And such euents as this are to be vnderstood in the rest of the Vials
also ; so that for one to take them as spoken properly, as the Iesuite
doth,is not so much to explane,as to cōfound all things,so as the light
of the Truth should be ouerwhelmed for euer.
